The excerpt is a structured table of contents for Chapter 2 (“Theoretical Principles”) of the AQB Design of Cross Sections manual (Service Pack 2025-4, Build 146). It lists eight main topics—each with nested subtopics—and their corresponding starting pages. Below is a hierarchical breakdown suitable for ingestion into a RAG‐style knowledge graph or vector store:

1. Chapter Title  
   • “2 Theoretical Principles” (page 2-1)

2. Section 2.1 External Forces and Cross Section (2-1)  
   2.1.1 Coordinate System (2-1)  
   2.1.2 External Forces and Moments (2-1)

3. Section 2.2 Stress Analysis by the Theory of Elasticity (2-3)

7. Section 2.6 Determination of the Required Reinforcement (2-17)

   2.6.2 Minimum Reinforcement of the Statically Required Cross Section (2-19)

   (Additional subsections—such as “Stress Range of the Reinforcement,” “Crack Width Check,” etc.—follow in the full manual.)

Key observations for RAG indexing:  
– Each heading is tagged with a numeric code (e.g. “2.7.2”) and a title describing the calculation or check.  
– Page references follow a “chapter-page” format (e.g. “2-23” means Chapter 2, page 23).  
– Topics progress from fundamental elasticity theory to advanced checks (non-linear, fatigue, code‐specific rules).  
– Uniform structure (major heading → decimal subheadings) makes automated parsing straightforward.  
– This table serves as the blueprint for linking input commands (records) in Chapter 3 to the theoretical principles detailed here.

The excerpted table is a fragment of Chapter 3 (“Description of Input”) from the AQB “Design of Cross Sections” manual (Service Pack 2025-4, Build 146) by SOFiSTiK AG.  It presents a structured listing of the input records (i.e. keywords and their associated sub-sections) that the user must specify in order to drive the automated cross‐section design routines.  Each record is shown with its short name, a brief title, and the page number where its full syntax and options are described.

Structure of the Table  
• Two-column layout:  
  – Left column: record identifier (numeric code + keyword), plus the title of that record or sub-record.  
  – Right column: starting page in the manual (all pages are in the 3-xx range, since this is Chapter 3).

Main Records (3.11 – 3.19) and Sub-Records  
3.11  S – Internal Forces and Moments  
    Defines which internal force envelopes and moment diagrams are to be transferred from the structural analysis. (p. 3-51)  

3.12  COMB – Definition of Load Case Combinations  
    Sets up factored or unfactored combinations of load cases for ultimate or serviceability checks. (p. 3-53)  

3.13  EIGE – Determination of Internal Stresses (AQBS only)  
    Calculates sectional stresses resulting from prestress tendon losses and other effects specific to AQBS tendons. (p. 3-59)  

3.14  STRE – Linear Stresses and Plastic Forces  
    Computes linear elastic stresses and plastic internal forces in concrete and reinforcement. (p. 3-62)  
    • 3.14.1  Shear Design – STRE UL  
        Ultimate‐limit shear checks according to the selected code. (p. 3-67)  
    • 3.14.2  Minimum Reinforcement – STRE RL  
        Serviceability reinforcement minimums and crack control requirements. (p. 3-68)  

3.15  REIN – Specification for Determining Reinforcement  
    User-defined reinforcement layouts or automated sizing rules. (p. 3-70)  

3.16  DESI – Reinforced Concrete Design, Bending, Axial Force  
    Performs combined bending-axial checks, design of longitudinal reinforcement. (p. 3-74)  

3.17  NSTR – Non-linear Stress and Strain  
    Iterative non-linear analysis of section behavior under large strains. (p. 3-79)  
    • 3.17.1  Design for Structural Steelwork (DIN 18800, EN 1993)  
    • 3.17.2  Design for Reinforced Concrete  
    • 3.17.3  Iteration Methods  
    • 3.17.4  Fatigue / Stress Range  
    (All p. 3-81 through 3-84)  

3.18  CAPA – Sectional Capacity Evaluation  
    Constructs capacity envelopes and interaction diagrams. (p. 3-86)  
    • 3.18.1  STR single values  
    • 3.18.2  MC moment-curvature relations  
    • 3.18.3  NM interaction of normal force with moments  
    (All p. 3-87)  

3.19  ECHO – Control of the Extent of Output  
    Toggles what results are sent to listing files or screen. (p. 3-88)  
    • 3.19.1  Output masks  
    (p. 3-92)  

Bibliography (p. 3-93)  
    Lists referenced design codes, standards and normative texts.

How It’s Used in RAG/VECTOR INDEXING  
• Each record name (e.g. “STRE”, “REIN”, “NSTR”) becomes a retrievable key.  
• Sub-sections (3.14.1, 3.17.3, etc.) allow fine‐grained retrieval for specific design checks.  
• Page references support pinpoint navigation.  
• The two-column structure simplifies parsing into “keyword ↔ description ↔ page” triples.

AQB is used for stress analysis and design of cross sections created with AQUA. The enhanced version AQBS allows the consideration of the special features of prestressed concrete and composite structures (prestressing tendons, imposed secondary stresses, creep and shrink- age). This manual is valid for both versions. The optional features which are operative only in AQBS are identified.
 The forces and the prestressing tendons can be defined directly or be imported from the database for beam, truss or cable elements. A whole series of design tasks can be carried out with the selected forces. These are:
 1. Creep and shrinkage analysis (AQBS only)
 AQBS can examine creep and shrinkage in up to 99 creep intervals. Different creep characteristics can be defined for each material, so that subsequently added cross section parts can be considered too. The internal forces due to creep are stored in the database and they are taken into account in later creep stages or stress determinations.
 2. Determination of the maximum stresses in the cross section according to the theory of elasticity.
 AQB can perform stress checks of any thick-walled or thin-walled cross section, including shear stresses and warping torsion in accordance with a great variety of codes for steel, timber, or prestressed concrete. Different stress limits can be considered for different materials in the same cross section.
 3. Determination of the required reinforcement or internal safety factor for unreinforced, re-
 inforced or prestressed concrete cross sections. AQB can design reinforced or prestressed concrete cross sections with an optimised dis- tribution of the reinforcement for axial force and biaxial bending. International codes can be taken into consideration. A shear design can be carried out following the bending design.
 4. Determination of the maximum stresses and actual stiffnesses for the defined material law.
 AQBS determines stress and strain distributions based on the material behaviour. This makes it possible to perform controls on crack width limits, reinforcement stress range, foundation pressures, and elastic-plastic design analysis. Also effective stiffnesses can be determined with that for a non-linear static calculation (plastic-plastic).

Determination of the maximum stresses and actual stiffnesses for the defined material law.. AQBS determines stress and strain distributions based on the material behaviour. This makes it possible to perform controls on crack width limits, reinforcement stress range, foundation pressures, and elastic-plastic design analysis. Also effective stiffnesses can be determined with that for a non-linear static calculation (plastic-plastic)..
 Computed stresses, reinforcement and stiffnesses can be stored back in the database, and they can both be graphically represented or be addressed by other modules.
 The functions for design and stiffness determination are also integrated into STAR2 in a sim- plified form. For this reason, tasks (3) and (4) can be also carried out directly with STAR2. This makes it possible to do a static design taking the material behaviour into account. When this procedure is used, however, only one design mode is possible for the entire structure. If columns and girders are to be designed with different parameters, one can make an iteration using the modules STAR2 and AQB by means of the command procedure PS (see general manual SOFiSTiK: ’FEA / STRUCTURAL Installation and Basics’).
 The small version of AQB is included in the general SOFiSTiK-Licence. It allows for a reduced
 number of functions only. These are:
 - Generally only uniaxial bending but for circular sections along the main bending direction (piles)
 - Stress checks for all cross sections
 - Elastic-plastic analyses (STRE E) for rectangular, circular sections and structural steel shapes
 - Uniaxial reinforced concrete design for rectangles and T-beams and for circular/annular sections.

The illustration shows an isometric view of a straight prismatic beam segment with a rectangular cross-section, annotated to define its local coordinate system, characteristic points, and applied internal forces and moments. The beam’s longitudinal direction is the x-axis (not explicitly drawn), which runs from the leftmost black circular marker to the rightmost black circular marker. These two filled-in circles at the beam ends indicate the “positive boundary” of the section—the face toward which the observer is looking—consistent with the DIN 1080 convention described in AQUA’s manual.

Beam Geometry and Reference Lines  
- The beam is drawn as a simple rectangular prism.  
- A dashed centerline runs along the top face, aligned with the x-axis, indicating the neutral axis of the section.  
- On the side face, another dashed line marks the projection of the beam axis onto that face.  

Characteristic Points in the Cross Section  
- A red dot located slightly inside the front cross-section face is labeled “S.” This marks the shear center of the section.  
- A second red dot on the near side face (on the left-hand long side) corresponds to the elastic center (or centroid) projection, with local coordinates y′s and z′s referenced to the beam’s cross-section.  

Local Coordinate Axes  
- The local y′ₛ-axis (shear-center y-axis) is shown as an arrow pointing diagonally outward to the left. It lies in the plane of the cross section, tangent to the side face.  
- The local z′ₛ-axis (shear-center z-axis) is shown as a downward arrow, also originating at the elastic center projection on the side face.  
- A global Z-axis is drawn vertically downward at the projected centroid of the section, signaling the conventional positive z-direction for bending.  

Applied Internal Forces and Moments (at the positive boundary)  
- N is depicted as a horizontal arrow pointing out of the cross section toward the viewer’s right, denoting the normal (axial) force.  
- Mᵧ is drawn as a diagonal arrow roughly in the plane of the screen, emanating from the section face and denoting the bending moment about the local y-axis.  
- M_z is a vertical arrow pointing downward from the section face, indicating the bending moment about the local z-axis.  

Additional Notations  
- The front cross-section face is hatched (45° lines) to indicate the cut surface.  
- Short leader lines and arrowheads connect each force/moment symbol (N, Mᵧ, M_z) to the exact point of application on the section.  
- Figure caption (“Figure 2.1: Coordinate system”) appears centered beneath the drawing.  

Overall, the graphic concisely communicates how, in the local y–z coordinate system of the beam (x being the longitudinal direction), one distinguishes three critical points—beam axis, elastic center, and shear center—and how the internal forces (axial load N) and bending moments (Mᵧ, M_z) are oriented. This layout follows DIN 1080 conventions, with the observer looking toward the positive end face of the beam.

Cross sections are described according to DIN 1080 in the local y-z coordinate system of the beam. Here the x-axis points in the longitudinal direction of the bar. The observer is looking at the positive boundary of the section (from the end of the bar to the beginning). For the description of the forces and moments and the support conditions, three points along the beam have to be distinguished within a section: Beam axis, elastic center and shear center. For more details see the manual for AQUA.

The external forces and moments are longitudinal or transverse forces referring to the elastic centre and the shear centre of the construction stage section used in the analysis.
 The elastic center is the point where an acting normal force will create only a centric strain and thus no moments.
 In special cases, one can select any other point in the cross section.
 For design purposes, the internal forces and moments are normally modified as follows.
 The longitudinal and transverse forces are converted to axial and shear forces. The torsional moment is dismantled in a Saint-Venant part and a secondary part from warping torsion.
 Within the defined support boundary, moments are smoothed under the assumption of a uni- form surface pressure (parabolic). The smoothing is done for each side of the beam, and the shear force at the end of the beam is set to zero.
 If the cross section is located within a haunch, the shear stress distribution will change consid- erably, however the practical design rules will account for that by changing the shear force in accordance with the following formula:

The computed stresses can be examined for limit values; a value exceeding the limit is iden- tified in the printout with * after the stress. All standard values (e.g. in steel-, timber- or prestressed concrete construction) can be invoked as limit stresses. The limit stresses are checked separately for each material.
 Depending on the declaration of the allowable stress type, additional specialities of the partic- ular codes can be taken into consideration too:
 • Check of the slenderness ratio c/t for steel plates according to the section classes 2 or 3 of EN 1993 or other design codes
 • Reduction of the axial force components by EN 1995 / DIN 1052 The combined check for axial force and bending moment is carried out by a bending stress check where the axial force components are reduced, which is equivalent with a multipli- cation of the utilisation equation in the design code with the allowable bending stress. In analog mode the check of the torsion occurs at the edge with correspondingly raised shear stresses from shear force.
 • Differentiation between compression zone and pre-compressed tension zone.
 • Reduction of the prestress components in the pre-compressed compression zone in accor- dance with DIN 4227 Sec. 15.3.
 • Shear design under ultimate loads in accordance with Zone a, DIN 4227
 • Check for the decompression limit state (e.g. according to EC 2, DIN 1045-1)
 Here it is verified that the concrete cross section has only compressive stress at the edge of the precompressed tension zone due to prestress for the determinant action combination.
 The decompression check is done with the input SPAN E STYP VH. The input STYP VH sets here the permissible tensile stressesin the concrete to 0.00. The check is filled, if the resistance factors are kept (≤ 1.0) → table: Maximum Degree of Utilization.

The decompression check is done with the input SPAN E STYP VH. The input STYP VH sets here the permissible tensile stressesin the concrete to 0.00. The check is filled, if the resistance factors are kept (≤ 1.0) → table: Maximum Degree of Utilization..
 AQB determines the check edge from the centre of gravity of all tendons. In the case of upper and lower tendons the check has to be done graphically.
 The stresses which are determinant for the decompression check can be checked graphi- cally with the WING input BEAM TYPE DECO or in WinGRAF with Design → Stress of the material → Decompression stress.

The figure is a two-dimensional chart entitled “Figure 2.2: Section classes.” Along the horizontal axis it identifies the five section classes defined in the design codes: (1), (2), (3) and (4a). The vertical axis is simply labeled “level,” which in context represents a nondimensional utilization or stress-to-limit ratio.  

A smoothly rising green curve is plotted from left to right.  Starting near zero at class (1), the curve rises gently through class (2), passes the critical value of 1.0 between class (2) and class (3), and continues upward into the region of class (4a).  A horizontal dotted green line is drawn at level = 1.0, marking the threshold between acceptable (below 1.0) and overstressed (above 1.0) conditions under linear-elastic checks.  

Two dashed arrows, one red and one red-dashed, illustrate two different “STRE” design approaches:

 • STRE C (red dashed arrow with a vertical drop) –  This arrow originates on the green curve at class (3) slightly above the 1.0 line, drops vertically down to meet the 1.0 threshold, then turns horizontally to the left pointing toward the region between classes (2) and (1).  The arrowhead and the red “STRE C” label sit just below the 1.0 level, indicating that under the STRE C variant the maximum permissible stress is defined by the green 1.0 cutoff but that higher-class sections (class 1 and 2) can be designed for their plastic capacities with interaction checks.  

 • STRE E (red-dashed horizontal arrow) –  A second arrow begins on the green curve just to the right of class (3), at a level modestly above 1.0, and points horizontally to the left under the black “STRE E” label.  This indicates that for the STRE E variant, sections of all classes up to 4a are checked purely for stresses (limit c/t usage) and low utilisation in class 4a is permitted if the actual stress remains below that shown by the arrow’s origin.  

Finally, surrounding class (4a) is a faint blue dashed rectangle whose top lies above the level of both the 1.0 line and the red STRE E arrow.  This stylized box suggests that in a non-linear analysis (NSTR) the non-effective portions of slender plates in class 4 can be “deactivated” automatically, effectively enlarging the allowable stress envelope for those sections.  

In combination, the green curve, the 1.0 limit line, the two STRE arrows, and the blue dashed outline visualize how different code-prescribed design procedures (elastic stress checks STRE E, combined stress-capacity design STRE C, and non-linear treatment of class 4 plates) map onto the section-class spectrum and interact with the key c/t limit.

Most newer design codes for structural steel and composite structures are based on a elastic- plastic or plastic-plastic design. To achieve this the sections are subdivided into four classes as follows:
 • Sections of class 1
 are suitable for plastic hinges and a non-linear analysis with distributed yield areas (Analy- sis option NSTR) and a detailed interaction of shear and normal stress.
 • Sections of class 2
 have limited deformation capacities. The analysis may be done according to linear theory but the design may be done up to ultimate plastic limits.
 • Sections of class 3
 have no allowance for yielding, i.e. the linear stresses are limited. Thus analysis and design are according linear theory.
 • Sections of class 4a
 are formal in class 4 but due to small stresses these sections may be treated as in class 3.
 • Sections of class 4b
 due to buckling of the plates, some parts of the section have to be treated as not effective for normal stress, which has to be accounted for either during the definition of the section or will be taken into account automatically within a non-linear analysis.
 The separation between the classes is rule by a width-to-thickness ratio c/t, defined in tables of the design codes. As the section class is not only depending on the stresses but also on the material strength, it is of little use to specify a single class for a complete section, and such a specification or evaluation of a section class in AQUA is not provided.
 The design in AQB reverts the viewing direction of the design to the consistent way and has considerable advantages for the checking and especially for the utilisation factors during plan- ning. AQB does not check that all sections are in class X, but it computes that the utilisation of the critical limit of c/t is less than the stress dependent required limit value. This allows also to use slender elements within a plastic design or non-linear analysis, if the stresses at these elements are sufficiently small.
 The check within AQB is done with the following possible variants:

AQB does not check that all sections are in class X, but it computes that the utilisation of the critical limit of c/t is less than the stress dependent required limit value. This allows also to use slender elements within a plastic design or non-linear analysis, if the stresses at these elements are sufficiently small.. The check within AQB is done with the following possible variants:.
 • Design for stresses only, checking the c/t ratio according to sectional class 1+2+3+4a and low utilisation of sections of class 4a (STRE E F)
 • Design for stresses for section class 3, and if the section is classified in 1 or 2 a design for sectional capacities with interactions according to Eurocode. (STRE C)
 • Non linear design with hardening effects for sections of class 1 and 2. (NSTR)
 • Design for stresses for sections of class 1-4 with a non-linear analysis, where the non effective parts of the plates in class 4 are deactivated automatically.(NSTR)
 For the design of sections of class 4 there are thus several possibilities:
 • For small stresses load cases not relevant for stability may use increased c/t-limits (EN
 1993-1-1 5.5.2 (9))
 • Defining NEFF areas in AQUA may create the effective sections directly.
 • Using automatic iterative evaluation of non effective parts with (NSTR)
 Due to the shortening of the c-values in AQUA by the NEFF definitions those sections are now classified as sections of class 1 to 3. Thus we encounter the question if those reduced effective sections may include yielding. EN 1993-1-1 describes in Chapter 6.2.1 (4) how to perform an elastic stress check based on effective sectional values. But then we have several hints:
 • Chapter 6.2.9.3 (1) requires only, that the stress should not exceed the yield stress.
 • Chapter 6.2.9.3 (2) defines a simplified check based on the interaction with the elastic sectional moduli Weƒƒ.
 • Chapter 6.2.2.4 describes how a section with a web in class 3 may be converted to class 2 with the introduction of non effective areas.

• Chapter 6.2.9.3 (2) defines a simplified check based on the interaction with the elastic sectional moduli Weƒƒ.. • Chapter 6.2.2.4 describes how a section with a web in class 3 may be converted to class 2 with the introduction of non effective areas..
 As a non-linear analysis including yield especially for the tensile parts but without hardening does not exceed the yield stress, this method is within the requirements of the first bullet. Chapter 4.6 on EN 1993-1-5 describes the simplified check according to 6.2.9.3 (2) as general rule, but it says also in chapter 4.2. (2): "‘Effective areas should be determined on the basis of the linear strain distributions with the attainment of yield strain in the mid of the compression plate."’

Figure overview  
The image is a two-dimensional line graph labeled “Figure 2.3: Utilization level of section classes.” Its purpose is to illustrate how the calculated utilization ratio of different steel‐section classes varies as the applied stress increases from zero up to and beyond the yield stress (fy).

Axes  
• Horizontal axis (x-axis): represents the applied stress level, marked from 0 on the left up to fy (the material’s yield stress) at a vertical reference line.  
• Vertical axis (y-axis): represents the utilization level (ratio of applied load effect to design resistance). A dashed horizontal line at y = 1.0 indicates the threshold of full utilization (100 per cent).

Curves and line styles  
1. Nonlinear growth below fy: Two smoothly rising, upward-curving (convex) green lines originate at the graph origin (0, 0). They rise gradually at first, then more steeply, reaching two distinct values at the yield stress mark:  
   – The darker, upper green curve reaches exactly the dashed line at y = 1.0 when x = fy.  
   – A lighter or slightly lower green curve levels off just below the dashed 1.0 line at fy.  
   Both curves are roughly quadratic in shape, reflecting the increasing geometric or effective cross-section limitations of a given class as stresses approach the yield.

2. Constant plateaus beyond fy: At the vertical fy line, each green curve transitions abruptly into a horizontal line:  
   – The lower plateau (continuing the lighter green) remains constant just beneath y = 1.0 for stresses beyond fy.  
   – A bright red horizontal line begins at fy at a utilization above 1.0 and continues flat to the right edge of the plot. This red line signifies a higher, fixed utilization ratio assigned once the material has yielded.

3. Dashed benchmark: A green dotted line runs horizontally at y = 1.0 across the entire width of the chart, marking the nominal full-capacity utilization level.

Interpretation in context  
• Below yield stress (x < fy), section-class limits are governed by plate slenderness and local buckling criteria, which produce a nonlinear (quadratic-like) increase in permissible utilization as stress grows. This reflects how highly stressed plates progressively lose effective width, causing the allowable utilization to drop more sharply close to fy.  
• At the yield point (x = fy), the effective limit for a given class jumps to a new constant value: for one class (green plateau), the limit remains at or just below 100 percent utilization; for another (red plateau), the design criterion enforces a higher fixed factor, for example to account for plastic reserves or safety factors.  
• The step-change nature of the curves demonstrates that once yielding begins, code provisions switch from elastic‐based section classification to geometric “effective width” or plastic interaction rules, hence the abrupt jump to a new utilization level.  
• The green and red plateaus beyond fy reflect two different design‐code treatments or section classes: the green plateau could represent class 3 (elastic limit), the red representing class 4 (inelastic or plastic capacity) with a specified overstrength factor.

Overall, this figure visually encapsulates the nonlinearity of utilization versus stress for different section classes, the code‐defined step at the yield stress, and the concept that after yield the allowable utilization is treated as a constant rather than following the earlier quadratic trend.

For an effective design the ultimate bearing capacity is checked by utilisation levels of the total forces. The interaction of the individual components is given on a simplified way in the design codes and in general there are clauses to use modified schemes if appropriate. Very often some parts of the section are reserved for a certain force component. An other severe drawback is the non linearity of the interaction utilisation levels, i.e.
 the utilisation of a combined action may be lower than that of the largest component
 • with half of the ultimate loading the utilisation value may be anything below 1.0, e.g. 0.25 or 0.75 for a quadratic expression
 • Utilisations larger than 1.0 cannot be treated at all in many equations
 AQB provides thus five types of interaction, the user may select. All interaction formulas try to calculate a utilisation level which is as close as possible linear, i.e. giving an indication for the possible load factor. For an utilisation level of 1.0 the expressions are equivalent.

The case of buckling will occur if an element will suffer from large forces due to small defor- mations induced by geometric non-linear effects. This will limit the ultimate load for slender structures.
 The design for stability can be done in either of two ways. The most common checks are done based on a single representative beam. The problem which persists is the determination of the buckling length. The other way is to perform a global analysis using second order theory and suitable imperfections. This is the general target of SOFiSTiK-Software. However there are two exceptions to this general concept:
 The design for axially compressed beams in accordance with DIN 18800 Part 2 / EN 1993 is also included under the stress design in AQB, since it is normally used for lateral buckling perpendicular to the plane of the structure and for single truss braces.  Eurocode EN 1999 uses in chapter 6.2.1 a unified design check based on admissible stresses and a national dependent combination constant C, increasing the admissible yield stress. This is comparable to a sectional check for sections of class 3 or 4 ( α = 1.0). This figure, entitled “Figure 2.4: Creep Intervals,” is a schematic illustration of a two-step loading history and the decomposition of resulting strain into a plastic (irreversible) part and a delayed (visco-elastic) part for each loading interval. The drawing is arranged in two sections:

1. Left-hand panel: step loading history  
 • A Cartesian plot with vertical axis labeled “P” (applied load) and horizontal axis labeled “t” (time).  
 • At time t = 0 an initial load step is applied suddenly, jumping from zero to a first level P₁.  
 • This level is held constant for the duration of the first interval.  
 • At the beginning of the second interval, the load is increased again by a discrete increment, rising to a higher level P₂.  
 • That second load P₂ is then held constant for the remainder of the time axis shown.  

2. Right-hand panel: strain‐time curves for the two intervals, split into fixed (plastic) and viscous (time‐dependent) components  
 The right side is organized as four small strain‐versus‐time plots arranged in a roughly two-column by two-row layout. In each sub-plot the vertical axis represents strain (denoted “e”) and the horizontal direction implicitly represents time (arrows pointing to the right). The four curves are labeled:
  
  • e1f (upper-left): the fixed (plastic yield) strain due to the first load step. This curve is drawn as a horizontal line immediately after t = 0, indicating that the irreversible strain appears nearly instantaneously and then remains constant throughout the first interval.  
  • e1v (upper-right): the viscous or delayed elastic strain under the first load. This curve starts at zero at t = 0 and rises in a concave fashion toward an asymptote, representing time-dependent creep within the first interval.  
  • e2f (lower-left): the fixed (plastic) strain component generated by the second load increment. At the onset of the second interval, e2f jumps by an amount equal to the incremental plastic strain produced by the new load. After that jump it remains constant for the rest of the interval.  
  • e2v (lower-right): the viscous/delayed elastic strain resulting from the second load. Beginning at the second step’s start time, this curve rises in a similar creep-type shape, reflecting rebuilding of the time-dependent portion in response to the fresh loading.

By superposing these four contributions—two plastic (e1f, e2f) plus two delayed elastic (e1v, e2v)—the total time-dependent strain history under multi-step loading can be constructed. The diagram thus visualizes how an initial load produces both instantaneous and delayed deformation, how the instantaneous part carries forward unchanged into subsequent stages, and how the delayed part “rebuilds” with each new loading interval.

 σsecondry
 The prestressing of the tendons is used with their values after creep and shrinkage taking into consideration the decompression due to the internal forces and moments on the reduced net cross section. The initial strain is determined by the actual values of the internal forces and moments, and then multiplied as a whole by the prestress factor.

The reinforcement in AQUA has been arranged in layers. The reinforcement of a layer is considered as tension reinforcement if the centre of the total reinforcement lies on the tension side relative to the centroid of the cross section. A reinforcement with its centre on the other side is regarded as compression reinforcement. The meanings of the layer types are as follows:
 M Minimum reinforcement
 The intended minimum reinforcement is defined by the basic reinforcement area. If the minimum reinforcement should be always applied and not be increased, the maximum reinforcement area must be set equal to the basic reinforcement area. If the maximum value is larger than the minimum value, the user may select for the design if the layer is always inserted with at least the defined minimum area for beams. Compressive members will always activate the minimum value, but the minimum reinforcement in the compression zone however is applied only when a corresponding tension reinforcement is also present.
 Z Supplementary reinforcement
 Layers of this type are optional. The layers are equivalent in ranking; the number serves only for identification. The value of the basic reinforcement area is only used to specify the reinforcement ratio between the individual positions, and it is not a specification of minimum reinforcement. If supplementary reinforcements are not permitted to exceed a certain value, an appropriate maximum value must be input.
 S Sequential layers
 This type of layer serves to control the sequential filling of the reinforcement layers known from older programs. When a maximum value is reached, the next higher layer number is addressed. The reinforcement of layer 0 can be defined as minimum reinforcement with layer type M; all other layers must be of type S and have no minimum reinforcement.
 Reinforcement with the same layer number is always increased by the same factor. The maxi- mum factor is given by the first element reaching the maximum reinforcement in the layer. The minimum factor is 0.0 for layers (S,Z) and 1.0 for active minimum reinforcement layers (M). Maximum values may be ignored in the determination of the minimum reinforcement of the statically required cross section.
 A design must find, by iteration, a strain estate and a reinforcement distribution by which exter- nal and internal forces match. Additional requirements for ductility trigger either safety factors depending on the tensile steel strain or establish limits for the height of the compressive zone. If the height of the compressive zone exceeds the specified limits, compressive reinforcements are required. But they should not be taken larger than the tensile reinforcements.

A design must find, by iteration, a strain estate and a reinforcement distribution by which exter- nal and internal forces match. Additional requirements for ductility trigger either safety factors depending on the tensile steel strain or establish limits for the height of the compressive zone. If the height of the compressive zone exceeds the specified limits, compressive reinforcements are required. But they should not be taken larger than the tensile reinforcements..
 The class of possible strain states is further limited in such a way that only the ultimate limit strain states are used. This reduces the number of unknowns in the strain plane to two. How- ever, as additionally unknown factors of the reinforcement distribution are also present, there might be more unknowns than conditions for the solution.
 For this reason, problems with more than one reinforcement layers do not always have one unambiguous solution. Even with all the possible additional conditions (3), one can find a unique solution for a maximum of 4 to 6 layers, depending on the strain range.
 The procedure runs in two steps. The limit strain state is iterated in the outer loop by the BFGS method, similarly to what was described in the previous section.
 • As a rule, a first attempt to achieve equilibrium is made with a strain variation between the optimum tensile strain S1 to the maximum compressive strain C1 and a variation of the reinforcement distribution. If this is successful while the limiting conditions are maintained, an optimum ductile solution has been found, where the limits on the height of the compres- sive zone (x/d) are fulfilled. If this does not happen, the further procedure is determined depending on the axial force.
 In case of compressive loading, the strain on the tension side is reduced to the point where equilibrium is reached with a symmetric reinforcement distribution. The compressive zone must be enclosed with shear links.
 •
 • In case of tensile loading, the following strain variations are successively used in search of equilibrium:
 a) Centric strain S2 per thousand
 b) Compressive strain between 0 and C1 Tensile strain between S1 and S2
 c) Fully tensioned cross section with variable tensile strain
 The distribution of reinforcement is found in the inner loop by means of a quadratic optimisation problem for minimum error between internal and external forces with supplementary conditions for the required reinforcement.
 • Compression reinforcement is inserted by a magnitude not greater than the tension rein- forcement. This requirement of the old DIN is generalised by making certain that the centre of the total reinforcement is located on the tensional side of the cross section relative to its centre.

The distribution of reinforcement is found in the inner loop by means of a quadratic optimisation problem for minimum error between internal and external forces with supplementary conditions for the required reinforcement.. • Compression reinforcement is inserted by a magnitude not greater than the tension rein- forcement. This requirement of the old DIN is generalised by making certain that the centre of the total reinforcement is located on the tensional side of the cross section relative to its centre..
 • Provided that a minimum reinforcement is defined either with the section or in the data base from former design, this in this respect partial one is considered than there is not any violation of the former paragraph. To prevent increasing reinforcements for cyclic loadings, minimum reinforcement becomes always active only with its symmetric part. A special option CTRL REIN REQU may even deactivate the minimum reinforcements completely.
 Even with these limiting conditions, the problem can still be ambiguous. If, for instance, several layers could function as tension reinforcement, the distribution of the reinforcement would be based on the defined base values of the steel areas. Since this is generally not desired, the program uses additionally the distance of the reinforcement from the neutral axis and the moment of inertia with respect to the neutral axis. A supplementary condition is formulated for that purpose, which prefers reinforcement which is located farther outwards. If two layers are at the same distance, they are treated in the same manner. If the distance of a layer is zero, it is given no consideration whatsoever. Interpolation is used between these two extreme situations. Thus, a layer which is half as far out as another can only increase up to about one half the value of the outer layer.
 If the centre of some layer is at the outer extreme, only the distance of the centre is considered;
 if all of the layers have zero centre distances, only the radii of inertia (./I/A) are considered.
 This condition too is interpolated linearly between the extreme values. Furthermore, the far- ther outward the reinforcement is positioned in the cross section, the more stringent the entire condition is formulated. This supplementary condition does not affect the area of the reinforce- ment, but rather the factors of increase. Therefore, any change in the AS-values defined in AQUA will have a certain influence on the reinforcement distribution.
 The procedure of activating the layer numbers in sequence, which was customary in older programs, can not handle changing loads. In special cases, such as multilayer peripheral reinforcement or additional densifications, this method can be applied by defining sequential layer numbers in AQUA.

Therefore, any change in the AS-values defined in AQUA will have a certain influence on the reinforcement distribution.. The procedure of activating the layer numbers in sequence, which was customary in older programs, can not handle changing loads. In special cases, such as multilayer peripheral reinforcement or additional densifications, this method can be applied by defining sequential layer numbers in AQUA..
 In such case, each layer is considered individually. Layer i is laid only after layer i-1 has reached its maximum value. If a layer is not needed (e.g. compression reinforcement), it can be passed over.
 Beside the information from the cross section program on the distribution of reinforcement, there are other parameters, especially the minimum reinforcement ratios, which are controlled with the record DESI.
 The program differentiates between bending and compression members. The sequence of criteria is as follows:
 first criteria is a definition specified for the beam or design element
 •
 second criteria is the specification with the section (most common case)
 third criteria is the orientation relative to the gravity (CTRL VERT)
 •
 last criteria is the magnitude and eccentricity of the normal force (e.g. e/d<3.5)
 •
 One constructional reinforcement value can be prescribed for each type. This is an important option in stability studies. The minimum reinforcement of the statically required cross section can also be considered for compression members.
 These minimum reinforcement values hold equally for all cross sections of an analysis run and they are input as percentages of the cross sectional area.
 The new reinforcement is the greatest of:
 reinforcement required by the current design
 - minimum constructional reinforcement
 - minimum reinforcement of the statically required section
 - minimum reinforcement defined in the cross section program
 - minimum reinforcement that has already been stored
 The so computed reinforcement is used in subsequent checks.

The minimum reinforcement of the statically required cross section is applicable to compression members. AQB recognises a compression member either by an explicit specification through the record BEAM or by the orientation relative to the gravity direction or, depending on the load
 case, by a relative eccentricity e/d < 3.5 and the limit axial force NLIM (record CTRL).
 The minimum reinforcement according to DIN is computed by the method of first determining the internal forces and moments that can be sustained by the cross section with an appropri- ate reinforcement (e.g. 0.8 percent), and then reducing the reinforcement in proportion to its relative strength.
 The minimum reinforcement for compression members according to EN 1992, on the other hand, is accounted as follows (distinct values are defined in the national annexes):
 Asmn = mn(0.10 · N/βs,0.002 · Ac)
 (2.33)
 As minimum reinforcement is used the one layer, in case there is only one, or the minimum reinforcement layer, in case there are many, or the supplements in cases of cross sections with supplements only. Any entered maximum values of layers are ignored in this case. If multiple layers are involved, the criteria of the previous section for the selection of the layers are used. Outer reinforcement is thus given preference.
 When the relative strength has been obtained, each layer is reduced by the same isotropic factor. If the minimum reinforcement were attained exclusively by means of a layer laying on one side only, at reduction by this method the minimum reinforcement ratio is not reached under circumstances. An alternative method which admits priority to the absolute steel area can lead to serious underdesign and is therefore unavailable.
 Clearly comprehensible results are obtained when only one layer with minimum reinforcement = maximum reinforcement is defined, with usable distribution and relatively small total quantity of steel, and all supplements lie on separate layers. The program changes then the minimum reinforcement onto the necessary value.

The truss analogy of the shear design requires a tensile force in the longitudinal direction!
 An optimal solution would introduce this force just from the beginning in the bending design, as the accounting of the compressive forces afterward is rather difficult. This design method is given in the Eurocode for the case of the transverse shear and may be selected in AQB with input CTRL VM.
 A drawback however is that the inclination of the struts has to be selected in advance or by iteration and that point loads may lead to excessive values of the reinforcements if the shear force changes the sign.
 But as there is no need to design for more reinforcements than required at the location of the maximum moment, it is quite common for best practice to use a shift rule with an offset for the required reinforcements. Then we get additional reinforcements on both sides for a zero moment which is a clear hint, that the longitudinal force is to be applied on the total section.
 For the torsional problem the standard workflow is to evaluate the utilisation of the provided total reinforcment for bending and to add the required torsional reinforcements. The true amount is only known if the inclination of the truss model has been selected. A required longitudinal
 reinforcement of 50 mm² for an inclination of 45° will yield for a cot of 1.75 thus a required longitudinal reinforcement of 875 mm² for Torsion. If then an existing reinforcement of 1000 mm² has a relative capacity of 2.5, the required reinforcement will be 1000/2.5 + 875 = 1275 mm². This reinforcement may be adopted to compressive forces within the section, which is not an easy task, but AQB will try to do so.
 As in many cases the torsional design uses an inclination of 45°, it is easier and much more economique, sometimes for existing structure possibly the only solution to go with an additional tensile force to the design similar to the transverse shear design.

content:
DIN 1045-1 contains in 10.2. (6) a regulation limiting the strain in the centre of plates of structured sections to the value of εc2. This will be accounted for in AQB at all centre points of shear cuts having the type FLAN. The default is to correct the maximum compressive strain. If this is not what you want to do, then an explicit definition of the DESI C2 will deactivate this behaviour. Then there are two possibilities:
 If nothing else is defined AQB will just check the strain and print an error message if its value exceeds the limit of the stress-strain-law.
 •
 • For critical cases, if the last sentence of this paragraph is needed, which imposes the pure web with the total maximum strains as an lower limit to the ultimate load, one has either to deactivate the plates via the CS-mechanism or define them with a special material without the rectangular block in the stress-strain-law.

The design is also suitable for unreinforced cross sections. In such case the program computes internal forces and moments which are in the same proportion to each other as the external forces and moments. The safety factors must be defined according to the particular code. The program then reports the relative strength and prints a warning if this becomes less than 1.0. A message is also printed when the strain at the gravity centre becomes positive, meaning that a gaping joint is extending beyond the centre.

In general the tendons are fixed. It is only the subdivision of the stress into a provided part and those parts induced by a strain increment which max become relevant for some design tasks.
 For the treatment of stress induced corrosion of prestressed bridges some enhancements are provided:
 • The extended print out of stresses (ECHO STRE FULL and selection of a relevant admis- sible stress check class with STRE STYP) has in the last row and last column an entry Az,r giving the estimated factor on the area and force of the prestressing yielding tensile stress of ƒctm. (the sectional values will be kept unchanged for this estimate)
 • Record BEAM has a new item PRED (after STYP) defining a factor to be applied on all
 tendon areas and forces.
 • For DESI an additional row will be printed with the relative bearing capacity based on the moments of the life load (Action L) with identifier (rel-tra(M-live))

To account for the shear forces there are multiple methods available.
 • AQUA will calculate the complete elastic shear stress by default with the Finite Element method (see CTRL STYP). This is used for all elastic stress checks, but it can be taken as a fallback or lower limit for the other methods if the values are reduced by a factor obtained from the internal lever in cracked condition to the uncracked condition.
 • The method of differences of longitudinal forces is mainly used for flanges and bond in composite sections (dowels)
 • The variable angle strut model is used for cracked conditions. It is the base for most design codes for uniaxial shear.
 The shear design for ultimate limit states is always defined as the resultant magnitude of the shear stress along the width b0. Thus we consider a shear flow T in [kN/m]. The torsional shear based on an equivalent hollow section Mt/2Ak may be added then easily. As a shear or principal compressive stress is valuable for the engineer we use and show these values too. The utilisation ratio for a total design force is not useful in general cases.
 No reduction is made of individual loads in proximity to the support. A consistent solution is extremely elaborate. Thus, only the reduction caused by the distributed pressure of the support is accounted for.

The drawing is a three-dimensional, axonometric sketch of a thin-walled flange element (essentially a rectangular plate) illustrating the principal internal force flow and reinforcement layout used in a strut-and-tie (truss analogy) shear design.  Below the image is the caption “Figure 2.5: Design of Flanges.”

Overall geometry  
• The flange is shown as a shallow box or plate of uniform thickness, viewed in perspective so that its top face, two side faces and bottom face are all visible.  
• Two cut-lines labeled “A–A” are drawn (one vertical at the left edge, one oblique over the top face) indicating the location of a section plane.  

Applied shear forces  
• On the top face at both the left and right ends two large horizontal arrows labeled “Fd” point inward toward the center of the flange, denoting the design shear force applied to the flange across its effective width b_eff.  
• At the bottom right edge another arrow is annotated “Fd + ΔFd,” showing that shear may increase along the span and that a small additional shear increment ΔFd must be carried.  

Shear flow notation  
• Along the lower edge on the visible side face, a thick arrow labeled “B” points horizontally, indicating the direction of resultant shear flow in the web or plate.  
• On the top face an arrow labeled “b_eff” spans from one loaded edge toward mid-span, marking the effective flange width over which shear is considered.  

Internal strut‐and‐tie system  
• Within the volume of the plate, a pair of dashed lines form an inclined “V” or strut pattern. One of these dashed lines (a concrete compression strut) runs from the loaded top edge down to the opposite bottom corner at an inclination labeled θ (theta).  
• At the intersection of these dashed lines a small solid-arrow box marked “A” denotes the compressive force vector in that strut.  
• This strut angle θ represents the angle of the compressive concrete strut relative to the horizontal (formerly denoted α in the code text).  

Shear reinforcement (ties)  
• On the bottom face of the flange a series of closely-spaced parallel straight lines represent steel shear reinforcement bars (stirrups or links) running longitudinally.  
• An arrow labeled “Asf” (area of shear reinforcement) points to this group of bars to identify their cross-sectional area.  
• Nearby, a slender vector arrow labeled “sf” indicates the shear flow carried by these reinforcement bars (shear flux in kN/m).  

Key relationships illustrated  
• The drawing embodies the “variable-inclination strut method.” The designer begins with a low strut inclination θ (around 0.4 rad or per standard) and increases it until the concrete’s principal compressive stress is just at its allowable limit or until the minimum shear reinforcement is exhausted.  
• The internal truss: top horizontal shear force Fd is transmitted into an inclined concrete strut (compression) which resolves into tension in the bottom reinforcement Asf (ties). Any increase in shear along the span (ΔFd) is likewise carried by the strut-tie system.  
• The effective flange width b_eff and the lever arm (vertical distance between strut apex and centroid of Asf) govern the magnitudes of internal forces.  

Section call-out  
• The cut-plane A–A, indicated both by heavy broken lines and by arrows pointing to it, shows where one would “slice” the flange to plot internal shear stresses, principal stresses σn, or to extract a 2-D cross-section for detailed design checks (e.g. verifying σc, σt against code limits).  

In sum, Figure 2.5 synthesizes the equilibrium of shear (change in normal stress vs. change in shear stress) by depicting how an external design shear force Fd acting over an effective flange width is carried through an internal concrete compression strut at angle θ and returned via longitudinal shear reinforcement (Asf), with notation for shear flow (sf) and additional shear increment (ΔFd). This perfectly visualizes the core of a truss‐analogy shear check for thin-walled composite flanges.

The image is a simple, two‐dimensional schematic (Figure 2.6) illustrating the internal shear‐flow equilibrium in a three‐layer composite element, in the absence of any external transverse loading. It is composed of three horizontal, rectangular “layers” (or materials) stacked one above the other and each spanning the same horizontal length “a.” Below the bottom layer is a dimension line marked “a,” with arrowheads at either end, denoting the constant bond length over which axial‐force differences occur.

Each layer is labeled in its interior:

• Bottom layer: “Material 1”  
• Middle layer: “Material 2”  
• Top layer: “Material 3”

At the left edge of each layer, an arrow points outward (to the left) and is labeled Ni (i = 1, 2, 3). At the right edge of each layer, an arrow points outward (to the right) and is labeled Ni + ΔNi. Thus:

• Bottom layer: left arrow N1; right arrow N1 + ΔN1  
• Middle layer: left arrow N2; right arrow N2 + ΔN2  
• Top layer: left arrow N3; right arrow N3 + ΔN3  

Between the bottom and middle layers there is a pair of opposing arrows (one on the underside of “Material 2,” one on the top of “Material 1”), each labeled T12. Between the middle and top layers is a similar pair labeled T23. These T‐arrows represent the shear flows (interface bond forces) that transmit differential axial forces from one material to the next.

To the right of the three‐layer stack, two boxed equations define these shear flows in terms of the axial‐force increments ΔNi and the bond length a:

• T23 = –ΔN3 / a  =  + (ΔN1 + ΔN2) / a  
• T12 = +ΔN1 / a  =  –(ΔN2 + ΔN3) / a  

These relationships enforce equilibrium: the sum of the shear‐flow contributions across all interfaces must balance the total change in longitudinal force across the composite section. In other words, any gain or loss of axial force in one layer must be offset by equal and opposite shear transferred through the adjoining interfaces.

Finally, centered beneath the drawing, is the caption:
“Figure 2.6: Equilibrium for Composite Shear (without loadings).”

Overall, the figure concisely demonstrates how differences in the normal (axial) forces in each bonded layer (ΔNi) give rise to internal shear flows T12 and T23, and how those flows are calculated by dividing the axial‐force differences by the length of the interface, a. This schematic underpins the theory—mentioned in the accompanying text—of shear‐transfer design in thin‐walled, composite or multi‐material beams, where bond‐length, layer stiffness, and the distribution of axial forces all enter into the determination of interface shear stresses.

The graphic, captioned “Figure 2.7: Shear distribution for cracked sections,” is laid out as a left-to-right sequence of five schematic panels connected by light-grey arrows. It illustrates how the true shear stress distribution in a cracked, solid rectangular section is transformed step by step into an equivalent constant-flux, thin-walled model.

1. Leftmost panel (original cross section)  
 ‑ A vertical rectangle represents the beam cross section under shear.  
 ‑ Its top region is shaded light-green (compression zone); the bottom region is left white (tension zone).  
 ‑ A horizontal dashed line marks the crack or neutral axis between compression and tension.  
 ‑ On the right face of the rectangle two blue, double-headed arrows point inward:  
   • The upper arrow, spanning from the top fiber down to the dashed crack line, is labelled “D.”  
   • The lower arrow, from the crack line to the bottom fiber, is labelled “Z.”  
 ‑ Between the crack line and a small dotted reference line above it is a dimension marked “z₁ᵢᵢ,” indicating the distance to the centroid of the cracked (tension-only) area.

2. Second panel (shear‐flow diagram)  
 ‑ A red-filled, free-form contour depicts the shear‐flow distribution q(z) obtained by integrating local shear stresses.  
 ‑ Its horizontal width at each elevation corresponds to the magnitude of q(z).  
 ‑ The profile bulges most in the compression zone and tapers down toward the tension side.

3. Third panel (overlaid traces)  
 ‑ Two outline curves are overlaid on a blank background:  
   • A dotted line shows the uncracked (idealized) rectangular‐section shear distribution (proportional to V·Q/I·b).  
   • A solid line gives the actual cracked‐section shear flow, scaled to have the same maximum value.  
 ‑ Their difference in curvature illustrates the empirical safeguard used when selecting the shear‐stress profile for cracked sections.

4. Fourth panel (reverse arrow)  
 ‑ A grey arrow points back toward the rightmost schematic.

5. Fifth panel (equivalent thin-walled model)  
 ‑ A slender vertical strip represents an open, thin-walled section whose constant shear flux T replaces the complex distribution of the cracked solid.  
 ‑ Two small horizontal arrows at the mid-height of that strip show the uniform shear flow direction.  

Together, these five panels demonstrate how a cracked rectangular beam under shear (with partial compression depth D, lever arm Z and eccentricity z₁ᵢᵢ) can be replaced by an equivalent thin-walled element carrying a single, constant shear flow T.

The figure is a schematic cross‐sectional sketch of a thin‐walled beam element used to illustrate the truss (strut‐and‐tie) model for shear design. It is labeled “Figure 2.8: Compressive or Tensile Forces” and shows a rectangular section of total depth “d,” with flange elements at top and bottom and an interior web zone carrying shear by inclined struts and ties.  

Overall Layout  
- The outer boundary (drawn with solid lines) defines a beam of height d. A vertical dashed line at the left marks a cut plane or control section. The distance between top and bottom faces is dimensioned by a double‐arrow labeled “d.”  

Flanges  
- Label A points to the top horizontal plate (the top flange).  
- Label C points to the bottom horizontal plate (the bottom flange).  

Web Region: Struts and Ties  
- Within the region between the flanges, a series of diagonal, cross‐hatched lines run from the bottom left toward the top right. These represent compressive struts—concrete compression zones—inclined at an angle θ to the horizontal (shown by an arc and the Greek letter θ near the red block).  
- Superimposed on the hatched struts are bold zig-zag lines inclined at a steeper angle α; these indicate tensile shear links or inclined longitudinal reinforcement. The angle α is shown near the left side of the web, measured between the link and the horizontal. Label D refers to this pattern of diagonal ties in the web.  

Spacing and Shear Link  
- Between two successive zig-zag lines there is a horizontal double-arrow labeled “s,” denoting the center‐to‐center spacing of shear links.  
- Label B identifies a single shear link element, highlighted as a red diamond (rotated square) located mid-depth in the web. Four small arrows point inward to that red shape, emphasizing its role as the tensile link resisting shear.  

Key Features Illustrated  
- The combination of inclined compression struts (hatched D) and tensile links (zig-zag lines at angle α) forms the classic strut‐and‐tie model for shear transfer in a beam section.  
- The angles α (link inclination) and θ (compression strut inclination) can be chosen to optimize required link area and compressive stresses. A gentle α reduces link area but increases longitudinal tensile forces, while θ is adjusted to respect compressive stress limits.  
- The red shear link (B) and the spacing s are design parameters in codes—minimum link reinforcement and maximum spacing are governed by concrete standards (e.g., EN 1992).  
- Top and bottom flange elements (A and C) serve as compression or tension anchorage zones for the web forces.  

Figure Caption  
Below the drawing, in plain text, is the caption “Figure 2.8: Compressive or Tensile Forces,” indicating the focus on internal force paths under shear loading.  

This schematic helps visualize how shear is carried in an open or thin‐walled section by a truss analogy: compressive struts in the concrete and tensile reinforcement ties, with geometry (d, s, α, θ) and material strength defining the interaction.

Figure Overview  
The image, captioned “Figure 2.9: Shear width in circular cross sections,” schematically illustrates how to determine the effective shear width under compression and tension for a circular member. A single circle represents the cross section of a structural element (for example, a column or a beam with a circular profile). Three horizontal lines are drawn across this circle to demarcate three key widths: shear width for compression-induced shear, shear width for tension-induced shear, and a minimum shear width.

Key Elements and Annotations  
1. Outer Circle – Cross Section Boundary  
   • Depicts the full cross-sectional outline of the member.  
   • All width measurements are taken between two vertical tangents of this circle at the chosen horizontal level.

2. Inner Points  
   • A point near the top of the circle is labelled “D.” This denotes the location of the resultant shear force’s line of action in the compression zone when the member is loaded.  
   • A point at the center of the circle is labelled “Z.” This represents the neutral‐axis or centroidal axis, commonly used in uniaxial design of bending and shear components.

3. Top Horizontal Band (Compression Shear Width)  
   • Two closely spaced horizontal lines near the top define the compression shear width.  
   • The region between these lines inside the circle is filled with diagonal hatching.  
   • Adjacent text reads “Shear width, compression force.”  
   • Interpretation: According to Feltham’s approach (cited in AQB methodology), the effective width for shear in compression is taken as the chord length of the circle at the elevation corresponding to the resultant shear force location D, related to the area above that level and the effective depth.

4. Middle Line (Tension Shear Width)  
   • A single horizontal line passes through the circle slightly below mid-height.  
   • It is labelled “Shear width, tension force.”  
   • Interpretation: For the tension side, the width is taken as the chord at a level symmetrically related to where the resultant shear crosses the section, measured from the neutral axis Z downward.

5. Bottom Line (Minimum Shear Width)  
   • A third horizontal line closer to the bottom of the circle is labelled “Minimum shear width.”  
   • This defines a lower bound for the chord length used in design, ensuring that even if the resultant shear branch shifts, the shear resistance is not underestimated.

Contextual Notes  
- Uniaxial Design: The figure isolates the shear width for either compression or tension branch so that design of shear reinforcement can proceed using only the relevant uniaxial component of internal forces or bending moments.  
- Shear Link Inclination: While this sketch shows only horizontal widths, any inclination of shear links (stirrups) is accounted for following the guidelines of Bender [2], which adjust the projected shear area according to link angle.  
- AQB Implementation: In a computational or code check (AQB), the widths extracted from this diagram feed into formulas that derive an equivalent rectangular shear area, ensuring conservative yet efficient shear reinforcement.

content:
In case of circular cross sections AQB uses as width according to a paper by Feltham a value derived from the area above the resulting shear force and the effective height.
 Design is always done for the uniaxial resulting components of the forces or moments.
 The inclination of the shear links will be accounted for according to Bender [2].

metadata.sections: 2.7.4 Shear Checks in Circular Cross Sections

content:
The determination of a stress state while accounting for the material properties is the basis for many further checks. For this purpose, one must follow the procedure described in Section 2.4 to determine the strain under service loads or increased service loads. No strain limits nor safety coefficients are in effect for this check. The user can apply a modified material law for this check.
 In general, this task can only be solved iteratively. To accomplish this, the strain level of the cross section, which is defined by the strain in the centroid and the curvatures in the two coordinate directions, must be varied until the internal forces and moments of the cross section sufficiently match the external ones.
 The so-called BFGS (Broyden-Fletcher-Goldfarb-Shanno) method is used for the non-linear iteration. From the differences between internal and external forces a direction of change is computed for the strain level, and iteration proceeds in this direction until it reaches an optimum point. This procedure is called line-search, and its precision can be controlled by some input for the CTRL record. Starting from the calculated optimum point, a new direction is determined in the next step of iteration, using all the information computed thus far.
 The mathematical prerequisite of convexity means, from mechanical perspective, that if the curvature increases the internal moment must increase too. If stress-strain curves with falling branches are defined, the solution can become ambiguous and the procedure may run into difficulties.
 Either the serviceability stress-strain curves or the ultimate stress-strain curves or an impute mean value stress-strain curve with or without safety coefficients defined in AQUA may be applied. As the choice of the correct curve may have considerable effect on the results, each user should carefully select the best curve along his knowledge or opinion. As a guide-line the EC2 states the following rules:
 • The evaluation of deformations and the distribution of forces should use the mean values (Ecm, fctm) in general. (A 2.1 (3))

As the choice of the correct curve may have considerable effect on the results, each user should carefully select the best curve along his knowledge or opinion. As a guide-line the EC2 states the following rules:. • The evaluation of deformations and the distribution of forces should use the mean values (Ecm, fctm) in general. (A 2.1 (3)).
 • For bracing elements, i.e. those where a lower stiffness is unfavourable, the mean values of the concrete have to be divided by a safety factor of the material. (A3.4 (6) und A3.1 (6)). As these factors do not coincide with those of the design itself, they have to be specified with the stress-strain law within AQUA.
 • For the evaluation of the ultimate limit state one has to use design values. (A 2.1 (4)).
 • For the design with the total system, reduced safety factors for the loading as well as for the concrete may be used. (A 3.1)
 The design takes into account any reinforcement possibly computed for the stored load cases. If no reinforcement has been computed, or if a single combination of forces and moments has been defined externally, the program uses the minimum reinforcement ratios set in AQUA.

A special case of non linear behaviour is the effect of local buckling as it is defined in Eurocode EN 1993-1-5. Depending on the slenderness ratio c/t and the acting compressive stress, parts of a thin walled section may become ineffective for the normal stress. AQB will account for this effect automatically. The values for c are defined in AQUA.
When some code requires observing certain maximum strains or checking that the neutral axis runs only as far as the gravity centre, these values can be taken directly from the results printout.

The stress range of the reinforcement is computed and verified, upon request, for all defined load cases or combinations thereof. The stress range is derived from the maximum and mini- mum steel stresses of all reinforcement elements in all of the examined load cases.

The basis of the check in accordance with many design codes is the calculation of a crack width by the expression:
 k = β · srm · (εsm − εcm)
 (2.47)
 where srm is the mean crack spacing, εsm the mean strain of the steel, εcm the mean strain of the concrete between the cracks and β an optional safety coefficient (old EC 2 = 1.7). The required design crack width wk is prescribed in AQB. The reduced coefficient for restraint must be defined for thick cross sections through the explicit input of this value.
 The two characteristic values are determined from the following expressions:
 ”local design checks” different rules are applied than for the total section where it is quite common to use k2 = 0.5 for bending despite of the real height of the tensile region.
 k3 = national definable boxed value (Recommendation = 3.4)
 k4 = national definable boxed value (Recommendation = 0.425)
