The figure is a schematic M–k plot (moment M on the vertical axis, curvature or rotation stiffness k on the horizontal axis) used to illustrate the concept of secant stiffness.  Key features are:

 1. Coordinate axes  
    - A vertical axis labeled “M” (moment).  
    - A horizontal axis labeled “k” (curvature or rotational stiffness), with a tick marking some nonzero k-value.  

 2. Nonlinear M–k curve  
    - A bold, gently convex curve starting at the origin and rising to the right.  This represents the actual (nonlinear) relationship M(k) for a cross section or structural member as it yields and then hardens.  

 3. Initial tangent stiffness line (tangent at zero)  
    - A straight, thin line through the origin with steeper slope than the nonlinear curve.  It is labeled “EI₀,” denoting the initial (elastic) flexural stiffness.  

 4. Secant line to the nonlinear curve  
    - A straight line drawn from the origin to a point on the nonlinear curve.  Its slope is indicated by the legend “EI = M/k.”  This secant line defines the secant stiffness at that working point.  

 5. Moment level indicator  
    - A dashed horizontal line drawn from the chosen point on the nonlinear M–k curve back to the vertical axis, marking the current moment M corresponding to that curvature k.  

 6. Angle marker  
    - A small angle drawn at the origin between the initial tangent and the secant line, visually emphasizing that the secant slope (EI = M/k) is shallower than the initial tangent stiffness (EI₀).  

 7. Caption  
    - Centered under the drawing is the text “Figure 2.10: Secant stiffness.”  

Interpretation in context  
  - The nonlinear curve is the actual moment–curvature response of a cross section undergoing elastic-plastic deformation.  
  - EI₀ is the initial (uncracked or purely elastic) flexural stiffness.  
  - At any working point (M, k) on the curve, one can define a secant stiffness equal to the slope of the line from the origin to that point (EI = M/k).  
  - The plot visually contrasts the faster initial response (tangent stiffness) with the reduced stiffness captured by the secant definition once yielding and plastic curvature have begun to accumulate.  

This diagram underpins the secant stiffness formulation often used in iterative nonlinear static analyses when a full incremental tangent stiffness is not available. It shows how the moment-curvature relation can be approximated by a linear “secant” stiffness through the origin, simplifying the computation of member stiffness updates under increasing loads.

sections: 2.8 Stress Checks with Non-linear Material Behaviour

content:
The image is a two-dimensional plot titled “Figure 2.11: Plastic curvature,” showing how an element’s curvature (horizontal axis k) develops under a bending moment (vertical axis M) when it yields and accrues plastic deformation.  Below is a detailed, element-by-element description:

1. Coordinate Axes  
   • Horizontal axis: labeled “k” for total curvature.  
   • Vertical axis: labeled “M” for bending moment.  
   • Both axes originate together at the lower-left corner.

2. Elastic Reference Lines (EI₀)  
   • From the origin two straight lines with equal, high slope emanate, each marked “EI₀.” These represent the purely elastic bending stiffness.  
     – The first of these lines (leftmost) is drawn unobstructed from the origin up toward the dashed moment level.  
     – The second is drawn through the point where the nonlinear (curved) response meets the dashed moment, serving as the tangent at that point; it is parallel to the first line.

3. Nonlinear (Secant) Response Curve  
   • A smooth, concave-down curve also starts at the origin, initially following the elastic slope but gradually bending over.  
   • This curve represents the actual secant stiffness of the cross section as plastic deformations accumulate: the effective stiffness falls off, so the curve flattens.  
   • It intersects a dashed horizontal line (the ultimate or applied moment level “M”) at a finite curvature value.

4. Dashed Reference Lines at the Point of Yield  
   • Horizontal dashed line: drawn at height M to indicate the target bending moment.  
   • Vertical dashed line: dropped from the intersection of the curved response with the dashed moment line, meeting the horizontal axis at a point labeled “k.” This is the total curvature reached under M.

5. Elastic Curvature Marker (k₀)  
   • On the horizontal axis, closer to the origin, there is a small tick and the label “k₀.” This denotes the purely elastic curvature corresponding to the same bending moment (i.e. M/EI₀).

6. Plastic Curvature Definition (k_pl)  
   • From the intersection point on the curve, the tangent line (second EI₀) is extended back to the horizontal axis, meeting it to the right of k.  
   • The distance between the two vertical projections (from k and from the tangent’s intercept) is marked and labeled “k_pl = k – k₀.” This is the plastic curvature: the extra curvature beyond the elastic portion.

7. Overall Interpretation  
   • The graph visually separates total curvature into its elastic and plastic parts.  
   • Up to k₀, the response is linear (elastic). Beyond k₀ and up to k, the material yields, stiffness degrades (curve flattens), and plastic curvature accumulates.  
   • The slope at any point on the curve is the secant stiffness M/k; the tangent at the yield point recovers the original elastic modulus EI₀.

By showing both the idealized elastic lines EI₀ and the actual secant response curve, the figure makes clear how to compute the plastic component of curvature (k_pl) in an iterative stiffness formulation.

sections: 2.8 Stress Checks with Non-linear Material Behaviour

content:
The figure is a stylized, black‐and‐white line diagram illustrating what the authors call the “Type N” secant‐stiffness update in an iterative nonlinear bending analysis (captioned “Figure 2.12: Type N method”).  It is drawn on a simple two‐axis coordinate system:

• Vertical axis (ordinate) is labeled “M” with an arrow pointing upward to indicate positive bending moment.  
• Horizontal axis (abscissa) is unlabeled but represents curvature (or a generalized rotation parameter), running from the origin at left to increasing curvature at right.

Several graphical elements appear:

1. Initial elastic branch (E₀)  
   – A thin, straight line of moderate slope is drawn from the origin upward and to the right, labeled “Eo.”  
   – This line represents the original elastic secant stiffness (moment = E₀ · curvature) before any plastic deformation.

2. Nonlinear moment‐curvature curve  
   – From the same origin, a heavier (bolder) curved line bows upward and to the right, reflecting increasing plasticity: initially steep (elastic), then gradually softening as curvature increases.  
   – This solid curve terminates at a distinct point (marked by a small solid circle or bullet) on the right side of the diagram, where a horizontal dashed line intersects it.

3. Horizontal load/reference line  
   – A dashed horizontal line is drawn at the height of that termination point. It denotes the current applied moment level Mₙ (the target external moment for the next iteration).

4. New secant stiffness (Eₙ)  
   – From the origin up through the same termination point runs another straight line, drawn thinner than the nonlinear curve but thicker than the initial E₀. This line is labeled “En.”  
   – Its slope is greater than E₀, reflecting a revised secant stiffness calculated from zero up to the current (plasticized) state.

5. Plastic tangent stiffness (Kₚₗ)  
   – A dashed oblique line also emanates from the origin with a relatively shallow slope, labeled “Kpl” on the horizontal axis.  
   – This represents the (constant) plastic tangent stiffness used in some formulations to account for incremental plastic curvature increments.

Together these elements convey the key idea of the Type N iterative update:  
– One tracks the nonlinear M–κ curve until it intersects the target moment level.  
– At that intersection, one may re‐linearize via a new secant stiffness En (passing through the origin and current point) or use a constant tangent/plastic stiffness Kpl (dashed line) to advance the solution.  
– The initial elastic stiffness E₀ remains fixed only for the very first step.  

The diagram’s caption (“Figure 2.12: Type N method”) sits below the drawing, centered, emphasizing that it is one of several possible secant‐stiffness schemes (Types S, K, etc.) described in the surrounding text.

sections: 2.8 Stress Checks with Non-linear Material Behaviour

content:
The figure is a schematic moment–curvature plot illustrating the “Type 1” secant‐stiffness update method in an incremental nonlinear analysis.  The vertical axis is labeled “M” (bending moment) and the horizontal axis represents curvature or a generalized deformation measure; both axes originate at the lower left corner.  

Starting from the origin, three straight lines of different slopes are drawn:
•  A lightly drawn line labeled “E0” radiates upward at a relatively steep angle; this represents the initial secant stiffness of the section, i.e. the ratio of moment to curvature from the origin to the first loaded state.  
•  A second lightly drawn line labeled “E1” is less steep than E0; this is the updated secant stiffness computed after the first iteration, connecting the origin to the new point on the nonlinear moment–curvature curve.  
•  A thin, more horizontal line at very small slope is labeled “Kpl” (plastic stiffness).  It originates at the origin and approximates the purely plastic branch or tangent stiffness when plastic curvatures are introduced as zero for certain members.  

Superimposed on these straight stiffness‐lines is a thick, smoothly rising curve that starts at the origin, initially rises steeply, then gradually levels off.  This thick curve is the true nonlinear moment–curvature relationship of the cross‐section, showing material and geometric softening as curvature increases.  

A horizontal dashed line at some intermediate height on the M‐axis marks the target external bending moment to be matched by the internal resisting moment.  Where this horizontal line intersects each secant‐stiffness line (E0 and E1) defines successive estimates of the curvature corresponding to the applied moment.  From the intersection on E1, a vertical dashed line is dropped down to the curvature axis, indicating the updated curvature estimate used in the next iteration.  

Under the plot is the caption “Figure 2.13: Type 1 method,” linking it to the discussion of secant formulations in an iterative static analysis.  In context, the image visualizes how, in the “curvatures‐and‐moments‐yield‐stiffness” variant (Type 1), the current moments and curvatures define a new secant stiffness through the origin; this new stiffness is then used to compute the next curvature increment.  The diagram thus conveys the geometric essence of the secant‐stiffness update loop: draw a radial line from the origin to the current point on the nonlinear curve, use its slope as the secant stiffness, apply the target moment to find the next curvature, and repeat until convergence.

The B 4700 is similar to the Eurocode, but there are deviations. The most significant is the different definition of concrete class based on the cubic strength.
 Some how uncertain is 2.4.2. (3). The steel strain will not be checked by AQB. We believe that the provision of symmetric reinforcements in those cases by AQB will cover the intended requests.
 For the inclination of the diagonals of the truss model we have the formulas (23) and (24) of OENORM. The lower limit of 0.4 is only allowed for continuous reinforcement. This has to be specified in REIN as SPAN.
 The serviceability check uses a given interpolation factor between tables 7/8 and 9/10. Table 9 and 10 have been extended for smaller stresses according to the theoretical base.
 The B 4750 has additional factors for the creep coefficients if the strength is higher than 35 MPa. The deductional areas of tendons is always the full duct area.

The mean value of permissible inclination for shear force and torsion is freely selectable be- tween 25 and 45 degrees within SIA 262, the maximum allowed shear is given by equation (40):
 VRd,c = bzkcƒcd(cosα + cotβsnα)snα
 (2.93)
 The coefficients kc will be selected based on the stress distribution and the CUT-properties WEB / FLAN.
 The coefficient kfor plates without shear links is taken as 3.0 and modified according to the steel strength and the grading of the longitudinal reinforcements. Modifications according to the maximum grain have to be specified explicitly.

Shear design according to BAEL-91 as modified in the year 1999 still uses the deductional stress method. The admissible stresses depend on the inclination of the shear links (A5.1,21), but have the same value for all type of shear. There is a factor k which modifies the shear force of the concrete depending on the normal force and bending stresses. (A5.1,23).
 The design for cracking is done via a limit for the stresses according to A.4.5,323.

The ministerial decret from 1996 allows the design according to the EC with the Italian material definitions. But there still exists the old method with a deductional stress. A special option is the parameter δ, which has a value between 0 and 2 depending on the normal force and the decompression moment. This value is then applied as a factor to the shear force of the concrete. Further it has to be noted that the admissible shear stress is depending on the inclination of the shear links. This document contains also a regulation for the use of the old EC2 with the formulas of the eurocode and the materials of the DM-1996. (Safety factor of concrete is 1.6, Inclination of struts in truss model is 0.5 < tan < 1.0 etc.).
 NTC (Norme Tecniche) of year 2005 was an intermediate solution, where material safety (1.9/1.5) was referred on the cubical strength Rck of the concrete. The crack width accord- ing Table 5.1-X is also depended on the sensitivity of the reinforcement, and the stresses had to be checked for the serviceability condition according to table 5.1-XI and 5.1-XII depending on the environmental conditions.
 The NTC (Norme Tecniche) of year 2008 is now nearly identical to the EN 1992 fast vollständig überein. Small deviations are in the material parameters only. Formulas for the crack width have to be taken from the comment however, they are not included in the design code itself. Also for non linear analysis detailed provisions are not given.

At the first glance the regulations for the EHE are very similar to those of the German DIN 1045-1, however the design is rather different as the EHE uses still a possible deduction of shear, which is for vertical links as follows:
 the case of the fine crack system.

The Swedish design code have the special provision that the safety factor for the material has two parts: First η • γm (= 1.5 for concrete) for the material itself, which is defined with the material in AQUA, then a second safety class factor γn dependant on the type of the structure which is defined when selecting the design code and thus will preset the safety factors for DESI.
 There are no special effects for the bending design, but for the shear a deduction method is foreseen where the concrete capacity is dependant on the normal stress, the prestress and the existing longitudinal reinforcement. (Sections 3.7.3 and 3.7.4.)

The table reproduced above is a matrix of nominal concrete cover requirements (in millimetres) for reinforced concrete elements, as specified by BS 5400 Part 4, Table 13. It cross-references four environmental exposure categories against four standard concrete grades. Concrete cover is the nominal distance from the surface of the concrete to the nearest reinforcement face and is critical in durability design for preventing corrosion and ensuring long-term performance.  

1. Structure of the table  
   • Columns:  
     – “Concrete Grade” header spans four sub-columns, labelled 25, 30, 40 and 50. These numbers refer to the characteristic cylinder strength of the concrete in N/mm².  
   • Rows:  
     – Four “Environment” categories, each with a descriptive note in parentheses explaining the type of exposure.  
       1. Extreme (Marine structures / moorland / pH < 4.5)  
       2. Very Severe (De-icing salts / sea water spray)  
       3. Severe (Driving rain / alternate wetting and drying)  
       4. Moderate (Fully sheltered / pH > 4.5)  

2. Interpretation of entries  
   • A numerical entry (e.g. 65, 45, 30) is the cover depth, in mm, required for that combination of environment and concrete grade.  
   • A dash “–” indicates that the combination is not applicable or not recommended by the standard (i.e., no published cover value).  
   • Parentheses around a number (e.g. (60) under Very Severe/grade 30) typically denote an alternative or less preferred recommendation, often used where data are limited or where conditions are borderline between categories.  

3. Data breakdown by environment  

   1. Extreme exposure (high chloride or acidic conditions):  
      – Grade 25: –  
      – Grade 30: –  
      – Grade 40: 65 mm  
      – Grade 50: 55 mm  

   2. Very Severe exposure (de-icing salts or sea spray):  
      – Grade 25: –  
      – Grade 30: (60 mm)  
      – Grade 40: 50 mm  
      – Grade 50: 40 mm  

   3. Severe exposure (driving rain, wetting/drying cycles):  
      – Grade 25: –  
      – Grade 30: 45 mm  
      – Grade 40: 35 mm  
      – Grade 50: 30 mm  

   4. Moderate exposure (fully sheltered, neutral or basic pH):  
      – Grade 25: 45 mm  
      – Grade 30: 35 mm  
      – Grade 40: 30 mm  
      – Grade 50: 25 mm  

4. Key trends and design implications  
   • As environmental aggressiveness increases, required cover increases. At the most extreme conditions, only higher-strength concrete grades 40 and 50 are given.  
   • Within each exposure category, cover requirements generally decrease as concrete grade increases, reflecting the better impermeability and lower permeability of higher-strength mixes.  
   • Where no value is given (dash), designers must either upgrade the concrete grade or reclassify the exposure severity before proceeding.  
   • The parenthetical value for grade 30 in “Very Severe” suggests that, although grade 30 might be marginally acceptable with 60 mm cover, designers are usually encouraged to use grade 40 or 50 to meet the unparenthesized requirements.  

This table is used in crack-width control and durability checks, notably when evaluating tension stiffening effects and prescribing nominal cover for reinforcement in BS 5400 design procedures. It ensures that cover is adequate for the environment to limit chloride ingress, carbonation, and other deterioration mechanisms over the intended service life.

 The depth d is according to the code the distance from the outmost compression fibre to the centre of gravity of the reinforcements, but not less than 0.8·h.
 There is no remark within the text of the standard if V/M includes forces from prestress. As it is generally intended to work on the ultimate forces and as there is no specific safety factor for prestress available, we use only external load contributions according to our technical knowl- edge: If you consider the ratio M/Mcr, the part of the shear force of the concrete will become zero if prestress and tensile strength is fully used from the external moment. From that follows that M must not include prestress while V is the shear force including parts of inclined tendons.
 According to the standard the shear part of the inclined tendons has to be added to the resis- tance Vc0 (uncracked) but not to the resistance Vcr (cracked), which is not followed by AQB. For the evaluation of the reinforcements V should include those parts.

According to the standard the shear part of the inclined tendons has to be added to the resis- tance Vc0 (uncracked) but not to the resistance Vcr (cracked), which is not followed by AQB. For the evaluation of the reinforcements V should include those parts..
 Theoretically one has to consider all beam sections for all load cases to select the side of the section to have compression or tension for the evaluation of Mcr and d. We use a bounding rectangle with its corners and midsides for this purpose.
 For the evaluation of the shear stress from torsion the standard has equation 9a for rectangular sections. This will provide for some ratios hmin/hmax lesser values than those provided by classical mechanics, which is compensated by much lesser admissible stresses compared to DIN/EC. AQB will not use this formula at all, due to unknown theoretical background. Instead the stresses from AQUA will be multiplied with a factor of 1.25 similar to equation 10a.
 Crack width may be evaluated according BS 5400 Part 4 5.8.8. For the tension stiffening effect a reduction is performed with an assumed tensile strength at the height of the reinforcement. What you need are the nominal cover values from table 13:

ACI and AASHTO have been published in a metric SI and in an imperial units version. SOFiSTiK uses the metric version where ever possible. The conversion of the constants within these standards is not very precise, thus you have to expect some small but remarkable devi- ations.
 As the AASHTO 2002 has foreseen allowable stress and STRENGTH-Design as alternate methods, and the appendix A of the ACI has been withdrawn 2002, we supply only the second variant. Checks for allowable stresses according to 9.15.2. for prestressed concrete members are not fully covered automatically (only 0.6 fc’).
 With the appearance of the ACI 02 several important changes have been introduced, however the old provisions still exist in Appendix B and C, which are available with a separate INI-file.
 Minimal moments according 8.17.1 of AASHTO may be selected via the literal MCR as load type at any combination. The factor is then to be defined as 1.2.
 The safety factors of the materials are expected with their inverse faktors (ACI and AAHSTO nearly identical):
 Tension, Bending and tensional bending: 0.90 Compression and compressive bending: 0.65 Shear 0.85
 Shear
 For small compressive forces the safety factor will be interpolated according to the steel strain. The old version based on the minimum from 0.1·fc·A and the normal force Pb of the ”balanced strain condition” is only available with the 318-99 version. This estate of ”balanced strain condition” will be evaluated first if the section is not fully under compressive stresses. The safety factor is then evaluated and will be kept despite of any changes of strain within the iteration.
 Minimum reinforcement according to 10.5.1 and 10.5.3 will be considered, 10.5.2 however not. The referenced area of the section will be scaled with d/h. If the relative bearing capacity is larger than 1.3 the minimum reinforcement will be reduced accordingly.

Minimum reinforcement according to 10.5.1 and 10.5.3 will be considered, 10.5.2 however not. The referenced area of the section will be scaled with d/h. If the relative bearing capacity is larger than 1.3 the minimum reinforcement will be reduced accordingly..
 Additional moments according to 10.12.3. will be only applied if a value for BETA at record BEAM is defined. We use Cm=1.0 and beta-d=0.6. Sway frames with slenderness ratios larger than 100 require a more detailed analysis via STAR2.
 Shear design will follow chapter 11.3.2. of ACI resp. 5.8.3. (2002: 8.16.6) of AASHTO. For prestressed sections we need according to 11.4.2. the values V and Mm of a different load case than that actually worked on, which is a problem for AQB. Also the evaluation of Mcr needs values from other combinations.
 To cope with all these requirements:
 1. The combination MAX-M has to be designed before the combination MAX-V. Then only AQB will remember the maximum values.
 For the calculation of Mcr uniaxial bending is assumed. The load cases of permanent
 actions have to be defined as such within the load combination to allow the evaluation of the ”unfactored dead load”.
 3. The shear part of inclined tendons will only be used for Vc. This is a deviation of the standard AQB procedure which implies that this part will have the security factor of 0.85 applied or if Vc < Vc will not be used at all.
 Shear-Friction according 11.7.4. is not yet accounted for.
 The depth d is according to the code the distance from the outmost compression fibre to the centre of gravity of the reinforcements, but not less than 0.8·h.
 AASHTO LRFD (2004) describes the shear design in chapter 5.8.3./4. in detail and rather complex. If AQUA has defined the crack spacing parameter se for a section, the design will be made using table 2, otherwise the values of Table 1 are used. The strain ε will be always taken for the mid of the shear cut.

If AQUA has defined the crack spacing parameter se for a section, the design will be made using table 2, otherwise the values of Table 1 are used. The strain ε will be always taken for the mid of the shear cut..
 Torsion within the ACI relies for the reinforcements exactly on the equivalent hollow section, but for the allowed stresses there is a simplified formula (11.6.1 resp. 11.6.3). AQB treats the value of Mt·U/1.7·A2 of 11.6.3 as real shear stress and factorises it for 11.6.1. Variant b of this formula is not accounted for. For the inclination of the struts there is always a value of 45 degrees. For prestressed sections this can be modified with input of DESI TANA 0.767 to the 37.5 degrees for the torsion. Minimum reinforcement according to 11.6.5.2. will be considered, 11.6.5.3 however not.

The input is done in a free format with the CADINP input language (see the general manual SOFiSTiK: ’FEA / STRUCTURAL Installation and Basics’).
 Three categories of units are distinguished:
 mm Fixed unit. Input is always required in the specified unit.
 [mm] Explicit unit. Input defaults to the specified unit. Alternatively, an explicit as- signment of a related unit is possible (eg. 2.5[m] ).
 [mm]1011 Implicit unit. Implicit units are categorised semantically and denoted by a cor- responding identity number (shown in green). Valid categories referring to the unit ”length” are, for example, geodetic elevation, section length and thickness. The default unit for each category is defined by the currently active (design code specific) unit set. This input default can be overridden as described above. The table summarizes all of the supported input records and their associated data‐items for one of the SOFiSTiK design modules.  It is intended as a “quick reference” that you can load into your RAG vector store so that you can retrieve, index or autocomplete record definitions when users build their input decks.  Below is a structured description of its contents.

1. Overview  
   • The table has two columns:  
     – Record: the keyword that begins each record (“ECHO”, “CTRL”, “BEAM”, “TEND”, “LC”, “S”, “COMB”)  
     – Items: all of the data‐fields or options that may appear on that record line or as continuation parameters.  
   • Input is organized in blocks (arbitrary number of records) that conclude with an END record.  An empty block (END/END) terminates the program.  The HEAD, END and PAGE records are defined elsewhere in the general manual.

2. ECHO & CTRL Records  
   • Purpose: control listing output, activate optional routines, toggle echoes  
   • Common fields:  
     – OPT    : option flag  
     – VAL    : numeric or logical value  
     – SELE   : selection code (ECHO only)  
     – VAL2   : second value parameter (CTRL only)  

3. BEAM Record  
   • Purpose: define a beam or a range of beams for design/analysis operations  
   • Indexing fields:  
     – FROM, TO, STEP  : start/end beam numbers and increment  
     – TYPE            : beam family/type code  
   • Geometric/section parameters:  
     – X, XE           : offset coordinate, end‐coordinate  
     – NCS             : section identifier  
     – BETA, BETS      : angular orientation at start/end  
     – STYP            : spring‐type or support type code  
     – PRED            : predecessor beam (for continuity)  
     – LAMS, LAMT, LAML, LAMC : warping or torsional stiffness factors at ends  
     – CS0 … CS31     : up to 32 custom section‐property overrides  

4. TEND Record  
   • Purpose: modify or read only the beam end‐point data of a previously defined BEAM  
   • Indexing fields:  
     – NO, NOB, MNO   : beam number or beam‐group number  
     – ICS1, ICS2, ICS3 : new cross‐section indices for the three local axes  
   • Coordinate shifts (local to global):  
     – X, Y, Z        : translational offsets  
     – ZZ, AZ, NY, NZ: rotational or geometric modifications  
     – YHR, ZHR, AHR, DZ, AR, UZ : additional rotation/hub‐rotation options  
     – TEMP           : temperature‐induced offset flag  

5. LC (Load Case) Record  
   • Purpose: define, reference or combine load cases  
   • Core identifiers:  
     – NO              : load‐case number  
     – TYPE            : type of load case (dead, live, wind, etc.)  
     – CST             : construction stage index  
     – REF             : reference to another load case (alias)  
     – TITL            : descriptive title text  
   • Load definition parameters:  
     – GAMU, GAMF      : partial safety factors for ULS/GLS  
     – PSI0, PSI1, PSI2: combination factors  
     – PS1S            : special combination factor  
     – GAMA            : global factor  
     – APAR, SUP, FAT  : appearance, support‐pattern, fatigue grouping  

6. S (Result Set) Record  
   • Purpose: select which section forces or results are to be printed or used in design checks  
   • Parameters:  
     – NCS             : section number or “all”  
     – NO              : load‐case number reference  
     – X, Y, Z         : nodal coordinates for result sampling  
     – N               : element‐normal orientation flag  
     – VY, VZ, MT, MY, MZ, MB : internal force and moment components  
     – MT2             : torsional moment about local 2‐axis (see context doc)  
     – REF             : reference to another result‐set  

7. COMB (Combination) Record  
   • Purpose: define linear combinations of results, or to generate design envelopes  
   • Fields:  
     – EXTR            : extraction code (min, max, envelope)  
     – SCOM            : secondary combination factor  
     – SFAC            : scale factor for design check  
     – LC1 … LC6       : up to six load‐case numbers to combine  
     – F1 … F6         : corresponding combination coefficients  

Additional context:  
– The keywords AS0 … AS9 may appear as alternate section‐type specifiers in some of the above records.  
– The record MT2 is explicitly called out in the “S” record to extract the torsional moment about the local‐2 axis.  

By capturing this table in your vector store, you enable quick retrieval of record names, allowable items, and their roles whenever a user composes or troubleshoots a SOFiSTiK input deck.

The table is the user‐input specification for defining the longitudinal reinforcement of beams in the SOFiSTiK design module.  All input records are grouped in “blocks” (which start with HEAD and end with END; the program stops on an empty block END/END).  Within each block you may select any load case and beam combination and then supply one or more of the following records.  Columns in the table are:

 • Record: the  identifier you type (MT2, AS0…AS9)  
 • Keyword: a brief English name of what the record does  
 • Format: Fortran‐style field specification (e.g. 10I3 means ten integer fields, width=3)  
 • Input: the sequence of fields you must supply for that record  
 • Description: fuller explanation of the record’s purpose  

----------------------------------------------------------------  
1.  Record = MT2  
    • Keyword: Definition  
    • Format: 10I3  
    • Input fields (10 integers, width=3):  
       1) record name (MT2)  
       2) continuous beam number  
       3) spanning‐element number  
       4) type number  
       5–14) ten bar-link positions (links 1…10)  
    • Description: Defines the longitudinal bar reinforcement in a beam (both construction-phase and service-phase).  You supply up to ten link numbers indicating specific rebar positions along the beam.  

----------------------------------------------------------------  
2.  Record = AS0  
    • Keyword: Top reinforcement left  
    • Format: 2I4  
    • Input fields (four‐digit integers):  
       1) record name (AS0)  
       2) continuous beam number  
       3) spanning‐element number  
       4) type number  
       5) first bar-link (distance for rebar layer)  
       6) second bar-link  
    • Description: Specifies the distances of the two top‐layer rebars on the left side of the beam’s cross-section.  These distances correspond to the Z‐profile definitions used for frame-surface reinforcement under positive bending moment (see general manual).  

----------------------------------------------------------------  
3.  Record = AS1  
    • Keyword: Area of top reinforcement right  
    • Format: I10  
    • Input fields (one 10‐digit integer):  
       1) record name (AS1)  
       2) continuous beam number  
       3) spanning‐element number  
       4) type number  
       5) cross‐sectional area of the top reinforcement on the right flange  
    • Description: Assigns the total steel area for the top-layer rebar at the right side of the beam.  

----------------------------------------------------------------  
4.  Record = AS2  
    • Keyword: Bottom reinforcement right  
    • Format: 2I10  
    • Input fields (two 10‐digit integers):  
       1) record name (AS2)  
       2) continuous beam number  
       3) spanning‐element number  
       4) type number  
       5) first bar-link distance for the bottom layer at the right side  
       6) second bar-link distance  
    • Description: Defines the locations (distances) of the two bottom-layer rebars on the right side of the beam.  

----------------------------------------------------------------  
5.  Record = AS3  
    • Keyword: Top reinforcement right  
    • Format: I10  
    • Input fields (one 10‐digit integer):  
       1) record name (AS3)  
       2) continuous beam number  
       3) spanning-element number  
       4) type number  
       5) steel area of the top reinforcement on the right side  
    • Description: Similar to AS1 but for the opposite flange or for a different design case (e.g. loaded vs. unloaded).  

----------------------------------------------------------------  
6.  Record = AS4  
    • Keyword: Bottom reinforcement right  
    • Format: 2I10  
    • Input fields (two 10‐digit integers):  
       Same field order as AS2, but used for the alternative load case or flange position.  
    • Description: As AS2 but for the alternate design scenario (e.g. unloaded side).  

----------------------------------------------------------------  
7.  Records AS5 through AS9  
    • Continue the same pattern: alternating “Top” vs. “Bottom,” “Left” vs. “Right,” choosing either bar-link distances (2I…) or steel areas (I…), according to the beam’s four flange corners and up to two design states (loaded/unloaded or phase 1/phase 2).  
    • Format and Input fields follow the same conventions already illustrated:  
       – bar-link distances always come in pairs (2I4 or 2I10)  
       – areas come as single fields (I10)  
    • The KEYWORD column for each will read “Top reinforcement left,” “Area of bottom reinforcement left,” etc., as required.  

----------------------------------------------------------------  
Notes:  
• All record names (MT2, AS0…AS9) must appear exactly as shown.  
• Blocks terminate on the record END; an empty block “END/END” stops processing.  
• For full explanations of HEAD, PAGE and END records and of the Z-profile conventions, refer to the SOFiSTiK “FEA / STRUCTURAL Installation and Basics” manual.

The table is organized into two columns—“Record” and “Items”—and defines six specialized SOFiSTiK input‐block records (EIGE, STRE, REIN, DESI, NSTR, CAPA) together with all permissible keywords (parameters) that may follow each record name. These records form part of a block‐structured input: each block ends with an END record, and an empty block (END/END) signals termination. HEAD, END and PAGE are covered elsewhere in the general manual. Below is a structured description of each record and its associated items:

1. EIGE (Geometry & Load Case Identification)  
   • F6: 6‐component force vector or related flag  
   • LCST / CST: Load‐case stamp or code  
   • TITL: Alphanumeric title for identification  

2. STRE (Section & Stress Definitions)  
   – Geometric transforms & orientation: MNO, PHI, EPS, REL, T, RH  
   – Thermal & initial conditions: TEMP, T0  
   – Grouping & load tracking: GRP, LCT  
   – Section model settings: SMOD (modification flag), STYP (section type), SC (section class), ST (steel grade)  
   – Buckling parameters: SBC, SBT (global/local), SBBC, SBBT (bending twist)  
   – Stress series & shear: SI, SII, TAU, SV, TAUS  
   – Time‐series & spectrum: SSTM (static time series), SSEM (seismic), SSKM, SSER, SSKR (series keys)  
   – Coordinate‐centroid control: CC, CBC, CBBC, LIMA (local inertia axis)  
   – Z‐axis modifiers: ZMAX, ZDIF  
   – Scaling & magnification: SCMG  

3. REIN (Reinforcement Parameters)  
   • MOD, RMOD: Reinforcement modification types  
   • LCR: Load case reinforcement reference  
   • ZGRP: Z‐group index  
   • SFAC: Reinforcement scale factor  
   • P6…P12: Positions or percentages of reinforcement layers  
   • TITL: Optional title for grouping  

4. DESI (Design & Code Check Settings)  
   – STAT: Status/control flags  
   – KSV, KSB: Shear design coefficients (vertical, bottom)  
   – AM1…AM4: Material partial safety factors  
   – AMAX: Maximum allowable factor

This table is the master definition of the SOFiSTiK “NORM” record, which you use to specify all the global defaults for material properties, load combinations, environmental parameters and—most importantly—the design‐code settings for a new project.  It would typically be one of the very first records in your input, because almost every other module will draw defaults from it.  Below is a breakdown of its structure and contents:

1.  Record Name  
    •  NORM – stands for “Normative settings.”  All subsequent fields tell SOFiSTiK which country, code family and code variant you want to apply.

2.  Primary fields  
    •  DC (Design Code family)  
       –  This chooses the broad family: EN (Eurocodes), DIN (German), OEN (Austrian), SIA (Swiss), AS (Australian), BS (British), IS (Indian), US (ACI, UBC…), CSA (Canadian), GB (China), NF (French), UNI (Italian), UNE (Spanish), SS (Swedish), DS (Danish), NS (Norwegian), SP (Russian), NZS (New Zealand), SFS (Finnish), NEN (Dutch), NBN (Belgian), NBR (Brazilian), ZA (South African).  
    •  NDC (National Design Code)  
       –  The specific standard designation, e.g. “EN 1992-1-1/EKS 12:2022” or “ACI 318-14.”  
    •  COUN (Country code)  
       –  For Eurocodes, some parameters (“boxed values” or national annexes) vary by country—e.g. HK/852 for Hong Kong.  
    •  CAT (Category or Class)  
       –  When a code differentiates building classes, bridge classes or safety/inspection levels, you pick one here.  The valid list of CAT entries comes from the matching INI file.  
    •  UNIT  
       –  Globally sets the unit system for input and output (only used by AQUA/TEMPLATE).  
    •  LON, LAT  
       –  Geographic longitude and latitude in degrees.  Used to calculate wind, snow or seismic actions if the loaded modules support it.  Defaults: LON = 0°, LAT = 45°.  
    •  G  
       –  Local gravity acceleration in m/s².  If omitted, the code‐default (usually 9.81 m/s²) is used; specify here only if you need a different value.

3.  How defaults are applied  
    •  On startup, SOFiSTiK reads NORM plus the country code and automatically picks an INI‐file named DC_NDC.INI (for example EN_EN1992-1-1.INI).  That file contains all default materials, partial safety factors, combination rules, load‐case coefficients, etc.  
    •  If you change DC/NDC after you have already defined actions or materials, the software issues a warning: you risk mismatches between design rules and defined loads.  Temporary redefinition for steel vs. concrete is possible but should be used sparingly.  
    •  “Boxed values” (national variants) can be manually overridden later with the TVAR record.  
    •  If you really want to ignore things like wind/snow/seismic elevations, set them to “NONE” in the INI file or record.

4.  Supported code families and variants (excerpt)  
    •  Eurocodes (EN)  
       –  EN 1990 through EN 1999 with national annexes for many countries.  Categories range from buildings (CAT A1–A3) to road bridges (B1–B4), footbridges (C1–C4), railway bridges (D1–D4).  
    •  German (DIN)  
       –  DIN 1045-1 (2008) for concrete, DIN 1052 (1988) for timber, DIN FB 102 (2009) boxed values for bridges.  
    •  Austrian (OEN)  
       –  OENORM B 4750 (prestressed concrete), B 4300 (steel).  
    •  US/ACI  
       –  ACI 318-08 and ACI 318-14 for concrete; UBC/IBC (UBC not explicitly listed but encompassed under “US Standards”).  
    •  Canadian (CSA S6-19) – Highway bridge code.  
    •  Indian (IS), Spanish (UNE), French (NF), Italian (UNI), Chinese (GB), Brazilian (NBR), South African (ZA), etc.  
    •  New Zealand (NZS) – with or without prestress (CAT 0).  
    •  Nordic (SS, DS, NS) – each has EN199X‐200X with national annexes and multi-tier safety/control categories.

5.  Implementation flags  
    •  For each DC/NDC entry, the table marks “A” if it’s implemented in AQUA (analysis) and “B” if in BEMESS (design).  
    •  If a feature (fatigue, buckling checks, creep/shrinkage, crack‐width, etc.) isn’t implemented for your chosen code, SOFiSTiK falls back to the Eurocode default behavior—though it may not cover every clause.

6.  Special notes  
    •  If you use historic codes without an INI file, you can still select them with CAT=USER and supply all partial factors yourself.  
    •  Unit definitions (UNIT record) and language (d_LANG) only propagate in AQUA/TEMPLATE; other modules read units from the INI files or assume the software default.  
    •  Page formatting (PAGE record) is local to each module.

In practice, your NORM record may look like this:

NORM  DC=EN  NDC=1992-1-1  COUN=EKS12  CAT=A1  LAT=60  LON=10  G=9.807  UNIT=MNmKN  

This tells SOFiSTiK:  
– Use Eurocode 2 Part 1-1 with the Swedish national annex EKS 12, building class A1, at 60° N, 10° E and use local gravity, plus MN–m–kN units. All material strengths, γ-factors, combination factors, etc. will then come from EN_EN1992-1-1.INI (with the EKS12 boxed values).

The table shown at the end of your input is the core “global settings” record for SOFiSTiK input files.  It defines six parameters that a user should specify at the very beginning of a project so that all subsequent modules (analysis, design, output) pick up the correct environmental and user‐preference data.  If left at their defaults (marked “*”), each module will read its default values from the matching INI-file (named by design code family and country code), but explicit specification here will override those defaults globally.  Below is a detailed description of each column and row:

Columns  
1. Item – the four-letter keyword that appears in the SOFiSTiK input stream.  
2. Description – a human‐readable label for that keyword.  
3. Unit – the unit or data type expected.  If it reads “–”, the parameter is unitless.  
4. Default – the value applied if the user does not explicitly supply one.  An asterisk (*) means “take the default from the active INI-file for the chosen design code / country.”

Rows  
1. ALT  
   • Description: Altitude above sea level.  Used by some codes (e.g. snow combinations that depend on elevation).  
   • Unit: meters (m).  
   • Default: 0.0 m.  If you leave it at 0.0, the program assumes sea level; if you specify “*”, the INI-file default (which may be nonzero for certain countries) is used.

2. WIND  
   • Description: Wind zone.  Many national codes define discrete wind regions or categories.  
   • Unit: Lit4 (a lookup code for a “boxed value”—see the INI file for the allowed zone labels).  
   • Default: *  (use the code’s default zone).

3. SNOW  
   • Description: Snow zone.  Defines the map region or category for snow load calculation.  
   • Unit: Lit4 (lookup category).  
   • Default: *  (take the snow zone from the design code’s national annex).

4. SEIS  
   • Description: Seismic zone.  Required by earthquake-design modules; identifies the local seismicity map region.  
   • Unit: Lit4 (lookup zone code).  
   • Default: *  (use the code’s built-in default or national annex).

5. WCAT  
   • Description: Terrain category for wind.  Many wind standards require the user to classify the local terrain roughness.  
   • Unit: Lit4 (lookup category A, B, C, D, etc.).  
   • Default: *  (pick the category defined by the active INI file).

6. UNIT  
   • Description: Selection of a set of units for all subsequent input and output (e.g. kN/m, MPa).  If omitted, each module’s INI file defines its own default unit system.  
   • Unit: — (unitless keyword list).  
   • Default: *  (use the INI-file’s default unit system).

7. LANG  
   • Description: Selection of an output-language default (e.g. EN, DE, FR).  Applied only in the AQUA and TEMPLATE modules.  
   • Unit: — (unitless).  
   • Default: *  (use the INI-file’s default language).

Key Points from the Full Context  
• All environmental parameters (ALT, WIND, SNOW, SEIS, WCAT) affect load definitions, combination coefficients and design values in the analysis and design modules.  
• Changing these after defining actions or load cases may lead to inconsistent results—set them at the start of your project.  
• “Lit4” and similar designations refer to “boxed values” in the INI files: national annex look-ups that vary by country.  
• By overriding the “*” defaults here, you ensure that every module sees the same values without having to repeat them in each individual record.  
• If you truly want to disable a category (for instance, ignore snow zoning), specify the keyword NONE instead of an actual zone code.

The excerpt you provided is part of SOFiSTiK’s “NORM” table, which governs how the program selects and applies design‐code defaults, national annexes (“boxed values”), unit systems, and implementation modules when you specify a particular design standard (via the NORM…DC/NDC record). Below is a breakdown of the table’s structure and its two sample rows for the generic Eurocode building and bridge families. 

1. Table Layout and Columns  
   • NDC (Design Code): A code identifier (e.g. “EN 199X-200X” or “EN 199X-200X-BRIDGE”). This value is entered in the NORM record’s DC and drives selection of the matching INI file (DC_NDC.INI).  
   • Description: A multi‐line text field summarizing:  
     – The overall scope (building vs. bridge construction)  
     – Which Eurocode parts are covered (e.g. EN 1992, EN 1993, EN 1994) for structural materials and safety formats  
     – Which “actions and combinations” documents apply (EN 1990, EN 1991‐x)  
     – Which material standards are included (timber EN 1995-1-1 or ‑2, brickwork EN 1996-1-1, aluminium EN 1999-1-1)  
     – Any special sub-parameters (e.g. COUN for country deviations).  
   • UNIT: A numeric code for the global unit system. “5” denotes the SI‐based set (kN, m, °C, etc.). If you define UNIT=5 in AQUA or TEMPLATE, that unit set applies to all modules.  
   • Design: One or more letters indicating in which SOFiSTiK modules this standard is implemented:  
     – “A” means AQB (the concrete/steel design engine) supports it  
     – “B” means BEMESS (reinforced‐and‐post‐tensioned concrete design) supports it  

2. Row 1 — EN 199X-200X (Eurocode Building Construction)  
   • Scope: General building works under the Eurocode framework.  
   • EN 1992-1-1: Ultimate and serviceability design of concrete structures  
   • EN 1993-1-1: Steel structures  
   • EN 1994-1-1: Composite steel‐and‐concrete structures  
   • Actions & combinations: per EN 1990 (Basis of structural design) and EN 1991-1-x (general actions)  
   • Material standards: EN 1995-1-1 (timber), EN 1996-1-1 (masonry), EN 1999-1-1 (aluminium)  
   • COUN IL/972: Special boxed values for Israel’s load‐train tables (only when COUN is set to IL/972)  
   • UNIT = 5 (SI units)  
   • Design = A,B (supported in both AQB and BEMESS)  

3. Row 2 — EN 199X-200X-BRIDGE (Eurocode Bridge Construction)  
   • Scope: Bridge structures—road, foot, and railway bridges under Eurocode annexes.  
   • EN 1992-2: Concrete bridges  
   • EN 1993-2: Steel bridges  
   • EN 1994-2: Composite steel‐and‐concrete bridges  
   • Actions & loads: per EN 1990 and EN 1991-2 (bridge‐specific actions)  
   • Material standards: EN 1995-2 (timber bridges), EN 1996-1-1 (masonry), EN 1999-1-1 (aluminium)  
   • CAT B/C/D: Category code to switch between road bridges (B), footbridges (C), and railway bridges (D), each invoking its own set of boxed values for load models and combination factors.  
   • UNIT = 5 (SI units)  
   • Design = A,B (supported in both AQB and BEMESS)  

4. How SOFiSTiK Uses This Table  
   • At project start you define NORM with DC=NDC (and optional COUN, CAT, LAT, LON, ALT, etc.).  
   • SOFiSTiK loads the matching INI file (e.g. DC_EN 199X-200X.INI) to pull all default coefficients, safety factors, partial factors, load models, climate data, etc.  
   • Changing the design code after load‐case definition is discouraged because many parameters (materials, combinations, national variants) are baked into those INI files.  
   • If a design code isn’t explicitly implemented for a given task or module, SOFiSTiK falls back to the Eurocode base provisions.  

By indexing these codes in a RAG‐friendly vector store, you can quickly retrieve:  
   – Which standards and sub‐documents a project is using  
   – What unit system has been set globally  
   – Which SOFiSTiK modules will actually execute that design code  
   – Any country‐ or category‐specific overrides.  

This structure ensures consistency across all actions, load combinations, material definitions, and national annex parameters throughout the SOFiSTiK analysis and design workflow.

This table documents the SOFiSTiK “NORM” input record, which you use at the very start of a project to tell the software which national or international design codes (and variants thereof) should govern materials, load combinations, safety factors, etc.  Its structure is as follows:

1. Columns (fields)  
   • NORM Item – the keyword you put in your input (e.g. LT, CAT, LON, LAT, G, COUN, NDC).  
   • Description – a brief human‐readable label.  
   • DC – short design‐code family key (e.g. EN, DIN, OEN, SIA, AS, BS, IS, US, CSA, etc.).  
   • Design code family – the full name of each code family in its own column.  
   • NDC – the code’s designation (e.g. EN 1992-1-1, DIN 1045-1, OENORM B 4750).  
   • COUN – country code for selecting “boxed values” or national annex variants under EN (e.g. HK/852).  
   • UNIT – unit group to use for input/output (only processed in AQUA/TEMPLATE).  
   • Default – default value applied if you omit the item.

2. Core Input Items  
   • LT – sets limit‐state identifier (default: EN Lt16).  
   • CAT – category or class within the chosen code (e.g. safety class, application class; defined per code in its INI file).  
   • LON, LAT – geographic longitude/latitude (decimal degrees; defaults 0 °, 45 °).  
   • G – local gravity acceleration in m/s² (default from code, override only for true local value).

3. How Defaults Are Selected  
   – SOFiSTiK reads an INI‐file named “DC_NDC.INI” (e.g. EN_1992-1-1.INI) to pick default material parameters, safety factors, combination rules and “boxed values” per country.  
   – You must supply NORM (with DC, NDC, COUN, CAT, etc.) before defining load cases or actions. Changing the code mid‐project is discouraged.  
   – Boxed values can be tweaked via the TVAR record; historic or unsupported codes may use CAT USER to accept free‐text categories.

4. Enumerated Code Families and Variants  
   For each DC column you find one or more rows like:  
   • DIN 1045-1 (2008) – concrete (A,B modules), CAT = A/B/C/D/E/F per Table 18.  
   • DIN FB 102-2009 – reinforcement classification (A,B).  
   • OENORM B 4750 (2000) – prestressed concrete (A).  
   • OENORM B 4300 (1994) – steel (A).  
   • US ACI 318-08, 318-14 – concrete (A).  
   • CSA S6-19 – Canadian highway bridge (A).  
   • SS EN199X-200X/EKS 12:2022 – Swedish building codes, with CAT A1/A2/A3 for safety classes.  
   • SS EN199X-200X-BRIDGE/TSFS 2018:57 – Swedish bridge codes, CAT B1–B4 (road bridges), C1–C4 (footbridges), D1–D4 (rail bridges).  
   • DS EN 199X/NA – Danish building and bridge annexes, CAT LE/NE/HE, LN/NN/HN, LR/NR/HR for combinations of safety & control levels, plus special CATs for road/foot/rail bridges.  
   • NZS, NEN, NBN, NS, SP, IS, UNE, etc., each with their own NDC and CAT definitions.

5. Supported Advanced Features  
   At the end, the table summarizes which advanced design features are implemented in each code family for steel/timber (e.g. F-ASD, LRD, c/t limits, λ buckling curves, σdyn fatigue, BDK lateral‐torsional buckling) and concrete (bending, shear, creep/shrinkage, tendon relaxation, crack‐width calculations). If a feature is not explicitly provided, SOFiSTiK falls back on the Eurocode provision where possible—but you must always verify manually that your chosen code’s requirements have indeed been honored.

In practice, you begin every project by inserting a NORM record that specifies at least DC, NDC (the exact standard), plus any country code (COUN) and category (CAT). The system then loads all matching defaults from the corresponding INI file, ensuring that material models, load combinations and safety factors conform to the selected code family and national annex.

The NORM record in SOFiSTiK serves as the central switch for selecting and parameterizing all code‐based design defaults—materials, load combinations, safety factors and so on. It is typically the very first record in any project (“must be specified at the beginning”) and should not be changed after actions or load cases have been defined unless the user fully understands the implications.  

Key Fields of the NORM Table  
• DC (Design code family) – Abbreviation of the standard series (EN, DIN, OEN, SIA, AS, BS, IS, US, CSA, GB, NF, UNI, UNE, SS, DS, NS, SP, NZS, SFS, NEN, NBN, NBR, ZA).  
• NDC (Designation) – Specific part or year of the code (e.g., EN1992-1-1, DIN1045-2008, ACI318-14).  
• COUN (Country code) – For “boxed values” (national variants) inside EN; for example “HK/852” for Hong Kong, “IL/972” for Israel, “00” for general EN.  
• CAT (Category/Class) – When a code requires classification (e.g. building-safety classes, bridge types). The valid CAT items are pulled from the matching INI file; “USER” can be used for legacy codes without an INI.  
• Lt4, Lt16, – Control flags for special options or warnings.  
• LON, LAT – Geographic longitude/latitude in degrees (defaults 0° and 45°). Some modules may adjust wind, snow or seismic loads based on these.

• UNIT, d_LANG, PAGE – Unit set, language and pagination controls (effective globally or per‐module in AQUA/TEMPLATE).  

Data Sourcing and INI Files  
Almost all code parameters—partial factors, combination rules, material properties—are drawn from INI files in the SOFiSTiK directory. The file name pattern is DC_NDC.INI (e.g. EN_EN1992-1-1.INI). When you change DC or NDC, the matching INI is loaded. National annex variants (boxed values) are overridden by country codes in the same way. If a code lacks an INI (e.g. some OEN 4200 series), built-in fallbacks inside AQB/BEMESS handle the minimal requirements.  

Examples of Implemented Codes and Features  
Codes implemented in both AQB (A) and BEMESS (B) include EN1992-1-1/EKS12 (concrete), EN1993-1-1/EKS12 (steel), SS EN1994-1-1/EKS12 (composite), and similar suite for bridges (SS EN199X-200X-BRIDGE). Each record lists the UNIT (“Design”), default COUN=0, whether A/B support, plus CAT values:  
– SS CAT A1–A3 for building safety classes  
– SS CAT B1–B4 for road bridges, C1–C4 for footbridges, D1–D4 for rail bridges  
– DS CAT LE/NE/HE (extended), LN/NN/HN (normal), LR/NR/HR (reduced) control levels  
– NZS/C.S.A./ACI entries cover New Zealand, Canada, US standards with basic support.  

Advanced Feature Matrix  
Where available, modules go beyond simple stress checks. For steel and timber they support:  
  • F-ASD (allowable stresses)  
  • LRD (limit-state factor design)  
  • c/t buckling slenderness, λ curves, σdyn fatigue, BDK lateral-torsional buckling.  
For concrete:  
  • SK slenderness moment effects  
  • CC creep/shrinkage, CZ relaxation, VB bond stress  
  • CW/CT crack widths, DY fatigue sway stress.  

If a code does not supply a given feature, Eurocode defaults are used. Users must always verify that all needed provisions (wind, snow, earthquake, load combinations) are indeed applied by their chosen module.

This table defines the SOFiSTiK “NORM” record and related fields used to select and parameterize national and international design codes in structural analyses. It is organized into three main parts: 1) general input fields and defaults, 2) code‐family entries with their country‐specific annexes and implementation flags, and 3) feature-support matrices for advanced checks.

1. General Input Fields  
• NORM (record name): selects overall design code family and variant.  
• Item/Description: human-readable name of the code or annex.  
• DC: shorthand code (e.g. EN, DIN, OEN, SS, DS, US, CSA, NZS, NEN, etc.).  
• NDC: designation of a specific code release (e.g. EN1992-1-1, ACI 318-14).  
• COUN: optional country code for “boxed” national values under Eurocodes (e.g. HK/852, IL/972).  
• CAT: category or safety/class level required by certain codes (values defined in matching INI-files, e.g. A/B/C…, A1/A2/A3, B1–B4, LE/NE/HE, etc.).  
• LON, LAT: geographic longitude/latitude in degrees for wind/snow/ seismic zone look-ups (defaults 0°/45°).  
• G: local gravity acceleration in m/s² (defaults to standard value).  
• UNIT (not shown above): global units set for AQUA/TEMPLATE modules.  
• LANG/PAGE: language or page definitions scoped to a module.

All defaults for materials, load combinations, partial factors and boxed values are drawn at startup from an INI-file named DC_NDC.INI (e.g. “EN_1992-1-1.INI”). Users must supply NORM, country code, location and material data at project start. Changing the design code after actions or load cases are defined is unsupported. Boxed values (national variants) can be overridden via the TVAR record.

2. Implemented Design Codes & Annexes  
Each entry lists: code family (DC), country standard reference, NDC release year, module support flags A (AQB) and B (BEMESS), and whether CAT applies. Examples:  
• DIN 1045-1 (2008) – German concrete – CAT A–F – A, B  
• OEN B 4750 (2000) – Austrian prestressed concrete – A  
• SS EN1992-1-1/EKS 12:2022 – Swedish concrete – CAT A1–A3 – A, B  
• DS EN 1990/NA:2007 – Danish combination rules – CAT LE/NE/HE/LN/NN/HN/LR/NR/HR – A, B  
• US ACI 318-14 – American concrete – A  
• CSA S6-19 – Canadian highway bridges – A  
• NZS – New Zealand standards – CAT 0 (no prestress) – A, B  
Older codes without INI-files (e.g. OEN 4200 series) are handled by AQB program logic.

Bridge variants are defined by appending “-BRIDGE” to the Eurocode or national code and carry specific CAT values for road, rail and pedestrian classes.

3. Advanced Feature Support  
For codes marked in the table, SOFiSTiK implements:  
• F-ASD and LRD factor methods  
• c/t plate slenderness limits and λ buckling curves  
• σdyn fatigue stress checks  
• BDK lateral-torsional buckling routines  
• Concrete creep/shrinkage (CC), relaxation (CZ), bond stress (VB), crack width (CW/CT) and fatigue (DY) models.

If a requested feature is not available for a specific code, the software falls back to the corresponding Eurocode implementation. Users should always verify that the module-level implementation covers the full regulatory requirements.

Below is a breakdown of its structure and contents:

1. Columns (Features)  
   • Design Code – identifier of the code or national annex. Bridge-specific variants are indicated by “-BRIDGE.”  
   • F-ASD – Factors for different permissible (allowable stress) design.  
   • LRD – Load Resistance Factor Design (limit-state partial-factor method).  
   • c/t – Limit slenderness ratio for plate elements (width-to-thickness).  
   • λ – Centric buckling curves (eigen-buckling-based section curves).  
   • σdyn – Fatigue-stress evaluation under dynamic loading.  
   • BDK – Lateral-torsional buckling check (program BDK integration).  

   An “X” marks a feature as implemented. A “–” means that feature is not supported for that code; in that case, Eurocode provisions are substituted if available. Parentheses, e.g. “(X),” indicate partial or conditional support (for instance only under certain country variants). Occasional text entries (e.g. “DIN 4132”) cite a reference standard used instead of the generic module.

The input defines two logically‐separate pieces of information. First comes the description of the “NORM” record, which is the mechanism by which SOFiSTiK selects its material, load and design‐code defaults. Immediately below that is a matrix that lists which advanced steel‐and‐timber design checks have been implemented for each code.  

1. NORM Record  
• Purpose: Specifies the overall design standard (DC), any national variant (NDC), geographic location (LAT, LON, altitude via CAT or load‐zone records) and unit conventions (UNIT) that the entire model will follow.  
• Key Fields:  
  – DC (Design Code Family): e.g. EN (Eurocodes), DIN, BS, ACI, NZS, etc.  
  – NDC (National Designation): boxed values for country variants (e.g. EN-1992-1-1/DE, EN-1993-1-1/UK, or HK/852).  
  – CAT: Category or Class within the code (e.g. safety class, building vs. bridge, user‐defined entries).  
  – LAT/LON: Latitude/Longitude in degrees.  
  – G: Local gravity acceleration in m/s², defaults per code if omitted.  
  – UNIT: Optional global units selection (length, force, stress) used by AQUA/TEMPLATE; otherwise defaults in INI‐files.  
• Mechanics: Once NORM is set, SOFiSTiK reads the matching INI‐file (named DC_NDC.INI) for default material properties, combination coefficients, load parameters (snow, wind, earthquake), and design‐code‐specific provisions. Changing NORM after defining actions or load cases is discouraged because defaults will not retroactively update. National or user‐specific “boxed values” may be overridden with TVAR records.

• LRD: Load‐resistance‐factor design capability

How to Read the Table:  
– A mark “X” under a column indicates that the code has native support for that check.

Usage in Workflow:  
• During model setup, specify NORM with the desired DC/NDC/CAT and geographic data.  
• The program automatically picks up which of the six advanced checks are truly code‐compliant.

Row-by-row summary  
1. EN 199X-200X (Eurocode base)  
   • SK: – (no slenderness-moment extension)  
   • CC, CZ: X (creep/shrinkage and tendon relaxation built in)  
   • VB: – (bond stress not separately treated)

2. EN 199X-200X-BRIDGE  
   • Mirrors the base Eurocode: creep/shrinkage (CC), tendon relaxation (CZ) and crack/fatigue checks are supported; slenderness and bond stress are not.

   • Exactly the same support profile as the EN 199X-200X row.  

4. DIN EN 199X-200X-BRIDGE

5. DIN 1045 (1988) (older German standard for concrete)  
   • SK, CC = X (includes slenderness-moment and creep/shrinkage handling)  
   • CZ, VB = – (no tendon relaxation or bond-stress routine)  
   • CT, CW = X (crack-width by tabulated and by calculation)  
   • DY = – (no fatigue-sway stress)

How to read and use this in practice  
• Before running a concrete design or checking module, the software checks this matrix.  
• If “X” appears, the code-specific clause (e.g. national annex formulas for creep) is used.  
• If “–” appears, the calculation defaults to the underlying Eurocode implementation.  
• Users relying on a “–” entry must verify that the fallback Eurocode method satisfies project or regulatory requirements.

The table is a feature‐support matrix showing, for a wide range of national and international design codes, which “advanced” analysis options have been implemented in the SOFiSTiK programs (beyond the basic bending‐and‐shear checks). Each row is a single design code (with year of issue), and each column is one of seven special features. An “X” means that the feature is available under that code; a “–” means it isn’t.  

Columns (features)  
• SK: Extra moments from slenderness (e.g. second‐order P–Δ effects)  
• CC: Creep and shrinkage coefficients (time‐dependent deformation)  
• CZ: Relaxation coefficients for prestressing tendons  
• VB: Bond‐stress calculation (interaction between concrete and reinforcement)  
• CT: Crack‐width by tabulated (code‐based) stress checks  
• CW: Crack‐width by detailed calculation  
• DY: Sway‐stress for fatigue checks  

Rows (examples)  
• DIN series (Germany)  
 – DIN 4227 +A1 (1995): supports CC, VB and CW.  
 – DIN 1045-1 (2001) and DIN 1045-2008 (2008): full set SK, CC, CZ, CT, CW, DY.  
 – DIN FB102-2009, FB102-2003: CC, CZ, CT, CW, DY (no SK or VB).  
 – DIN FB104-2009/2003: same as FB102 but crack‐tabulation only in 2009 version.  

• OEN (Austria) and SIA (Switzerland)  
 – OEN EN199X-200X (general Eurocode family): CC, CZ, CT, CW, DY.  
 – OEN 4700 (2001): SK, CC, CT, CW (no CZ, VB or DY).  
 – OEN 4750 (2000): CC, CT, CW.  
 – SIA 26X (SIA 262 2013): CC, CT only.  

• BS (UK), SP (Spain), UNE (Spain), UNI (Italy)  
 – BS EN199X-200X and trunk “‐BRIDGE” annex: CC, CZ, CT, CW, DY.  
 – BS 8110 (1997), BS 5400 (1990), SP 63-13330 (2012), UNE EHE (1999): only CW.  
 – UNI DM-2018: CC, CT, CW, DY.  

• NF (France)  
 – NF EN199X-200X and “-BRIDGE”: CC, CZ, CT, CW, DY.  
 – NF BAEL (1999): CZ, CT, CW only.  

• Nordic countries (SS, DS, SFS, NEN, NBN, NS)  
 – General EN 199X codes (“building” and “bridge” national annexes): CC, CZ, CT, CW, DY.  

• US and Canada  
 – US ACI 318-08 and ACI 318-14: SK only (no creep, crack or fatigue modules).  
 – CSA S6-19 (Canadian Bridge Code): design not supported in current release (all “–”).  

Key observations  
• Most Eurocode-based national annexes (EN1990–199X) support ∙CC, CZ, CT, CW and DY, with only a handful supporting SK or VB.  
• Legacy codes (e.g. BS 8110, SP 63, UNE EHE) only offer crack‐width by calculation (CW) and no other advanced features.  
• US ACI codes only implement second‐order effects (SK) but lack time-dependent or crack/fatigue checks.  
• If a specific code lacks a feature, SOFiSTiK falls back to the Eurocode provision (where implemented).

The table defines how the three design-check routines (STRE, NSTR, DESI) treat bending demands on a cross-section, depending on whether principal‐axis rotation (FSYM) is allowed or suppressed. It is most often used in AQUA’s RAG workflows to tag sections for either biaxial or uniaxial bending checks. Below is a structured description of its contents, column by column and row by row, including all relevant notes:

1. Key Parameter  
   • FSYM (flag) – “Suppress rotation of principal axes”  
     – FSYM = NO (default): the cross‐section is free to rotate its principal axes under combined bending.  
     – FSYM = YES: the principal axes are fixed in orientation; one bending direction is suppressed.

2. Column Headings (Design Routines)  
   • STRE – Stress check under combined actions (e.g. interaction formula level)  
   • NSTR – Ultimate strength check (no rotation of principal axes if FSYM = YES)  
   • DESI – Detailed design check (same bending assumption as for NSTR)

3. Table Rows  
   A. cross-section with FSYM = NO (default in AQUA)  
     – STRE: biaxial bending  
     – NSTR: biaxial bending  
     – DESI: biaxial bending  
     Interpretation: when axes are free, all three checks account for bending about both principal axes (M_y and M_z).

   B. cross-sections with FSYM = YES (rotation of principal axes suppressed)  
     – STRE: biaxial bending  
     – NSTR: uniaxial bending ⁽¹⁾ (Mz = Vy = 0)  
     – DESI: uniaxial bending ⁽¹⁾ (Mz = Vy = 0)  
     Interpretation:  
       • STRE still evaluates both M_y and M_z (for stress interaction), but  
       • NSTR and DESI treat the section as loaded in a single plane (uniaxial), setting moment about the minor axis (M_z) and corresponding shear (V_y) to zero.

4. Footnote  
   (¹) “Uniaxial bending” here means a bending check about the principal axis that remains active; the other axis is held at zero moment and shear. This is an enforced simplification that avoids principal‐axis rotation in strength and detailed design checks.

5. Contextual Linkage  
   • This table ties directly into the broader “Type of bending” controls under the “3.6.2 Forces” section of AQUA’s input language. In particular:  
     – AXIA +1 / AXIA –1 governs whether uniaxial or biaxial bending is invoked and whether rotations of principal axes are allowed.  
     – FSYM = YES corresponds to AXIA –1 (suppress rotation).  
   • Users choose one of the material‐group codes (MSEL: CONC, STEL, COMP, TIMB, ALUM) then specify the bending mode via AXIA and the smoothing/conversion rules (SMOO, VRED, VM, VAL, etc.). The FSYM flag finalizes whether NSTR and DESI collapse to a simpler uniaxial check.

6. Practical Implications  
   – For complex, two‐way bending demands on reinforced sections, leave FSYM = NO so NSTR/DESI preserve biaxial checks.  
   – For members known to carry bending predominantly about one axis (e.g. simply supported beams with negligible torsion), setting FSYM = YES can streamline design without sacrificing safety under the chosen design code (EN 1992–1999).  
   – The choice impacts reinforcement layout, principal stress calculation, and the use of shift‐rule coefficients (VM, VAL, VAL2) downstream in AQUA.

By capturing this table in your RAG vector store, you enable rapid retrieval of the correct bending‐mode logic whenever a user’s AQUA input includes an FSYM flag.

The input table and accompanying notes define a compact yet comprehensive set of switches and numeric parameters used to control cross-section design and action combinations in a structural analysis or design program. Below is a structured description of each entry, grouped by logical function:

1. MSEL – Type of design  
  • Governs which classes of material sections are included in the design process.  
  • Default treats all materials; restricting the range is possible by choosing one of the codes below:  
    – CONC: reinforced concrete only (EN 1992)  
    – STRS (or STRE): structural steel only (EN 1993)  
    – COMP: composite steel-concrete only (EN 1994)  
    – TIMB (or TIM): timber only (EN 1995)  
    – ALUM: aluminum only (EN 1999)

2. 3.6.2 Forces – how bending, shear and torsion are combined and processed  
  A. AXIA – axis of bending  
    • “AXIA +1” enables uniaxial bending only.  
    • “AXIA –1” suppresses the rotation of principal axes (keeps axes fixed, yz = 0).  

  B. Action grouping (for load combinations AQB/AQBS)  
    • Each distinct basic action identifier is treated separately.  
    • By default, actions of the same category (e.g. dead loads) are merged into one group.  
    • Setting “2” forces all actions listed in the same table row at record LC to be treated as one group.

  C. STRE / NSTR / DESI – bending mode for strength (STRE), normal‐force design (NSTR) and design checks (DESI)  
    • STRE: biaxial bending is considered in cross-section strength verification.  
    • NSTR: only uniaxial bending is used (Mz = Vy = 0), principal axes fixed (unless AXIA allows rotation).  
    • DESI: same as NSTR—uniaxial bending checks only (Mz = Vy = 0).  

  D. SMOO – moment smoothing at supports  
    • 0: no smoothing.  
    • 1: smooth principal bending moments only (default).  
    • 2: smooth both principal and lateral bending.  
    • Flags +128, +256, +512 can suppress reference‐system conversion of shear or moments at inclined axes.  
    • Smoothing applies only if a support edge is defined; shear at that edge is set to zero.

  E. VRED – maximum inclination (cot θ) for converting shear in haunched sections (default 0.3333)  
    • 0.0: no conversion.  
    • +512: suppress moment conversion at the inclined axis.  
    • Note: smoothing rules from SMOO still apply at supports.

  F. SVRF – non‐prestressed reinforcement factor for concrete sections CS0–CS15  
    • Default 0.0 or inherited from AQUA CTRL RFCS (gross section only).  
    • If CTRL EIGE 64 is set, reinforcement effects on creep and shrinkage are suppressed.

  G. VM, VAL, VAL2 – shift‐rule parameters to account for shear and torsion in longitudinal reinforcement design  
    • VM: coefficient for combined shear and torsion.  
    • VAL: from shear, default 0.0 (ignored). Otherwise specify cot θ or percentage factor. “STD” means offset only.  
    • VAL2: from torsion, similarly—negative values apply only to NSTR.

3. Cover, member classification and limit values  
  • CNOM: a single fixed cover value applied to all sections.  
  • In AQB’s BEAM record the user flags each member as bending or compression; the default is auto‐determined by gravity-axis orientation, eccentricity (ED) and axial force ratio (NGRE·A·βr).  
  • VERT: maximum vertical deviation of the beam axis to still treat it as bending (default 0.3333).  
  • NLIM: lower limit of axial force (relative to the plastic axial capacity) below which a member is no longer classed as a compression member (default 0.001).  
  • ED: relative eccentricity threshold (e/d) for distinguishing compression vs. bending members if not overridden in the BEAM record (default 3.5).
