The input table provides a concise overview of the key fields accepted by the TVAR command (with SCOP = DESI) when temporarily overriding boxed-value variables defined under Eurocode pseudovariables. It enumerates four items—NAME, VAL, SCOP and CMNT—together with their intended meaning, data‐type (“Unit”) and default fill‐in value when omitted. Detailed breakdown follows:

1. Column headers  
   • Item  
     – The literal keyword used in the AQB/INI file record (e.g. NAME, VAL, etc.).  
   • Description  
     – A plain‐language explanation of the item’s purpose or content.  
   • Unit  
     – The internal data type or maximum storage length for that field (Lit16, Lit64, Lit32 or no specific unit).  
   • Default  
     – What value the system substitutes if the user omits this item in a TVAR statement.  

2. Row definitions  

   a) NAME  
      • Purpose: Specifies the identifier of the boxed‐value variable to be adjusted. These names correspond to entries in master.ini under the DESI scope (e.g. ALF-CE, GAM-CE, GAM-SF, etc.).  
      • Data type: Lit16 → up to 16 characters text.  
      • Default: “!” → An exclamation mark signals a mandatory field; omission triggers a syntax or semantic error.  

   b) VAL  
      • Purpose: Assigns either a literal numeric factor or a formula (prefixed by an equals sign “=”) to define how the variable is modified. For example, VAL 0.85 or VAL "=1.0+0.05" are both valid.  
      • Data type: Lit64 → allows up to 64 characters, accommodating fairly complex expressions.  
      • Default: “!” → Like NAME, VAL is mandatory and cannot be skipped.  

   c) SCOP  
      • Purpose: Indicates the scope or domain in which this overridden variable applies. In the context of temporary AQUA batch commands, SCOP must explicitly be set to DESI to target design‐phase factors.  
      • Data type: none (—) → free‐form keyword.  
      • Default: “*” → If omitted, the asterisk acts as a wildcard, but best practice is to specify SCOP DESI explicitly to avoid ambiguity.  

   d) CMNT  
      • Purpose: Free‐text comment field allowing the user to document the reason or context for the override. This can help with traceability when multiple TVAR statements are used in complex load‐combination setups.  
      • Data type: Lit32 → up to 32 characters.  
      • Default: “–” → A dash denotes no comment was provided.  

3. How this ties into the RAG / NORM workflow  
   • “See also: NORM” reminds users that nationally determined parameters can also be handled through NORM definitions. NORM typically carries permanently adopted national values, whereas TVAR with SCOP DESI lets you stage temporary overrides within an AQB calculation script.  
   • The TVAR mechanism (and the table above) is crucial for advanced users who need to:  
     – Adapt partial factors (e.g. “ALF-CE” for modulus reduction, “GAM-SF” for load factors) on the fly.  
     – Run parametric studies without editing the master.ini.  
     – Document overrides in comments for compliance checks.  

4. Practical example (referenced in context)  
   • To reduce the elasticity modulus for the calculation curve, two TVAR lines might appear at the top of an AQB file:  
     – TVAR NAME "ALF-CE" VAL 0.85 SCOP DESI  
     – TVAR NAME "GAM-CE" VAL 1.25 SCOP DESI  
   • Here, NAME and VAL are both mandatory, SCOP is explicitly set to DESI, and a CMNT could be appended if desired.  

By capturing each column’s role and default behavior, this table ensures that users of the RAG‐powered vector store and TVAR command have an unambiguous reference for on‐the‐fly Eurocode parameter adjustments.

The table summarizes a selection of the most commonly used design (“DESI”) scope variables defined in the Eurocode‐based AQUA master.ini file and, where permitted, adjustable via the AQB TVAR command. Each entry consists of three fields—NAME, default VALUE, and a brief COMMENT explaining its role in strength and safety calculations. Below is a row‐by‐row breakdown:

1. GAM-C  
   • VALUE: 1.50  
   • COMMENT: Safety (partial) coefficient for concrete in ultimate limit state (ULS) design. Multiplies characteristic concrete strength to account for material variability and modeling uncertainties.

2. GAM-CE  
   • VALUE: 1.20  
   • COMMENT: Safety coefficient specifically for concrete elasticity (modulus of elasticity). Alters stiffness‐related calculations (e.g., deflection checks). In AQB one may override this via  
     TVAR NAME "GAM-CE" VAL <new> SCOP DESI.

3. GAM-B  
   • VALUE: 1.15  
   • COMMENT: Safety coefficient for reinforcing (passive) steel. Applies to yield and ultimate strengths of rebar in ULS.

4. GAM-Y  
   • VALUE: 1.15  
   • COMMENT: Safety coefficient for prestressing steel (tendons, strands). Similar to GAM-B but tailored to the properties and failure modes of prestressed elements.

5. GAM-S  
   • VALUE: 1.10  
   • COMMENT: Safety coefficient for structural (mild) steel sections. Used when designing steel‐framed structures, affecting moment capacity, shear capacity, etc.

6. GAM-A  
   • VALUE: 1.30  
   • COMMENT: Safety coefficient for structural aluminium. Captures its higher variability compared to steel and brittle failure characteristics.

7. ALF-CC  
   • VALUE: 1.00  
   • COMMENT: Long‐term reduction factor for concrete compressive strength, as per EN 1992-1-1 §3.1.6(1). When calculating sustained load effects, the characteristic strength is multiplied by ALF-CC.

8. ALF-CT  
   • VALUE: 1.00  
   • COMMENT: Long‐term reduction factor for concrete tensile strength (EN 1992-1-1 §3.1.6(2)). Governs cracking and serviceability assessments under sustained loads.

9. ALF-LCC  
   • VALUE: 0.85  
   • COMMENT: Long‐term reduction factor for lightweight concrete compressive strength (EN 1992-1-1 §11.3.5(1)). Reflects the increased creep and relaxation characteristics of lightweight mixes.

10. ALF-LCT  
   • VALUE: 0.85  
   • COMMENT: Long‐term reduction factor for lightweight concrete tensile strength (EN 1992-1-1 §11.3.5(2)). Used in serviceability and cracking analyses for lightweight sections.

Key points for RAG vectorization and on‐the‐fly adjustment in AQB:

- “DESI” scope: All variables listed belong to the design partial‐factor category and must be set with SCOP DESI when using TVAR in AQB.  
- Not all variables in the overall master.ini can be changed at runtime; this table highlights those that typically are.  
- Example override syntax for reducing concrete elasticity modulus in AQB:  
  TVAR NAME “ALF-CE” VAL 0.85 SCOP DESI  
  TVAR NAME “GAM-CE” VAL 1.25 SCOP DESI  

By indexing these entries in your RAG vector store, you capture both the Eurocode origin (master.ini boxed values) and the dynamic AQB‐TVAR mechanism, enabling intelligent retrieval of default design coefficients and their runtime‐adjustment syntax.

The input table is a concise reference of “boxed values” for Eurocode design variables (DESI scope) that can be overridden via TVAR commands in AQUA (AQB). It consists of three columns—NAME, VALUE, and Comment—and lists the most common DESI‐scope parameters that govern reinforcement ratios, stress–strain curve adjustments, and strut inclinations in concrete and composite members. Only a subset of these parameters can be temporarily redefined at run‐time in an AQB script by issuing TVAR statements with SCOP DESI. Below is a breakdown of its structure and content:

1. Table Structure  
   • Columns  
     – NAME: The identifier used with TVAR (e.g. “ALF-CE”, “AS-MAX”, “TANMINT”).  
     – VALUE: The default numerical factor or limit.  
     – Comment: A concise description of what the variable controls, including the relevant Eurocode clause reference (EN 1992-1-1).

2. Entries Related to Stress–Strain Curve Reduction  
   • ALF-CE (0.85)  
     – Reduces the elastic modulus for the calculatory (design) stress–strain curve.  
     – Typical usage: TVAR NAME “ALF-CE” VAL 0.85 SCOP DESI.  
   • GAM-CE (not shown in table but mentioned)  
     – Alters the partial factor on the modulus of elasticity for design curves (e.g. increase to 1.25).

3. Entries Governing Reinforcement Ratios  
   • AS-MAX (8.00)  
     – Maximum longitudinal reinforcement ratio based on gross cross‐section Ac (EN 1992-1-1 9.5.2 (3)).  
   • AS-MINB (0.13)  
     – Minimum longitudinal reinforcement ratio in bending members (EN 1992-1-1 9.2.1.1 (1)).  
   • AS-MINC (0.20)  
     – Minimum reinforcement ratio in compression members based on Ac (EN 1992-1-1 9.5.2 (2a)).  
   • AS-COMP (0.10)  
     – Absolute minimum reinforcement in compression members under axial load (EN 1992-1-1 9.5.2 (2b)).

4. Entries Governing Strut Inclinations in Shear and Flange Regions  
   All inclination terms refer to the tangent of the angle between compressive struts and the member axis:  
   • TANMIN (0.40)  
     – Minimum web‐strut inclination (EN 1992-1-1 6.2.3 (2)).  
   • TANMAX (1.00)  
     – Maximum web‐strut inclination (EN 1992-1-1 6.2.3 (2)).  
   • TANMINC (0.50)  
     – Minimum inclination in compressive flanges (EN 1992-1-1 6.2.4 (4)).  
   • TANMAXC (1.00)  
     – Maximum inclination in compressive flanges (EN 1992-1-1 6.2.4 (4)).  
   • TANMINT (0.80)  
     – Minimum inclination in tensile flanges (EN 1992-1-1 6.2.4 (4)).  
   • TANMAXT (1.00)  
     – Maximum inclination in tensile flanges (EN 1992-1-1 6.2.4 (4)).

5. Usage Notes & Context  
   • These default values originate from the master.ini (or national annex INI files) and can be overridden globally or locally.  
   • To adjust one of these in an AQB input script, precede each TVAR with SCOP DESI, e.g.:  
       TVAR NAME “ALF-CE” VAL 0.85 SCOP DESI  
       TVAR NAME “GAM-CE” VAL 1.25 SCOP DESI  
   • Not all DESI‐scope variables are adjustable in AQB—this table highlights the frequently used ones.  
   • References to “NORM” in AQUA documentation denote the broader normalization settings (global Eurocode parameters), while TVAR allows targeted changes within the DESIGN (DESI) scope.

By indexing this table in a RAG setup, you provide a ready lookup for design‐stage adjustments—linking each NAME to its default VALUE, comment, and Eurocode clause—facilitating dynamic generation of TVAR commands in parameterized analyses.

See also: NORM
 TVAR
 There is a range of variables in the Eurocodes allowing to adopt national factors called boxed values. They are defined in the INI files in general, but it is possible to adjust them in AQUA using the TVAR command. An overview of the accepted names and subjects (DESI,COMB etc.) is given in the file master.ini.
 For special cases, these values may also be defined temporarily with the TVAR command in AQB. For the input in AQB it is important to set SCOP explicitly to DESI. If for example a reduction of the elasticity modulus for the CALC curve is required, it is possible to specify factors ALF-CE and GAM-CE :
 TVAR NAME "ALF-CE" VAL 0.85 SCOP DESI
 TVAR NAME "GAM-CE" VAL 1.25 SCOP DESI
 Some names of the DESI SCOPE and frequently used values are given in the following table. Note that only some of them can be adjusted in AQB.

 The selection can be done with BEAM FROM ... via element numbers. Alternatively it is possible to select with BEAM FROM GRP ... all beams of a primary or secondary group, with BEAM FROM SLN ... all beams of a structural line and with BEAM FROM REF ... all beams of an axis. (Important: An explicit selection of secondary axes is not possible! If a primary axis is selected, all beam elements along the primary axis and the related secondary axes are taken). The group or axis designation is to be specified at position TO, INC has no meaning in those cases. If the referenced element is an axis, the values CS0 to CS1 may be specified as the name of a variable at the axis with a maximum of 4 characters, defining the values along the axis.
 Only one type of elements can ever be processed in one input block. Thus the definition of BEAM should precede the selection of the load cases. The following are considered to be of the same type:
 BEAM,FLEX,COMP beam elements of database
 DSLN,DBEA,DCOL results at design elements in the data base

 These types can be defined in detail:
 BEAM = beam elements
 FLEX = beam elements as bending members

 SLN = structural lines

 = structural lines as compression members
 TRUS = truss elements
 CABL = cable elements
 SECT = external section in bending members

 FACE = support face
 HFAC = support face, hinged support
 IFAC = support face, indirect support
 SHEA = external section, shear section
 With the types FLEX and COMP, the otherwise valid differentiation between compression and bending members with respect to the orientation to the gravity is overwritten. AQB checks however eccentricity and magnitude of the axial force in every section against the selection. If CS0 is selected, the default of TYPE is changed to FLEX.

In general, the user processes only the results of the database or individual external forces and moments of the load case zero. In order to be able to use the extensive possibilities for forming combinations, of creep stages and of shear designs, it is possible to define an external static system which is defined and managed independently of the existing system.
 This system is described by means of the external sections. The user must define every section with a beam number FROM and with an x value in increasing order and a section number. When such a section has been defined, all further inputs of TYPE SECT are interpreted as the defaults.
 The system is stored separately in the database, and can be reactivated for later computing runs with BEAM TYPE SECT.
 Since tendons and internal forces and moments are also stored under the defined beam type in the database, both the load cases and the tendons must be entered after the beam sections.
 For an example of this, see example t-beam-bridgesection.dat.

For the description of construction stages the user has to select an arbitrary but unique num- bering scheme. Each change of the section, installation or grouting of tendons should have its own number. The recommended scheme is to use numbers 10,20 etc. for constructional phases, while 11,21 are used for post stressing and 15,25 for the grouting process. With AQBS every beam or beam section can be assigned up to 31 different cross sections for determining stress (e.g. gross, net, ideal). These are designated as gross and construction stage sections CS0 to CS31.
 Each section in AQUA may have up to 9 construction phases, each with a construction stage number. If CS0 is defined with the literal AUTO, all CS values defined in AQUA will be used to define the construction stages, for literal AUTX the values in AQUA will trigger the stages +0,+1 and +5. The definition of higher construction stages may be done with multiple continuation lines as described below. Every row with the literal CS+X will shift the assigned CS numbers by 10, i.e. the second line defines the values for CS10 to CS19:
 BEAM 1001 1099 CS0 10 CS1 11 ......
 CS+X CS0 101 CS1 102
 Hint
 When using this option none of the records must contain generation or list expressions!
 Every load case is also assigned to a distinct construction stage. Its forces are acting on the section with the highest construction stage less or equal than the stage of the load case. It is also possible to assign a load case to an explicit stage (e.g. CS3), this allows to use different construction stages in one load case or to select always the second construction stage for the post-stressing.
 Further for every tendon three construction stage numbers are defined (values ICS1 to ICS3). Each tendon can be installed, grouted, or extended to a particular stage. Only the very first tendon should have ICS1=ICS2, because the program has to distinguish between the estates before and after the extrusion very carefully. The following conventions are in effect for the stage CSi:

Further for every tendon three construction stage numbers are defined (values ICS1 to ICS3). Each tendon can be installed, grouted, or extended to a particular stage. Only the very first tendon should have ICS1=ICS2, because the program has to distinguish between the estates before and after the extrusion very carefully. The following conventions are in effect for the stage CSi:.
 Tendons with CSi < ICS1 or CSi > ICS3 are present only with their duct as deductional area.
 Tendons with CSi > ICS1 and CSi < ICS2 are calculated with their steel area without bond and with their duct as deductional area. In ultimate load design, the prestressing is calculated with a constant value, without a strain increment.
 Tendons with CSi > ICS1 and CSi > ICS2 are calculated with their steel area into the com- pound and with a deductional area of the same size. ICS1=ICS2=0 defines tendons with immediate bond. These tendons are always active.

 These properties can also be defined in different ways, so that the user can hold to a method- ology which suits him in large systems with many stages of construction progress. The order in which tendons are considered depends only on the relative positions of the ICS numbers with respect to the CS numbers.
 Always the highest used CS number of the load cases will be employed for calculations at the total section (e.g. nonlinear, creep and shrinkage etc.) Checks for building stages should therefore be checked or include the CS value as specification at COMB. Forces and primary strains will be converted to the selected reference if necessary.
 The stress of tendons is active only for those cases where the tendons are really active. This is rather complex as the forces from prestress are acting on the section just before the one where they enter. For the definition of the prestressing sequences CSi following points are to be considered therefore:
 is strongly recommended to supply two construction stage numbers for any post-

 • The default for the CS-section of a combination is now derived from the load cases used in that combination. (This might have an severe impact on those cases, where the desired section type is not addressed by any load case for EIGE, ULTI or NSTR.)
 • If a tendon is not yet used in a CS-section, it will not have its initial stress value. If it is included, there is still the factor of prestress effective especially for the very first construction phase.

BEAM may be also used to specify a discrete reinforcement pattern for a system as needed for non-linear analysis or the determination of relative bearing capacities. When selecting the beams by number and x-value you may specify at CS the literals AS for the longitudinal rein- forcement or ASV for the shear links. At Position CSi you may now enter the reinforcement values in AS[mm2] 1020 resp ASV[mm2/m] 1021 for the layers of reinforcement with the num- ber i. Instead of a value a name of a variable (with up to 8 characters) may be specified. This variable must have the appropiate unit, but it may be defined also along an axis. As a further enhancement, missing x-values will be interpolated.
 BEAM SLN 1 X 0 XE 5 CS AS CS1 5[cm2] BEAM SLN 1 X 5 XE 20 CS AS CS1 20[cm2] BEAM SLN 1 X 20 XE 25 CS AS CS1 5[cm2] REIN RMOD SAVE
 When using a selection via axes (BEAM FROM REF), be aware that only primary axes are supported. In this case the reinforcement is set for all beams belonging to this primary axis and all corresponding secondary axes. Rotated placements are not considered (no longitudinal offset of the specified reinforcement). For such cases, please use the input via structural lines (BEAM FROM SLN).
 A benefit of this approach is that during the system generation the same section may be used. It has to be noted, that for accounting the existing reinforcements for the sectional values with STRE and EIGE, the intended reinforcement distribution case LCR has to be selected with record REIN!

The input table defines all of the input parameters required by the AQB “TENDON” record used to specify individual prestressing tendons in a beam.  It is intended as a companion to the BEAM and LC (load-case) records and must be entered in ascending order of beam number (NO) and then tendon number (NOB).  Unless noted otherwise, all units follow the current AQB unit system (default: mm for lengths, kN for forces, etc.).  Any field marked with “–” in the Unit column is dimensionless.  An asterisk (*) under Unit or Default indicates that the value is inherited (see notes below).  

Column headings:
•  Item:  the mnemonic used in the input file.  
•  Description:  a brief English label of its purpose.  
•  Unit:  the physical unit in which the value is interpreted.  
•  Default:  the value assumed if the field is omitted.  

List of parameters:

1.  NO  
 •  Beam number  
 •  Unit: – (integer index)  
 •  Default: 1  

2.  NOB  
 •  Tendon number within that beam  
 •  Unit: –  
 •  Default: 1  

3.  MNO  
 •  Material number of this tendon, plus 1 000 × deductional-material index  
 •  Unit: –  
 •  Default: 1  

4.  ICS1  
 •  Prestress stage “building in” (time stage when tendon is cast in)  
 •  Unit: –  
 •  Default: 0  

5.  ICS2  
 •  Prestress stage “extrusion” (time of jacking or transfer)  
 •  Unit: –  
 •  Default: 1  
 •  Note: Use 0 for immediate bond; use NONE or 9999 if external and to be excluded from shear-check; for post-tensioning specify ICS2 > ICS1.  

6.  ICS3  
 •  Prestress stage of removal (only for tendons to be removed)  
 •  Unit: –  
 •  Default: 0  

7.  X  
 •  Longitudinal coordinate along the beam axis  
 •  Unit: m (converted to the current length unit, normally mm)  
 •  Default: 0  

8.  Y  
 •  Lateral coordinate in the section’s local y-axis  
 •  Unit: * (inherits section coordinate unit, normally mm)  
 •  Default: 0  

9.  Z  
 •  Vertical coordinate in the section’s local z-axis  
 •  Unit: *  
 •  Default: 0  

10.  ZZ  
 •  Applied (initial) tendon tension force  
 •  Unit: kN  
 •  Default: 0  

11.  AZ  
 •  Cross-sectional area of the tendon steel  
 •  Unit: mm²  
 •  Default: 0  

12.  NY  
 •  Slope (gradient) of tendon path in y-direction: dY/dX  
 •  Unit: –  
 •  Default: 0  

13.  NZ  
 •  Slope of tendon path in z-direction: dZ/dX  
 •  Unit: –  
 •  Default: 0  

14.  YHR  
 •  y-coordinate of duct (or profile) center within section  
 •  Unit: *  
 •  Default: Y (copies the Y field if omitted)  

15.  ZHR  
 •  z-coordinate of duct center within section  
 •  Unit: *  
 •  Default: Z  

16.  AHR  
 •  Cross-sectional area of the duct surrounding the tendon  
 •  Unit: mm²  
 •  Default: AZ (uses tendon steel area if omitted)  

17.  DZ  
 •  Effective diameter of tendon or duct (used for sheathing checks)  
 •  Unit: mm  
 •  Default: * (inherited from overall beam default)  

18.  AR  
 •  Reference area for calculation of crack widths  
 •  Unit: m²  
 •  Default: – (no default; set to a large negative value to exclude this tendon from crack-width design, or positive to enable crack-width checks)  

19.  UZ  
 •  Circumference length around the tendon used in crack-width calculations  
 •  Unit: mm  
 •  Default: * (inherited: can use formula U = 16 − n − VAZ in sections with bundled strands)  

20.  TEMP  
 •  Temperature used for “hot design” effects on prestress losses  
 •  Unit: °C  
 •  Default: 0  

Additional context:  
- Older AQB versions assumed meters for X, Y, Z; since v12.47 these fields follow the global unit setting (typically mm). Old-unit entries will trigger errors 13 or 14.  
- Tendons must lie within the section’s cross-section for proper shear checks; external unbonded tendons to be excluded must use ICS2 = 9999.  
- When combining load cases of TYPE PR with adjustment factors, tendon forces (ZZ) are scaled by the same factor.

See also: BEAM, LC
 TEND
 TEMP
 Temperature for a hot design

 Tendons are generally defined with the program TENDON. For special cases and especially external sections, however, they can also be specified directly. The tendons need to be entered in order by beams and beam sections. The x values need to be specified with a precision of 1 mm. A use of this feature combined with forces directly defined with record S in load case 0 is not possible. (See example aqb2_3_t-beam-bridgesection.dat and aqb2_4_precastbeam.dat)
 The stress phases are the numbers of time stages in the progress of a construction stage, and are assigned to individual sections during the CS inputs of the BEAM record. For tendons with immediate bond, the correct specification is ICS2 0. For tendond without bond, the correct specification is ICS2 NONE or ICS2 9999, For post tensioning i.e. tendons with a delayed extrusion it is strongly suggested to specify ICS2 > ICS1.
 If a load case of TYPE PR is given an adjusting factor in a combination, then the tension forces are also multiplied by this factor.
 For the shear check it is necessary that the tendons lie within the cross section. Otherwise the proportional tensile force is computed wrongly. It is not therefore possible to combine all tendons into one single one which lies then outside of the cross section. AQB checks the situation of the tendon with a tolerance which corresponds to the radius of the prestressed steel area. External tendons without bond that are supposed to be excluded from this examination must be defined with ICS2 9999.
 The values DZ and UZ are preset to the corresponding values of an individual beam. For UZ, the literal BUND can be used to call the formula
 U=16-n- VAZ
 (3.1)
 If AR is defined as positive, then an additional calculation of the crack width is done for this tendon alone. For this design, tension members are calculated into the total reinforcement with the factor min(1.0,0.09/AR). This is to satisfy the requirement that tension members with delayed bond can only be calculated within a square with sides of 30 cm. AR can be input as a negative value, if only the amount to be calculated is desired. If individual tendons are not to be calculated in or designed at all for the crack width, then AR should be defined with a large negative value.

This is to satisfy the requirement that tension members with delayed bond can only be calculated within a square with sides of 30 cm. AR can be input as a negative value, if only the amount to be calculated is desired. If individual tendons are not to be calculated in or designed at all for the crack width, then AR should be defined with a large negative value..
 NY and NZ are the corresponding inclinations of the prestress cable in respect to the axis of the beam (tangent) :
 NY = dY/dX
 NZ = dZ/dX
 NZ = dZ/dX
 (3.2)
 Hint:
 Older versions of AQB used only m as basic unit for this record. This has been changed from Version 12.47 to the more common unit mm (or others selected via PAGE UNII) as within TENDON. Old definitions will be flagged with an error 13 or 14.

The table under discussion defines the input fields (items) for an “LC” (load-case) record in AQB, showing for each item its purpose, the expected data type or unit, and any default value used when the item is omitted. It is arranged in four columns:

1. Item  
   – The keyword or mnemonic used in the LC record.  

2. Description  
   – A brief explanation of the role or meaning of that keyword.  

3. Unit  
   – The data type or unit expected by the parser (e.g. literal string “LIT,” numeric, or “–” for dimensionless).  

4. Default  
   – The value assumed if the field is not explicitly supplied.

Below is a detailed walkthrough of each row:

• NO  
  – Number of the load case.  
  – Unit: “–/LIT” (either a numeric ID or a literal string pattern, including wildcards).  
  – Default: none.  
  – Usage: Identifies a single case, a range (via wildcards), or a set by action type (D, A, E, P, F, N, R, H, HZ, PT, LT, MT, ST, VT).  

• TYPE  
  – Name of the action to which the load case belongs (for example G, Q, A, E, etc.).  
  – Unit: “LIT” (literal).  
  – Default: none.  
  – Usage: Overrides or temporarily redefines the default action types defined in the design-code INI-file, possibly with category suffixes (_A…Z).  

• CST  
  – Cross‐section type used in stress computation.  
  – Unit: “–/LIT” (numeric stage index or literal keyword).  
  – Default: “*” (system default).  
  – Accepted values:  
    • nnnn = construction stage number  
    • GROS = gross section  
    • CS0, CS1, …, CS255 = specific construction‐stage sections  

• REF  
  – Reference point for stored internal forces and moments.  
  – Unit: “LIT.”  
  – Default: “PART” (construction stage section).  
  – Keywords: STD (no conversion), GROS (final gross section), EFFE (effective section), NULL (coordinate origin).  

• TITL  
  – Descriptive name of the load case.  
  – Unit: “Lit24” (up to 24-character literal).  
  – Default: “*” (no title).  

• GAMU  
  – Unfavourable safety factor.  
  – Unit: “–” (dimensionless).  
  – Default: “*” (inherit).  

• GAMF  
  – Favourable safety factor.  
  – Unit: “–.”  
  – Default: “*.”  

• PSI0, PSI1, PSI2, PS1S  
  – Combination coefficients for standard, frequent, quasi-permanent, and infrequent actions, respectively.  
  – Unit: “–.”  
  – Default: “*” (use code defaults).  

• GAMA  
  – Safety factor for accidental action.  
  – Unit: “–.”  
  – Default: “*.”  

• APAR  
  – Partition within the action family (one of G, P, Q, A or E).  
  – Unit: “LIT.”  
  – Default: “*.”  

• SUP  
  – Superposition rule within the same action.  
  – Unit: “LIT.”  
  – Default: “*.”  

• FAT…DIN  
  – Special amplification factor for fatigue checks per DIN FB 102 A 106.2.  
  – Unit: “LIT.”  
  – Default: none.  

Taken together, these fields allow precise control over which load cases are processed, how they reference sectional data, how internal forces are interpreted, and which safety or combination factors apply. When omitted, most parameters fall back on defaults drawn either from the action type definitions in the INI file or from AQB’s built-in conventions.

sections: 3.10 LC – Selection of the Load Case to be Designed

content:
The table organizes the way each fundamental load‐case “action” is named and combined in AQB, under three different combination modes—Normal, Additive (Add.), and Specific (Spec.)—and provides a short Remark describing the physical origin of each load.  A small superscript on each code flags its combination rule:  
- g (permanent): always included;  
- q (conditional): only included when unfavourable;  
- x (mutually exclusive or special‐sign): only one of this group may act at a time or it carries a special sign rule.  

Columns  
1. Normal  
   The base code used when the action is taken alone or as part of a general combination without separation into additive vs. specific sub‐groups.  

2. Add. (Additive)  
   The same code prefixed by “Z” when loads of that type are treated as additive superpositions within one action category (APAR/SUP settings).  

3. Spec. (Specific)  
   The same code prefixed by “S” when loads of that type are pulled out into a specific selection group—only included if they turn out to be the most unfavorable case.  

4. Remark  
   A plain‐English description of the load case.  In some instances the note also indicates a special rule for bridge design (e.g. using ZW/ZW^x for wind).  

----------------------------------------------------------------------  
1. Permanent Loads (superscript g)  
   • Gᵍ   / ZGᵍ   / SGᵠ  dead load  
   • G1ᵍ  / Z1ᵍ  / S1ᵠ  primary dead load  
   • G2ᵍ  / Z2ᵍ  / S2ᵠ  secondary dead load  
   • Pᵍ   / ZPᵍ   / SPᵠ  prestress  
   • Cᵍ   / ZCᵍ   / SCᵠ  creep and shrinkage  

2. Variable or Service Loads (superscript q or x)  
   • Qᵠ   / ZQᵠ   / SQᵠ  variable live load  
   • Lˣ   / ZLˣ   / SLˣ  life load (e.g. permanent‐except‐for‐maintenance)  
   • Wˣ   / ZWˣ   / SWˣ  wind load  
       – remark: “use ZW” for bridge main‐girders  
   • Sᵠ   / ZSˣ   / SSˣ  snow load  
       – remark: “use ZS” for bridge decks  
   • Rᵍ   / ZRˣ   / SRˣ  earth or water pressure  
   • Fᵠ   / ZFˣ   / SFˣ  settlements  
       – (ZF = expected, SF = possible)  
   • Tˣ   / ZTˣ   / STˣ  temperature effects  

3. Exceptional or Accidental Loads (superscript x)  
   • Aˣ   / ZAˣ   / SAˣ  accidental action  
   • Bˣ   / ZBˣ   / SBˣ  construction/maintenance loads  
   • Eˣ   / ZEˣ   / SEˣ  earthquake  
       – (ZE = service‐level seismic, SE = design‐level seismic)  

How to read one row, e.g. the wind load row:  
- Normal code   = Wˣ (wind action treated on its own)  
- Additive code = ZWˣ (wind as an additive superposition among variable loads)  
- Specific code = SWˣ (wind isolated into a “specific” case if it proves governing)  
- Remark        = “wind (use ZW for Bridges)”  

Key points from the wider context:  
- AQB groups load cases by action type (G, Q, A, E, etc.) and may subdivide each type into categories (A…Z) to apply different γ factors or ψ coefficients.  
- By default, any load case marked with g is “always added” (permanent), with q “only if unfavourable,” and with x triggers special exclusion or sign‐rules.  
- Prefix “Z” tells the solver to superpose that action across several load cases within the same category; prefix “S” isolates it as the single most unfavorable case.  
- The table drives both single‐case design (when LC is not specified) and combination design (when COMB records are used), ensuring each physical action is accounted for with the correct safety or combination factor.

The illustration is a schematic cross-section of a structural member (for example a reinforced-concrete beam or steel channel) with superimposed force and moment symbols and two special points marked inside the section. Visually, the drawing can be broken down into three zones—from left to right—plus a caption below.

1. Cross-Section Geometry (left two-thirds)  
   - The outline is rendered in thin grey lines; the top flange and bottom return flanges are shaded in a pale cyan.  
   - At the very top, a wide horizontal slab (the “flange”) extends beyond the section’s web on both the left and right. These overhangs are shown as rectangular blocks of equal thickness.  
   - Beneath this flange, a vertical web drops down and then turns inward at the base, forming a U-shaped channel. The bottom of the web also has two short horizontal flanges (shaded cyan) that mirror the overhangs at the top.  
   - Inside the U-shaped cavity, two small filled circles represent characteristic points of the cross section:  
     • “Sb” (the shear centre or barycentre point) is the upper dot.  
     • “Seff” (the elastic centre or effective point) is the lower dot.  
   - Each dot is connected by a light dashed horizontal line that extends to the right, indicating their horizontal alignment.

2. Applied Force and Bending Moment (right third)  
   - A thick solid arrow labeled “N” points leftward along the same horizontal dashed line as “Seff.” This denotes a normal (axial) force being applied to the section.  
   - Directly above that, a large red curved arrow annotated “M” wraps around a fictitious hinge point, indicating a bending moment applied about an axis perpendicular to the plane of the drawing.  
   - The arrow for “M” is rendered as a quarter-circle arc with arrowheads, reinforcing the idea of rotation (clockwise in this view).

3. Caption  
   - Centered beneath the graphic is the legend:  
     Figure 3.1: Stresses and elastic centre  
   - This ties the visual elements back to the discussion of how axial forces and bending moments produce stress distributions referenced to the elastic centre of the section.

Overall, the figure highlights:  
- The geometric configuration of the section (U-shape with flanges).  
- The distinction between the shear/barycentric point (Sb) and the elastic-centre (Seff).  
- How an axial force N and a bending moment M act relative to these key internal points. This sets the stage for deriving the normal stress formula σN = … in subsequent analysis.

sections: 3.10 LC – Selection of the Load Case to be Designed

content:
See also: COMB, S
 LC
 LC is used to select the load cases to be designed. The first item NO may be specified with a number, an expression with wildcard symbol (eg. "‘1??00"’) for load case numbers or the name of a load case type (action). In the latter cases all load cases matching the criteria will be selected. Especially interesting are:
 (D) Ultimate Design combination
 (A) Ultimate Accidental combination
 (E) Ultimate Earthquake combination
 (P) Service: Quasi-permanent combination
 (F) Service: Frequent combination
 (N) Service: Infrequent combination
 (R) Service: Characteristic (rare) combination
 (H) Comb. of principal loading
 (HZ) Comb. of principal+supplemental loading
 (PT) permanent load combination e.g. for timber
 (LT) long term load combination e.g. for timber
 (MT) middle term load combination e.g. for timber
 (ST) short term load combination e.g. for timber
 (VT) very short term load combination e.g. for timber
 The load type is the name of the action to which the load case belongs. The default are the already defined values, but it is possible to redefine all properties temporarily.
 The most important actions are predefined with the INI-file of the design code. Further it is possible to subdivide each action in categories selected with a character from A to Z, each having distinguished combination coefficients or safety factors. This will be appended with an underscore to the name of the action.
 However 48 reserved names with designated meanings are used to trigger special effects in AQB for historical superpositions. AQB saves results in the data base of the design for all combinations (COMB) with an explicit LCST given and for all single load cases with one of the above types assigned. If a load case should be classified only temporarily the type (-) may be used.
 Normal Add.
 Spec.
 Remark
 g
 Load case is permanent (always added)
 q
 Load case is conditional (added if unfavourable)

If a load case should be classified only temporarily the type (-) may be used.. Normal Add.. Spec.. Remark. g. Load case is permanent (always added). q. Load case is conditional (added if unfavourable).
 Load cases are conditional excluding each other
 TITL can be used not only to title a load case which is to be newly defined, but can also make a later change or expand the name of a load case which is stored in the database.
 Prestressing is only taken into consideration when a load case with that type of action is se- lected. The factor in the combination will be also applied to the tension force itself if the action does not have a category. With category 0 or 1 these define the factor for pre-tensioning or post-tensioning only. Beside this the factor max not be specified differently, only the first definition is taken.
 When designing individual load cases with prestressing, therefore, all load cases must be given a prestress action type.
 For the check STRE U according the "‘Nachrechnungsrichtline"’ we have reduction factors rcp derived from the shear links provided. They will be applied as additional factors.
 With a definition of FAT DIN the sectional forces of this load case will be magnified based on the location of the section with a factor between 1.40 and 1.75 according to paragraph A 106.2 of DIN FB 102. Unfortunately the information about the start and the end of a span is hardly defined. AQB will use the higher factors therefore only if the beam contains a section with the attribute ”face” towards the respective end of the span.
 The definition of the section type and reference is an essential input to calculate the stresses with the appropriate section.
 Within the static analysis all forces should be referenced to the elastic center of the appropriate construction stage section as caclculated in AQUA. This is the point within a section where an acting normal force will create only centric strains and thus no moments:
 The association of the correct section type can be done either by a global construction stage number or by the section designation defined explictly in the BEAM record. The default for CST is CS1 for all load case types except G1 and PR; for these the default is CS0. Load cases with undefined CS sections are assigned to the gross section. Therefore, when the CS values are not defined in the BEAM record, all load cases operate on the gross section.

metadata.sections: 3.10 LC – Selection of the Load Case to be Designed

content:
The default for CST is CS1 for all load case types except G1 and PR; for these the default is CS0. Load cases with undefined CS sections are assigned to the gross section. Therefore, when the CS values are not defined in the BEAM record, all load cases operate on the gross section..
 For special cases, the specified sections may be taken to other reference points via REF or via explicit coordinates within the S-record.
 For the calculation of the stresses ideal sections including ducts, tendons and current amount of reinforcements will be used, thus the specified moments will be adjusted then to account for the final shift of the elastic center.
 AQB has various ways of using load cases:
 1. No specification for LC
 If nothing is specified for LC, all load cases stored in the database are designed individu- ally. External forces and moments S are processed separately as load case 0.
 2. Specification for LC only
 When LC is specified, only these load cases are designed.
 3. LC and S
 If internal forces and moments are defined after any LC record, they are saved under this load case and are included in the remaining calculation. This option not only permits the definition of load cases for sections, but also allows the inclusion of additional forces and moments in the calculation for individual sections, even without static design to an existing system. This causes deletion of results stored under the same load case number.
 4. LC and COMB
 If design combinations are selected in addition, then only these combinations are de- signed. The load case types are evaluated only in connection with these combination regulations. The input of COMB supplements the possibilities of the program MAXIMA, and allows calculation with divided safety coefficients, or selection from among traffic load cases.
 The internal forces and moments of the load case, if any, must be input immediately following the LC record. Internal stresses are automatically deleted when internal forces and moments are input.
 The combination coefficients and safety factors will be usually defined with the generation of the load case. A definition in AQB will be only of temporarily influence and will not account for any defaults by specifying a load case type. Only in those cases where forces and moments are defined in AQB explicitly, the defaults from the corresponding INI-file will be taken.
 The items APAR and SUP define the superposition of load cases within an action. The default will be taken from the action. However if only one of the values is specified, the other value will be reset to its default value.

content:
The table defines the set of keywords and their parameters used to prescribe arbitrary internal forces and moments along beam‐type elements in a RAG-driven finite‐element workflow. Each row corresponds to one input “item,” with four columns indicating  
 1. Item name (the keyword used in the data file)  
 2. Description (what physical quantity it represents)  
 3. Unit (the display or interpretation unit, often subscripted by an internal code)  
 4. Default value (used if the keyword is omitted)  

Below is a detailed walk-through of each parameter and how it fits into the broader load‐case framework:

1. NCS (Cross section number)  
   – No unit.  
   – Default “–” (mandatory if specifying a reference coordinate system explicitly).  
   – Identifies which cross‐section profile (from the section library) the following forces and moments refer to. When using LC records, NCS only sets the reference coordinate system and must still be present.

2. NO (Element number)  
   – No unit.  
   – Default = 1.  
   – The element (beam line) index to which the forces/moments apply. Serves as the primary sorting key.

3. X (X value)  
   – Unit: meters [m] (code 1001).  
   – Default = 0.  
   – Specifies the longitudinal coordinate along the beam (from its local 0‐point). Negative X is interpreted from the opposite end. Entries must be ordered by NO ascending, then X ascending. Duplicate locations are not allowed.

4. N (Axial force)  
   – Unit: kilonewtons [kN] (code 1101).  
   – Default = 0.  
   – Positive tension pulls away from the section centroid.

5. VY, VZ (Shear forces)  
   – Unit: kilonewtons [kN] (code 1102).  
   – Default = 0.  
   – VY is shear in local Y, VZ in local Z, both measured about the shear centre unless overridden by a reference point.

6. MT (Total torsional moment)  
   – Unit: kilonewton‐meters [kNm] (code 1103).  
   – Default = 0.  
   – Sum of primary Saint‐Venant torsion plus secondary warping torsion. By default, warping is kept as MB but the full MT is stored here.

7. MY, MZ (Bending moments)  
   – Unit: kilonewton‐meters [kNm] (code 1104).  
   – Default = 0..  
   – MY bends about local Y‐axis, MZ about Z‐axis, both referenced to the centroid unless Y/Z offsets are given.

8. MB (Warping moment)  
   – Unit: kilonewton‐meter² [kNm²] (code 1105).  
   – Default = 0.  
   – Represents pure warping torsion. Treated as an eigen‐stress state: omitted in DESI output but included as primary strain in NSTR analyses (though not varied in nonlinear runs).

9. MT2 (Secondary torsional moment)  
   – Unit: kilonewton‐meters [kNm] (code 1103).  
   – Default = 0.  
   – An auxiliary torsional component (beyond MT) for advanced warping‐torsion superposition.

10. Y, Z (Reference coordinates)  
    – Unit: millimeters [mm] (code 1011).  
    – Default = “*” (must be explicitly specified if used).  
    – Shifts the origin in the section plane. If provided, all N, V, M quantities are first referenced to this point then internally transformed to centroid/shear‐centre.

11. REF (Designation of a sectional point)  
    – Unit: Lit8 (an 8-character literal).  
    – Default “–”.  
    – A user‐defined label for this exact location (e.g. “TOPFLG” or “BOTWLN”), useful for post‐processing or matching external design checks.

Additional context on usage:  
• Records prefaced with “S” are stored under the special load‐case number 0 (static, user‐defined forces). For other load‐cases (LC), the forces/moments attach to the most recent LC declaration.  
• Pre‐ and post‐tensioning forces must reflect only the statically determined prestress component; for second‐order (geometric) analyses, prestress from creep & shrinkage (via AQUA) is excluded unless construction‐stage tracking is active.  
• Ordering rules (by element and X) and the prohibition on duplicate locations ensure unambiguous interpolation of internal loads along the beam.  
• The distinction between centroid and shear centre references, plus optional Y/Z offsets, enables fully general definition of section‐specific loadings and supports complex warping‐torsion fidelity in advanced analysis modules.

See also: LC
 S
 These records can be used to define individual internal forces and moments for a separate design.
 The forces and moments defined with S are normally saved under load case number 0. The values NO and X are then needed only for identifying the output.
 If a load case is given with LC, the internal forces and moments are stored under the latest defined load case. In this case the section NCS is used only to define the reference coordinates but must be specified explicitly The forces and moments must be input in increasing sequential order by beam number and x value. Multiple definitions for the same location are not possible. Negative x values are interpreted as dimensions from the beam end.
 Axial force and bending moments are referenced to the centroid, torsional moment and shear- ing forces to the centre of shear of the section. If a specification for Y or Z is made, however, then all internal forces and moments are relative to the so-defined reference point in the section coordinate system. They are immediately transformed to the centroid or the centre of shear. The torsional moment is the total moment as the sum from the primary Saint-Venant and the secondary part from warping torsion. The warping moment MB is an eigen stress state, thus it will not be included in DESI. However for NSTR it will be included as primary strain, but will not varied within a nonlinear analysis.
 Forces and moments for the load case pre- and post tensioning have to be defined always with the static determined part of the prestress forces.
 As the second order analysis must not include the prestressing force in the geometric stiffness, there is an exception: Prestress including creep and shrinkage effects defined with the section (AQUA) is not to be included with the forces and moments if no construction stages have been selected.

The table shown defines two of the optional parameters you can specify on a COMB-EXTR record in AQBS/AQB when you want to control which sectional “stage” and what title is associated with each block of load-case combinations.  In a RAG/vector-store schema you would typically extract from this table the following fields:

1.  Item  
    •  Code used on the COMB record.  
    •  This becomes the “parameterName” or “fieldName” in your JSON schema.  

2.  Description  
    •  A human-readable explanation of what the parameter does.  
    •  For CST, it tells you which construction-stage section to use when computing internal stresses (EIGE), design forces (DESI) or non-linear stresses (NSTR).  
    •  For TITL, it specifies the user-defined name of the combination.  

3.  Unit  
    •  The expected data type or literal domain.  
    •  “Lit/—” means a literal token (free text) or, if omitted (—), the parameter may default.  
    •  “Lit24” means a literal text up to 24 characters in length.  

4.  Default  
    •  The value applied if the user does not supply one.  
    •  In both cases here, “*” denotes a blank or system-assigned default.  

–––  

Detailed breakdown of each row:

•  CST  
   –– ParameterName: “CST”  
   –– Description: “Section type for EIGE / DESI / NSTR”  
       ◦  EIGE = determination of internal stresses  
       ◦  DESI = design force calculation  
       ◦  NSTR = non-linear stress computation  
   –– Domain / Allowed Values:  
       •  GROS  → “Gross section” (the full cross-section before any construction staging)  
       •  nn    → “explicit construction stage” (where nn is an integer code from 0 to 255)  
       •  CS0  → “Construction-stage section 0” (same as nn=0)  
       •  CS255 → “Construction-stage section 255” (maximum user-defined stage)  
   –– Unit/DataType: “Lit/—” (a literal token or blank)  
   –– Default: “*” (omit to let AQB assume its own staging)  

•  TITL  
   –– ParameterName: “TITL”  
   –– Description: “Name of the combination”  
       ◦  If you do not supply a name explicitly, AQB will automatically construct one from the list of load cases involved.  
   –– Domain / Allowed Values:  
       •  Any printable string, up to 24 characters long (letters, digits, punctuation)  
   –– Unit/DataType: “Lit24”  
   –– Default: “*” (blank → triggers AQB’s auto-generated name)  

–––  

Usage in context:  
When you define a COMB EXTR block to generate a set of combined actions (for example to find the maximum bending moment My or the minimum axial force N across a set of permanent, live, prestress and accidental cases), you can:  
  – precede your SCOM lines by “CST GROS” or “CST 2” (to pick stage 2), and  
  – add “TITL My–N combo” (so your vector store entry can carry a human-readable label).  

By extracting these two fields into your RAG/vector database, you ensure that downstream tools know both which stage of the section to evaluate and what to call the combination for traceability (e.g. reporting, filtering or re-execution of the design check).

sections: 3.12 COMB – Definition of Load Case Combinations

content:
The table presents the symbols and algebraic definitions of the partial‐safety factors and combination coefficients used by AQB in defining load combinations per EN 1990.  It is organized in four columns: the first and third columns list the factor names (symbols), and the second and fourth columns give their mathematical expressions.  At the foot are references to the source clauses in EN 1990 (Table B.3 and equation 6.6).

1. Columns and Layout  
   • Column 1 (“Symbol”) – names of the factors as used in AQB input.  
   • Column 2 (“Definition”) – the formula combining fundamental safety factors γ (for loads) and ψ (for combination coefficients), or ξ for accidental‐action factors.  
   • Columns 3–4 – a parallel set of symbols and definitions, reflecting alternative notation (for example, using γₐ or γ_f instead of γ_u).  

2. Fundamental Factors  
   • γ_u, γ_f, γ_a: Partial safety factors for unfavourable (γᵤ), favourable (γ_f), and accidental or complementary loads (γₐ).  
   • ψ₀, ψ₁, ψ₂, ψ₁,infq: Combination coefficients for permanent/transient load pairing:  
     – ψ₀ (quasi‐permanent coefficient)  
     – ψ₁ (frequent coefficient)  
     – ψ₂ (rare coefficient)  
     – ψ₁,infq (infrequent/transient coefficient for leading variable action)  

3. Derived Coefficients  
   These are simply products or ratios of the fundamental γ and ψ factors, used when building design or accidental combinations:  
   • PSIG = (γᵤ/γ_f)·ψ₀  
   • PSIU = γᵤ·ψ₀  
   • PS1G = (γᵤ/γ_f)·ψ₁  
   • PS1U = γᵤ·ψ₁  
   • PS2G = (γᵤ/γ_f)·ψ₂  
   • PS2U = γᵤ·ψ₂  
   • P1SG = (γᵤ/γ_f)·ψ₁,infq  
   • P1SU = γᵤ·ψ₁,infq  

   The right‐hand block shows the same constructs with γₐ or γ_f replacing γᵤ, and notation PS1A, PS1F, PS2A, PS2F, P1SA, P1SF, etc.

4. Accidental and Seismic Factors  
   • ξ (XSI) – the accidental‐action factor for rare events (e.g. explosion or seismic).  
   • XSIG = ξ·(γᵤ/γ_f)  
   • XSIU = ξ·γᵤ  
   • XSIA = ξ·γₐ  
   • XSIF = ξ·γ_f  

5. Factors Including k_fi (“KFI”)  
   • k_fi – factor accounting for load inclination or influence‐line effects in certain codes.  
   • KFG = k_fi·(γᵤ/γ_f)  
   • KFG0 = k_fi·ψ₀·(γᵤ/γ_f)  
   • KFG2 = k_fi·ψ₂·(γᵤ/γ_f)  
   • XKFG = ξ·k_fi·(γᵤ/γ_f)  
   • XKGU = ξ·k_fi·γᵤ  
   • And analogous variants combining k_fi with ψ₁, ψ₁,infq, γₐ or γ_f (e.g. KFGS, XKGA, XKGF).  

6. References  
   – “EN 1990, Tab. B.3” for the base values of γ and ψ.  
   – “EN 1990 equ. 6.6” for the accident‐action (ξ) expressions.  

Usage in AQB: when defining a COMB record, the user can refer to any of these symbols to apply the corresponding factor to a particular load case or to discriminate favourable vs unfavourable contributions. If explicit values are given, they override defaults. The table thus encapsulates all combinations of global safety factors and ψ-coefficients necessary for limit‐state design according to Eurocode load combination rules.

sections: 3.12 COMB – Definition of Load Case Combinations

content:
The image is a scan of a technical manual page describing how the AQBS/AQB software handles combinations of structural load cases (“COMB”) and illustrating the addition of control moments to prevent cracking. It is divided into two main regions: a dense block of monospaced text (top and center-left) and a smaller diagram plus equations (bottom and center-right), all set in a fixed-pitch font.

Top section  
• A header line reads “See also: LC.”  
• The narrative explains that AQBS normally processes individual load cases but, by using the COMB command, the user can define combinations of those cases per partial-safety theory (as in international codes and prestressed concrete design).  
• It lists what results can be stored under a user-defined load case number LCST:  
  – Combined forces and moments (including all special effects),  
  – Material stresses at selected points or shear-cut centres,  
  – Eigenstresses (EIGE),  
  – Nonlinear stresses (DESI, NSTR).  
• Users may also specify GMAX and GMIN numbers to capture the maxima and minima of those results. If no title (“TITL”) is given, AQB generates one automatically from the involved cases.

Mid-section  
• Describes addressing cases by number or by type (record type LC), e.g. G1, G2, P, C (summed permanent loads), Q/S/F (only unfavorable contributions summed), and other types where only the worst-case is used.  
• Notes that INI-file settings can alter this default behavior.  
• Introduces a “special superposition type” allowing explicit safety factors and combination coefficients (design, accidental, seismic combinations), with formula snippets (e.g. “S = γg·Gk + γq,1·Qk,1 + …” and seismic factor from EN 1990 Eq. 6.10b). A warning states that any explicit factor will override defaults and disable automatic leading action selection.  
• Cites the ACI requirements for investigating three standard combinations:  
  1. 1.4 G + 1.7 L  
  2. 1.05 G + 1.275 L + 1.43 E  
  3. 0.9 G + 1.43 E  
• Explains how moment factors may be set proportionally when axial-force factor = 1.0, and gives sample input lines:  
   COMB EXTR MAX SCOM MY 1.0  
   COMB EXTR MAX SCOM N 0.15 LC1 G F1 1.0 LC2 L F2 1.0  
• Defines EXTR keywords (FSUM, FMAX, FMIN, FMAM, FSOL, FSMA, FSMI, FSMX) for cases where factors should act also on combination forces.  
• Shows further commands for setting one factor per section force (FSOL before combination records).

Lower left  
• Introduces additional design-code moments (type MCR for control of cracking, via ACI/AASHTO/DIN, with variants MCRM, MCRL, MCRH; type DMRZ specifically for cracking control under DIN 4227 or DAfStb).  
• Begins a brief section on EIGE (internal stress determination), noting dependencies on humidity, temperature, concrete age, cement class, effective thickness A/U, with a “CTRL EIGE” switch to choose a material-code method.

Bottom right  
• Two simple equations appear:  
   ΔM₁ = ±5·10⁻⁵·(EI/d)  
   or  
   ΔM₂ = ±15·10⁻⁵·(EI/d)  
  with a note that R (or DMRZ) creates only additional MY moments per 1 °C temperature difference.  
• Directly beneath is a small line drawing of a bending-moment distribution along a simply supported beam (horizontal axis). On the right vertical axis, “M.” A bold curved line labeled “M” shows the primary moment diagram. Two secondary curves—one labeled DM1 (smaller amplitude) and one DM2 (larger)—are drawn in solid and dashed styles, peaking near mid-span. Short vertical ticks mark the amplitudes of DM1 and DM2 at two locations.  
• The caption reads “Figure 3.2: Additional moments for control of cracking.”

sections: 3.12 COMB – Definition of Load Case Combinations

content:
See also: LC
 AQBS normally performs its design operations for the selected load cases. With COMB, com- binations of the load cases can be defined instead, as are used in partial safety theory in many international codes or prestressed concrete.
 Compared to the superposition in MAXIMA, we need to know the part of the permanent loading, the prestress or the life load for many design tasks. Furthermore it is very common that we have extreme values for different targets, thus the load cases of the same type ar now mutually exclusive.
 The combinations must be input before the particular design request is specified, and will stay in effect for later operations as well, until a new definition is made.
 For each combination you may define a load case number LCST to store results. Then the results are stored under this load case number. These are:
 • Combined forces and moments (not at EIGE) (incl. all special effects and transformations)
 • Stresses for each material and selected stress points or the centre of every shear cut for STRE. For shear stress in concrete we store for the reference stress the shear stress due to lateral shear stress only.
 • Eigenstresses in case of EIGE
 non-linear stresses for DESI and NSTR
 •
 You may also define for every block of combinations two special load case numbers via the combinations GMAX and GMIN with LCST. Then the maximum and minimum values of the results will be stored via this load case numbers in the same format.
 If TITL is not selected, AQB constructs a name of its own from the involved load cases.
 For each load case a number can be specified; then the load case which is addressed thereby is added up without regard for its type. As an alternative, a load type can also be addressed (see record type LC); then all load cases of this type are addressed and combined as selected within the action definition. e.g:
 • For the types G1, G2, P and C, all of the contributing components are added together (permanent loads). Load type G includes all of the G1 and G2 load types.

If the factor of the axial force is defined as 1.0, then the factors of the moments are given by the ratio of area to moment of resistance.. These factors do not act on the forces of the combination itself. They will be considered only to decide if a load case acts favourable or not. The seldom case where the factors act also on the combination forces, can be accomplished through the input of the following EXTR values:.
 FSUM, FMAX, FMIN, FMAM, FSOL, FSMA, FSMI and FSMX
 The following input defines a combination of a moment multiplied by 1.5 and an axial or shear force multiplied by 1.0.

 The factors do not act on secondary forces and from reasons of consistency on internal forces of type prestress.
 Other variations are possible, there is however only one factor per section force allowed. In the case where more factors have been defined, they must be set before the actual combination record with the keyword FSOL.

 For Bridges EN 1992-2 defines in section B.105 safety factors for delayed long term strains to be used, "‘However, when safety would be increased by overestimation of delayed strains, and when it is relevant in the project, the creep and shrinkage predicted on the basis of the formulas or experimental determinations should be multiplied by a safety factor."’ Thus the user has to select these factors via a definition of CTRL EIGE SAFE. The provisions of the German NA to apply these factors always for the shrinkage is activated automatically if a bridge class has been selected.
 If T is defined, these basic values PHI and EPS will be modified according to the evolution in time given by tables or formulas in the design codes. For those design codes relying on the summation approach (DIN 4227, Japanese and Chinese Code) the delayed elasticity will be incorporated automatically. If one wants to apply the time evolution function to be applied to the explicit given PHI/EPS-values, one has to use a negative value for T. For the first creep interval, the value T0 will control the age for the concrete for creeping and the amount of shrinkage which has been occurred between TS and T0. If we need the total shrinkage (e.g. for deformations or stresses with reinforcements) a separate unloaded shrinking time interval has to be introduced.
 The value of TEMP defines then either the temperature in Celsius (1 to 80 degree) during the creep step or, if defined negative the temperature of a thermal treatment before the creep step. For special cases a definition with an explict unit − allows to specify an explicit scaling factor for the effective age of the concrete.
 The influence of the temperature on the tendon relaxation (EN 1992-1-1, 10.3.2.) should be accounted for with an explicit Factor for PHI. The formula (10.2) given in EN 1992-1-1 is not implemented as it yields for Tmax equal to 80 degrees a rapid (43.3 times accelerated) re- laxation, so the method given in many technical papers to apply an immediate loss of 4% is preferable. For very special cases a definition with increased time increment values according to that formula can be specified.

The formula (10.2) given in EN 1992-1-1 is not implemented as it yields for Tmax equal to 80 degrees a rapid (43.3 times accelerated) re- laxation, so the method given in many technical papers to apply an immediate loss of 4% is preferable. For very special cases a definition with increased time increment values according to that formula can be specified..
 For analysis SUM with delayed elasticity (old DIN and Japan and China) the parts from delayed elasticity are always added if T is specified and applied for all primary creep results with the corresponding negative value. The order of the load numbers must correspond to the chrono- logical course in this case. Higher load case numbers must describe therefore later creep stages. If the PHI value is given as 0.0, the part from delayed elasticity is suppressed. If one wishes to determine only the re-creep, a small value must be entered at PHI.
 Further it has to be taken care of, that the effective concrete age is based on the slowly harden- ing cement, instead of the new coefficients (kz = 0.5, 1.0, 1.5), the original factors from Rüsch (kz = 1.0, 2.0, 3.0) have to be used.
 If an Indian design code is selected, than RH will be treated as maturity according to table 2 of IRC 18 defining PHI, while EPS is derived from the time T0 according to table 3. There are no time effects available however in this case.
 AS 3600 / 5100 provide curves and final factors for creep and shrinkage based on the effective
 depth, the environmental conditions and the concrete strength. Not included are temperature, cements with other sulphate contents or high stresses. With a definition of EC at PHI a switch to the Eurocode-Formulas may be achieved.
 With the setting CTRL EIGE 1, curvature loads for calculating the statically indeterminate shares from creep and shrinkage are stored. As a rule, multiple creep stages are required in that case (e.g. 3 to 5) because STAR2/ASE do not know the stresses or the forces at the end of an interval. If necessary, the relaxation parameters can be altered in AQB. If this load case is not calculated with STAR2/ASE, the calculation for AQB remains unrestrained i.e. statically determined.

The table defines the input parameters for a “STRE” record (stress‐checking module) in a structural‐analysis program, covering (a) the type of check or material selection, (b) an optional preset of limiting stresses by code, and (c) the numerical values of all stress limits used in utilization and resistance calculations.  Fields are grouped logically as follows:

1.  SMOD / STYP  
    •  SMOD (LIT / –) – Type of check or, if numeric, a material number.  
       –  E (default): compute elastic stresses only (required for sectional classification).  
       –  B: resistance for individual force effects and simple linear superposition (option P).  
       –  C: resistance for cross‐sectional interaction using complex interaction rules.  
       –  D: suggested dimensions based on allowable stresses or plastic capacities.  
       –  DG: select a section from a user‐defined group.  
    •  STYP (LIT) – A literal key that presets all limiting stresses according to a chosen code or material standard (e.g. “H,” “HZ,” “S,” “ZMAX,” etc.). If STYP is supplied, individual stress limits need only be overridden in special cases.

2.  Normal and bending stresses  
    All units: N/mm²   Defaults refer back to a previously entered limit.  
    •  SC – Maximum normal compressive stress (no default)  
    •  ST – Maximum normal tensile stress (default = SC)  
    •  SBC – Maximum edge‐fiber bending compression (default = SC)  
    •  SBT – Maximum edge‐fiber bending tension (default = ST)  
    •  SBBC – Maximum corner bending compression (default = SBC)  
    •  SBBT – Maximum corner bending tension (default = SBT)  
    •  SI – Maximum principal tensile stress (no default)  
    •  SII – Maximum principal compressive stress (no default)

3.  Shear and equivalent stresses  
    •  TAU – Maximum shear stress (no default)  
    •  SV – Maximum von Mises (equivalent) stress (no default)  
    •  TAUS – Maximum longitudinal shear stress in welds (no default)

4.  Combined shear/tension checks  
    All default to TAU if not specified:  
    •  SSTM – Shear/tension in middle area  
    •  SSEM – Shear/tension separate middle area  
    •  SSKM – Shear/tension combined middle area  
    •  SSER – Shear/tension at edge  
    •  SSKR – Shear/tension combined edge

5.  Compressive‐zone stresses (for cracked or prestressed sections)  
    •  CC – Max normal stress in compressive zone (default = SC)  
    •  CBC – Max edge stress in compressive zone (default = CC)  
    •  CBBC – Max corner stress in compressive zone (default = CBC)

6.  Special limits  
    •  LIMA – Limit for decompression or neutral‐axis zone “a/b” (* = no default)  
    •  ZMAX – Maximum prestressing‐steel stress (* = user must define)  
    •  ZDIF – Maximum stress range in prestressing steel (no default)  
    •  SCMG – Global safety‐class multiplication factor (no unit, no default)

Usage notes drawn from contextual documentation:  
–  STRE records are used in tandem with load‐case or combination records (COMB, LC type D, GMAX/GMIN) to store extreme elastic stresses and utilization factors.  
–  For section classes 1–2, EC 3/EN 1993 or BS interaction formulas are applied; for class 3, stresses are compared directly to allowable values.  
–  A global safety factor (SCMG) can multiply internal safety factors.  
–  SMOD can override material‐group defaults; if only SMOD is given, an E-type stress check is run.  
–  STYP literals streamline code‐based stress assignments (e.g. DIN 18800, EN 1995, BS 5400).  
This table therefore provides a comprehensive framework for defining every stress limit needed in elastic, plastic, or interaction‐type structural design checks.

sections: 3.14 STRE – Linear Stresses and Plastic Forces

content:
STRE
 Evaluation of maximum stresses for every force principal and von Mises yield stress in all sectional points.
 E:
 B: Evaluation of the utilisation factors for every individual component and a simplified linear superposition of the linear total utilisation.
 C: Evaluation of the utilisation factors for every individual component and a complex interaction of these components.
 In all cases the elastic stress will be evaluated, as this is required to define a sectional class. If the section is in class 3, the allowable stresses will be checked and their utilisation is save to the data base as relevant utilisation. If the section is in class 1 or 2, the resistance of the cross section for any individual force is calculated and for option P a simple linear addition of all utilization degrees will be saved to the database as total utilisation, while option C will store a complex interaction based on the provisions of the Eurocode (1993/1999).
 Additional tables for every section if ECHO TABS has been set which is also the default value. Loadcases with the extreme values of stresses or utilisation factors may be created in the data base by a preceding COMB GMAX/GMIN. If stress points have been defined in the cross- section, then the stress ranges occurring in the points are saved in the load case specified for GMAX. The stress ranges result from the difference between the maximum and minimum occurring stresses in the analysed load cases or combinations.
 D: Suggested dimensions
 Depending on the section class an estimate for the required dimensions of the cross section is made based on allowable stresses or plastic sectional capacities. For rectangle, circle, and steel shapes a rather detailed analysis is performed, while for all other sections, a linear scaling factor for the dimensions factor is evaluated. In the cases of rectangular sections, the width or height can be fixed when defining the section. Option DE will use only the allowable stresses for the dimensioning.
 Similar to option D. However sections will be selected from a group of sections. A group is defined via a sequence of cross section with continuous section numbers and increasing load capacities. The first section of a group will differ only in the last digit of the current section number. If sections with numbers 8,9,10,11 and 12 are defined, then the program may select instead of section 8 and 9 any of these numbers while for sections 10, 11 and 12 only the last three sections will be used. This Option is especially useful if one wants to select a different sequence for British or American shapes (e.g. UC 305 x 305 x 97 before UC 254 x 254 x 132). Option DGE will use only the allowable stresses for the dimensioning.
