content:
Some design codes allow a design for shear of concrete sections based in an uncracked model. These are the old German DIN 4227 or the first amendment to the German "‘Nachrech-
 nungsrichtlinie"’ of the German Ministry of Transport (2015). In all cases the stress at the extreme fiber of the section is not allowed to exceed a certain value.
 For the latter the definition of STRE U has to be selected. As in the "‘Nachrechnungsrichtlinie"’ the allowable stresses depend on the existence of flanges in the tensile zone and the provided shear links, AQB checks the center of all shear cuts for flanges to decide which value is to be taken for the values SBZ and SI. ECHO SHEA YES will print only the maximum values and the obtained limit values. With ECHO SHEA FULL, the shear cuts are printed for those sections fulfilling the longitudinal stress limit, wit ECHO SHEA EXTR all shear cuts will be printed.
 For DIN 4227 the input of define STRE E UL does not only start the design of the stresses in Zone a, but also the limiting stresses for shear design under cracked condition in Zone b using DESI. For this reason, the meanings of some values have been changed. Here the values TAU, SV and TAUS stand for values from Table 9, lines 56, 59 and 61, and the values SSTM to SSKR stand for the values from lines 53, 50, 54, 52, and 55. So a design is done when one of the shear stress or principal tensile stress components exceeds the following limits:
 τV > SSEM
 or τT > SSTM or SSER
 or τV+T > SSKM or SSKR
 As the value SSEM is also used for the specification of the inclination of the truss model, a full shear analysis should be triggered by specifying SSKR 0.001.

τV > SSEM. or τT > SSTM or SSER. or τV+T > SSKM or SSKR. As the value SSEM is also used for the specification of the inclination of the truss model, a full shear analysis should be triggered by specifying SSKR 0.001..
 The base values for shear stress for phase 2 require
 τV < TAU
 and τT < SV
 and τV+T < TAUS
 and σ < CC (Webs) resp. CBC (Flanges)
 If no record STRE has been defined with ULnn, the entire shear design is done by DESI in cracked conditions. Otherwise a differentiation is made between Zones a and b depending upon the maximum uniaxial extreme fibre stress LIMA, and only sections in Zone b are de- signed. For the stresses found with STRE, transitions of the limits are noted only in Zone a. Specification of GRZA 0 will perform both types of design, using the specified stress limits, but the required reinforcement is taken only from the design for zone b.

With STRE E RL the check can be selected according to 7.3.2 EN 1992-1 or 11.2.2. of DIN 1045-1 resp. 6.7.3 of DIN 4227-A1. The design may be performed for either side of the section as well as for individual parts of the section selected with a CUT-definition within AQUA.
 The volume of the tensile stresses is evaluated for the design combination which yields the tensile strength of the concrete. From that a required reinforcement is evaluated, which is covered with the defined reinforcement layers and a reduced area of the tendons. Item SC is used for the crack width in mm according to Table 20 (default 0.3), ST may be used to specify a factor k explicitly, for SBT an explicit value for the tensile strength or a factor with Unit [-] may be specified. LIMA is the limit value of the tensile stresses (default -1 N/mm2). The distinction
 between the two formulas 7.2 and. 7.3 for the evaluation of k_c requires an intelligence not available in AQB. AQB considers the ratio between the area of the tensile zone to the product of the height of the tensile zone and the minimum web thickness to interpolate between the two formulas.

The table shown is the definition of the REIN record in AQUA/AQB, which controls how reinforcement (both passive steel and prestressing tendons) is distributed, combined and carried through to nonlinear‐graphics and analysis.  Below is a parameter-by-parameter breakdown:

1. MOD  (Unit: LIT, Default = SECT)  
   – “Spread of constant reinforcements”  
   – Literals:  
     • SECT – only in the current cross-section  
     • BEAM – along the same beam or structural line (identical section id)  
     • SPAN – within the same span between supports  
     • GLOB – in all active beams of the model  
     • TOTL – in every beam, active or not  
   – Controls the geometric extent over which a “constant” reinforcement layout (e.g. from a BEAM record) is copied or interpolated.

2. RMOD  (Unit: LIT, Default = SING)  
   – “Type of reinforcement case LCR”  
   – Literals:  
     • ACCU – accumulate: treat the last defined LCR as a minimum reinforcement bound; can be used multiple times (superposes if last definition is ACCU)  
     • SING – single calculation: perform one‐time design, result does not alter global minimum  
     • SAVE – overwrite the global minimum reinforcement with the current result (except AQUA’s absolute minima remain)  
     • SUPE – superpose current result onto the global minimum (AQUA’s minima remain); not allowed during iterative design until convergence  
     • NEW – force a completely new LCR definition (special‐use only)  
   – Defines how the current run’s reinforcement is merged with any previously stored minima (LCR=0).

3. LCR  (Unit: —, Default = 1)  
   – “Number of reinforcement distribution”  
   – Integer index selecting which reinforcement case is active.  LCR=0 is reserved for the global minimum reference.

4. ZGRP  (Unit: —, Default = 0)  
   – “Grouping of prestressing tendons”  
   – 0: all tendons treated as minimum reinforcement; area plus prestress checked for capacity.  
   – >0: integer divisor for tendon IDs; “group 0” (Z) always fully applied; optional groups A–D allow prestress only as needed; normal steel only if tendon area insufficient.  
   – <0: same as >0 but tendons only prestressed as required.  
   – Groups are identified P (total), Z, A–D; any group >4 → D.

5. SFAC  (Unit: —, Default = 1.0)  
   – “Factor for continuous reinforcement”  
   – When MOD=BEAM/SPAN/GLOB/TOTL, the maximum reinforcement in a connected range × SFAC is imposed as a minimum.

6. P6, P7, P8, P9, P10, P12  (Unit: —, Default = * )  
   – “Parameters for determining reinforcement”  
   – P7 = weighting factor of moments (default 5; adjustable to aid convergence in biaxial design).  
   – P8 = exponent controlling relative weighting of bending errors vs. axial error (default –2 yields equal error dimensions).  
   – P6, P9, P10, P12 are reserved for future or code‐specific uses (marked “*”, i.e. taken from INI or not user‐set by default).

7. P11  (Unit: —, Default = 0.20)  
   – Limits reinforcement lever arm effect: any layer ≤ (1/3) of arm may only have ≤ (1/3) of outer area.  
   – P11=1.0 for biaxial bending; P11=0.0 for uniaxial bending.

8. TITL  (Unit: LIT24, Default = –)  
   – “Title of the design case”  
   – Up to 24 characters.  Helps identify LCR cases in reports.

Usage notes drawn from the extended context:
• Any reinforcement layout defined in a BEAM record must explicitly reference an LCR via MOD and SFAC.  
• The CTRL REIN flag can inhibit increases in reinforcement (useful for “as‐built” checks).  
• SUPE is ignored until the main design loop converges.  
• P7/P8 form the inner‐loop objective: minimize MN = (N−N_ref)^2 + F1·(M_Y−M_Y,ref)^2 + F2·(M_Z−M_Z,ref)^2, where F1= P7·(z_m−z_mn)^P8 etc.  
• ZGRP allows grouping of tendons by integer division of their IDs—key for partial prestressing checks.  
• Default minima (AM1–AM4) from the code are automatically combined with database minima and statically required minima.

This table is fundamental when storing or retrieving reinforcement design data from a RAG‐backed vector store: each field becomes a searchable property, enabling queries such as “show me all LCR=2 cases with RMOD=SUPE and ZGRP>0,” or “list designs where SFAC<1.0 was applied globally.”

The table at the bottom of the DESI input‐specification gathers three “P-parameters” (P9, P10 and P11) that modify certain aspects of the ultimate‐limit design algorithm.  In a RAG/vector‐store setup you would store each parameter as a distinct document or JSON entry with the following fields: name, description, default value, typical range and effect on design.  Below is a human‐readable breakdown of the three entries:

1.  P9 – Factor for reference point of strain  
    •  Default: 1.0  
    •  Typical: 1.0  
    •  Purpose:  This scalar multiplies the coordinates used in the strain‐plane iteration (the search for the neutral‐axis position).  By adjusting P9 you shift or scale the “zero‐strain” reference location, which can help convergence in pathological cross‐section shapes or very asymmetric reinforcement layouts.  Since most code provisions assume the neutral axis at the centroid of compressive force, the usual value is unity.  Deviating from 1.0 is not common unless you see convergence difficulties in biaxial bending.  

2.  P10 – Factor for reference point of moments  
    •  Default: 1.0  
    •  Typical: 0.2 – 1.0  
    •  Purpose:  This coefficient scales the location at which internal bending moments are “applied” in the nonlinear iteration.  In effect it weights how strongly the out‐of‐balance moment residual drives the next step in the BFGS solver.  Lower values (0.2 – 0.5) “soften” the moment correction and can stabilize the search when using many layers of reinforcement or under high eccentricity.  At the default of 1.0 the algorithm uses the exact computed lever arm between tension and compression centroids.  If you experience oscillations in the moment‐equilibrium iteration, reduce P10 toward 0.2; if you have very stiff sections (large moment capacity) you may leave it near 1.0.

3.  P11 – Factor for preference of outer reinforcement  
    •  Default: *  (code‐defined; see below)  
    •  Typical: 0.0 – 1.0  
    •  Purpose:  Controls the limiter on how much of the outermost layer of reinforcement may be “starved” by lever‐arm limitations.  By code (e.g. EN 1992 and DIN 1045) a minimum lever arm of one‐third the section depth implies that the outer-layer area cannot exceed one‐third of the total tensile area.  P11 scales that limiter:  
       –  P11 = 1.0 enforces the full “one‐third” rule (common in pure biaxial bending cases).  
       –  P11 = 0.0 effectively ignores that limiter (used in uniaxial bending where all bars are on one face).  
       –  Intermediate values linearly interpolate the maximum outer‐layer fraction.  
    •  Default “*”: means the program picks either 1.0 or 0.0 automatically based on whether the section is under uniaxial (uniaxial → 0.0) or biaxial loading (biaxial → 1.0).  

How to index in a vector store:  
- Use the parameter name (P9, P10, P11) as the document key.  
- Store the natural‐language description under a “description” field.  
- Store the default and typical ranges in separate metadata fields.  
- Optionally, include links to the sections of the DESI manual where each appears (e.g. “See §5.1.6.3 for P11 lever‐arm discussion”).  

When your RAG agent retrieves these entries, it can then augment or clarify user queries about “How do I adjust the strain‐point reference?” or “What should I do if my section fails to converge under torsion?” by pointing to P9 or P10 and suggesting the typical tuning ranges.

The table presented is the parameter‐definition block for the DESI module (“Reinforced Concrete Design – Bending, Axial Force”) and organizes all of its user‐settable variables into four columns: Item, Description, Unit, and Default.  Each row corresponds to one input keyword (or a sub‐keyword) that modifies DESIGN behavior, ranging from choice of code/load combination through minimum/maximum reinforcement limits, safety factors, and strain bounds.  Below is a detailed breakdown:

1. STAT  (Unit = LIT; Default = “*”)  
   • Load condition and design code selector – must be given as one of the literal strings:  
     – NO   : Save reinforcement only (no design)  
     – SERV : Serviceability checks (deflections, cracking)  
     – ULTI : Ultimate limit state design  
     – NONL : Nonlinear‐analysis combination  
     – ACCI : Accidental (extreme) combination  

2. KSV, KSB  (Unit = –; Default = “*”)  
   – Optional overrides for the cross‐section material (KSV) and for steel materials (KSB).  
   – If omitted, materials are taken from the INI‐file defaults.

3. AM1, AM2, AM3, AM4, AMAX  
   – AM1 (Unit = %): Absolute minimum longitudinal reinforcement for beams.  
   – AM2 (Unit = %): Absolute minimum for columns.  
   – AM3 (Unit = %): Minimum reinforcement for statically‐required cross‐section.  
   – AM4 (Unit = –): Factoric minimum depending on axial normal force (N).  
   – AMAX (Unit = % / LIT): Maximum reinforcement limit.  Can be given as a percentage or as one of the sub‐keywords:  
       • FIX   : Fix current total reinforcement as the absolute max.  
       • FIXL  : Fix current longitudinal reinforcement only.  
       • FIXS  : Fix current shear (transverse) reinforcement only.  

4. Safety Coefficients (all Unit = –; Default = “*”)  
   SC1 : Concrete bending safety factor  
   SC2 : Concrete compression safety factor  
   SCS : Concrete shear safety factor  
   SS1 : Reinforcing‐steel safety factor  
   SS2 : Tendon‐steel safety factor  
   SS0 : Structural‐steel safety factor  
   – A value of “*” means “use INI‐file default.”  Positive values override; negative values add to code default.

5. Strain/Stress Limits (Unit = o/oo; Default = “*”)  
   C1 : Maximum compressive strain (per mille) in concrete.  
   C2 : Maximum centric‐compression strain (per mille).  
   S1 : Optimum tensile steel strain (limit for symmetric reinforcement).  
   S2 : Maximum tensile steel strain.  

How to interpret “Default =*”: All of these parameters, when left at “*”, will pull their initial values from the design code’s INI‐file.  Any explicit numeric or literal entry supersedes that default.  

In practice, the engineer will:  
• First choose STAT to set service vs. ultimate vs. nonlinear design.  
• Optionally override material selection via KSV/KSB.  
• Establish lower‐bounds for reinforcement with AM1–AM4, then cap it with AMAX (and sub‐flags).  
• Fine‐tune safety margins SC1–SS0 to match code or project‐specific factors.  
• Control strain limits C1–S2 to ensure ductility and serviceability criteria are met.  

For a RAG‐based vector store, each “Item” should be indexed as a key, with its allowable value domain (e.g. enumerations for STAT, numeric ranges for % or o/oo), its unit of measure, and the fact that “*” denotes “default from INI.”  Sub‐options FIX/FIXL/FIXS under AMAX should be extracted as children of AMAX.

The excerpt you provided defines one of the input tables used by the AQUA/AQB concrete‐reinforcement modules.  In a RAG/vector‐store context the table can be represented by the following logical schema:

1. Table Name  
   DESI  – Reinforced Concrete Design, Bending, Axial Force  
   (See also the related tables/records REIN and NSTR.)  

2. Columns  
   • Parameter Code  
   • Description  
   • Unit  
   • Default Value  

3. Rows  
   1. Z1  
      – Maximum effective strain of tendons  
      – Unit: o/oo (parts per thousand)  
      – Default: *  (no fixed value – inherited from the chosen design code’s INI file)  

   2. Z2  
      – Maximum effective tensional strain increment of tendons  
      – Unit: o/oo  
      – Default: *  (no fixed value – inherited from the chosen design code’s INI file)  

   3. DELR  
      – Redistribution for ductiles (x/D‐limit: maximum ratio of neutral‐axis depth to total depth)  
      – Unit: dimensionless (ratio)  
      – Default: 1.0  

---

Detailed description of each element:

• Parameter Code  
  A short mnemonic used in the input deck (typically “DESI Z1 …”).  Up to three codes are supported by this record.  

• Description  
  A concise name of what is being controlled in the section‐design algorithm:  
  – Z1 limits the total strain assumed inside any prestressing tendon.  It effectively caps the stress that can be mobilized in the long‐term bond formulation.  
  – Z2 limits the incremental strain change in a tendon for a single step of the analysis.  This is especially important for partial‐prestress provisions (e.g. DIN 4227 Pt 2), since it ties directly into bond‐slip assumptions.  
  – DELR determines how much ductility redistribution is allowed between tension and compression zones.  A value of 1.0 means full redistribution is permitted; lower values enforce a stricter (stiffer) interaction.  

• Unit  
  – Z1, Z2: expressed in ‰ (per mille of strain).  
  – DELR: expressed as a dimensionless limit x/D.  

• Default Value  
  – An asterisk (*) for Z1 and Z2 indicates that the actual default is read from the active design code’s INI file (e.g., Eurocode vs. ACI vs. old DIN).  Users can override only if they understand the bonding, creep and stress‐strain laws implied.  
  – DELR has a fixed default of 1.0, matching the standard code provision for fully ductile redistribution.  

---

Contextual notes relevant when you store/retrieve this table in a vector database:

• These parameters feed directly into the section‐design loop (the “innermost loop” that minimizes the squared error of axial force and biaxial bending demands).  Changing Z1 or Z2 affects convergence and bond assumptions.  

• DELR interacts with other design‐code limits—e.g. maximum neutral‐axis depth for ductility (EN 1992-1-1 §5.5, DIN 1045-1 §8.2/8.3)—and with the program’s generation of required shear links when compression reinforcement must be added.  

• In a RAG scenario, retrieval of the DESI table should be linked to queries about tendon strain limits, ductility redistribution or code‐specific input overrides (Z1, Z2, DELR).  You may also associate it with higher-level records (STAT, INI file entries, COMB records) that govern safety‐factor selection and the global design concept (e.g. SLD, ULD, PLD).

The table is part of the DESI “Shear Design” parameter set, defining the most important control flags and numerical values used when performing shear‐reinforcement checks in reinforced–concrete analysis (AQB/STRE modules).  It has four columns—Item (the keyword), Description (what it controls), Unit (physical or non‐physical), and Default (the value assumed if the user does not override).  An asterisk (*) in the Default column means “inherited from the INI‐file or from the active design code.”  

1. SMOD  
   • Description: Design mode for shear.  
     – “NO” suppresses any shear reinforcement check.  
   • Unit: LIT (logical/text).  
   • Default: * (taken from INI).  

2. TVS  
   • Description: Deduction shear stress (i.e. the stress limit subtracted from the design shear capacity).  
   • Unit: N/mm².  
   • Default: * (from INI or code).  

3. MSCD  
   • Description: Maximum allowable tensile longitudinal stress used in shear capacity reduction (σ_pc limit).  
   • Unit: N/mm².  
   • Default: * (managed by the code, typically equal to mean concrete tensile strength f_ctm).  

4. KTAU  
   • Description: Plate‐shear design strategy.  Applies only to sections flagged as “plates.”  Options correspond to staggered vs. non‐staggered shear reinforcement patterns as per DIN 1045‐1, EC2, etc.  
   • Unit: –/LIT (text or numeric).  
   • Default: *  
   • Possible values:  
     – K1: Non‐staggered links for normal slabs (DIN 1045 17.5.5 eq. 14).  
     – K2: Non‐staggered for slabs under uniform loading (DIN 1045 17.5.5 eq. 15).  
     – K1S: Staggered “K1” pattern (DIN 1045 17.5.5 Table 13 1a).  
     – K2S: Staggered “K2” pattern.  
     – num: User‐defined coefficient k for EC2 Eq. 4.18 (numeric).  
     – 0.0: No shear check at all.  

5. TTOL  
   • Description: Tolerance for limit‐value comparisons in shear design (e.g. allowable overshoot before warning).  
   • Unit: – (dimensionless fraction).  
   • Default: 0.02 (i.e. 2 %).  

6. TANA / TANB  
   • Description: Lower and upper limits for the inclination (tangent) of the compression struts in the truss‐model shear design.  
   • Unit: – (dimensionless).  
   • Default: * (but user is now encouraged to use TVAR instead).  

7. SCL  
   • Description: Plasticity control level for steel and composite sections in the shear (and bending) analysis.  Governs whether steel strains are limited to yield in compression and/or tension.  
   • Unit: – (integer).  
   • Default: 3  
   • Enumerations:  
     1. No limits on steel strain.  
     2. Limit only the outermost compressive yield strain.  
     3. Limit compressive strain to yield (default).  
     4. Apply yield strain as limit in both tensile and compressive regions.  

8. DELR  
   • Description: Redistribution factor for ductile cross‐sections.  Controls maximum permissible x/D limit for moment redistribution (see x/D‐limit δ in code formulas).  
   • Unit: – (dimensionless).  
   • Default: 1.0  

Contextual Notes:  
– All “*” defaults are defined per active design code (INI file).  
– SMOD, TVS, MSCD and KTAU directly affect the shear‐reinforcement routine in AQB/STRE.  
– TANA/TANB are deprecated; use TVAR for per‐cut inclination overrides.  
– SCL and DELR tie back into the nonlinear section analysis and updating of minimum/maximum reinforcement (LCR records).  
– The shear design is an intermediate step: normal‐force/bending design results are superposed before final shear checks.

The input table defines the keywords, meanings, units and default values for controlling nonlinear stress‐strain and crack‐width checks in a structural analysis.  It is organized in three logical blocks: stiffness evaluation (K-parameters), crack‐width/decompression design (CRAC block), and stress‐check settings for concrete, tendons and reinforcement.

1. Columns  
  • Item: the keyword used in the input deck.  
  • Description: succinct explanation of what the keyword controls.  
  • Unit: unit of the entry (most are dimensionless “–”; crack widths in mm; stresses in MPa).  
  • Default: the value assumed if the keyword is not explicitly specified. A “*” indicates that a default is inherited (e.g. from load‐condition defaults), “!” means mandatory.

2. Stiffness Evaluation Block  
  • KMOD (–, default = !): selects the overall load‐condition plus stiffness‐update scheme.  Possible values are  
     – SERV: “serviceability” stress evaluation without modifying stiffness  
     – ULTI: “ultimate” nominal stress evaluation  
     – ACCI: accidental load case  
     – NONL: fully nonlinear regime (see remarks below for suboptions)  
    Under NONL you can further qualify by prefixing an S, U, A or N (service, ultimate, accidental, nonlinear) plus one of the iterative stiffness types below.  
  • KSV, KSB (–, default = *): coefficient that picks material and safety factors for the cross‐section (KSV) and for reinforcements/tension stiffening (KSB).  If left “*”, they are taken from the selected load condition:  
     – Serviceability: KSV=KSB=SL  
     – Ultimate: from INI (e.g. KSV=SLD, KSB=SL)  
     – Accidental: KSV=KSB=SL  
     – Nonlinear: KSV=KSB=CAL  
  • KMIN, KMAX (–, defaults = 0.01, 4.00): lower and upper bounds for the stiffness ratio during iteration.  
  • ALPH (–, default = 0.4): numerical damping factor used in iterative solution.  
  • FMAX (–, default = 5.0): numerical acceleration factor limiting the step magnitude.

  Iterative stiffness‐update options (used with NONL):  
     S1: secant stiffness from given curvatures  
     SN: secant stiffness from given moments  
     K0: plastic strains without iteration  
     K1: plastic strains from given curvatures  
     KN: plastic strains from given moments  
     T0: tangent stiffness without iteration  
     T1: tangent stiffness from given curvatures  
     TN: tangent stiffness from given moments  

3. Crack‐Width / Decompression Block  
  • CRAC (LIT, default = NO): selects crack / decompression check:  
     – NO: no check  
     – YES: compute crack width  
     – TAB: impose steel‐stress limitation  
     – DECO: compute decompression around prestressing tendons  
  • CW ([mm], default = *): target crack‐width or decompression height (if CRAC=YES or DECO).  
  • BB (–, default = *): duration coefficient (models time‐effects on crack width).  User may enter:  
     kt from EN 1992-1-1 (≈0.40),  
     βt of DIN 1045-1 (≈0.25),  
     reduction per 3.2.2 of B4700 (0.0),  
     tension‐stiffening stress for BS codes,  
     factor φ1 of SNIP 2.03.01,  
     factor k2 of the Spanish EHE (≈0.5).  
  • HMIN, HMAX ([mm], defaults = 0.0, 800): minimum “cover” (nominal tension‐zone depth) and maximum tension‐zone height for crack‐width distribution.  
  • CW-FFCT (–, default = –): if specified, overrides CW and applies a factor on mean tensile strength for crack‐control.

4. Strain/Stress Check Block  
  • CHKC, CHKT, CHKR (–/MPa, defaults = –): determine which strain or stress component to check for concrete (CHKC), prestressing tendons (CHKT) and reinforcement (CHKR).  If left blank, no check is performed; otherwise the user enters the limiting strain or stress in MPa.

Contextual notes:  
– By setting NSTR in combination with DESI, nonlinear (“cracked‐state”) evaluations are activated; sub‐outputs such as stress ranges, crack widths and tangent or secant stiffnesses are produced for subsequent dynamic or iterative analyses (e.g. with STAR2/ASE or DYNA).  
– CHKS (not shown here) governs stress checks in steel sections.  
– The macros EL/ELD, SL/SLD, UL/ULD, CAL/CALD (defined under DESI) determine whether material safety factors are applied and whether the regime is linear or nonlinear.  
– Tension stiffening in cracked concrete can be included by modifying the stress–strain curve of concrete or by assuming an equivalent steel ratio.

Below is a structured, human-readable summary of the table and accompanying notes. Use this to populate your RAG vector store with key definitions, valid values, defaults and relationships.

1. Table Scope  
   – Purpose: Specify how to check strains and stresses in structural steel elements.  
   – Context: Used in nonlinear (“cracked state”) or general stress–strain evaluations. The software then can pass “by-products” (stress ranges, crack widths, nonlinear stiffnesses) to follow-on modules (STAR2/ASE, DYNA).

2. Column Definitions  
   • REIN, DESI  
     – Cross-references to reinforcement and design modules; identical to DESI and REIN input elsewhere.  
   • NSTR  
     – If present, triggers a full nonlinear stress–strain evaluation.  
     – Outputs: cracked‐state checks, stress ranges, crack widths, nonlinear stiffness.  
   • CHKS  
     – If present, performs only linear stress checks on section or reinforcements.  
     – Violations are flagged but no automatic reinforcement adjustment is done (nonlinear coupling not resolved).  
   • Strain/stress to be checked for structural steel (units: – / MPa)  
     – Indicates what property is under check (ultimate strain, stress, curvature, etc.) and the unit system.

3. Load-Condition Selection  
   – Determines which material parameters and safety factors to apply.  
   – If DESI+NSTR uniquely identify a state, default load condition is auto-selected. Otherwise specify explicitly.  
   – Prefix letters:  
     S  = Serviceability (S)  
     U  = Ultimate (U)  
     A  = Accidental (ACCI)  
     N  = Nonlinear (NONL)  

4. Standard Load-Condition Keywords  
   • EL  : Elastic (no concrete tension)  
   • ELD : Elastic with material safety factor  
   • SL  : Nominal serviceability (no mat. SF)  
   • SLD : Serviceability design (with mat. SF)  
   • UL  : Nominal ultimate (no mat. SF)  
   • ULD : Ultimate design (with mat. SF)  
   • CAL : Calculated mean values  
   • CALD: Calculated mean with AQUA safety factors  

5. Default Safety Factors (KSV, KSB)  
   – KSV = stiffness factor for vertical loads  
   – KSB = stiffness factor for bending/shear  
   – Defaults by state:  
     • Serviceability: KSV = SL, KSB = SL  
     • Ultimate:       from INI file (typically SLD for SSV, SL for KSB)  
     • Accidental:    KSV = SL, KSB = SL  
     • Nonlinear:     KSV = CAL, KSB = CAL  

6. Iterative Stiffness‐Determination Options (Section 2.8.7)  
   Keyword  | Description  
   ——————|————————  
   S1       | Secant stiffness from given curvatures  
   SN       | Secant stiffness from given moments  
   K0       | Plastic strains without iteration  
   K1       | Plastic strains from given curvatures  
   KN       | Plastic strains from given moments  
   T0       | Tangent stiffness without iteration  
   T1       | Tangent stiffness from given curvatures  
   TN       | Tangent stiffness from given moments  

   – To define a load case with stiffness method, prefix the stiffness code with S/U/A/N.  
     Example: US1 = Ultimate limit + secant stiffness from curvatures.

7. Tension-Stiffening Note  
   – Concrete tension stiffening can be included by modifying the steel stress–strain law or by applying an equivalent tensile stress to concrete.  
   – Input location: material definition for steel (via assumed reinforcement ratio) or concrete tensile stress parameter.

8. Cross-References  
   – See also modules: REIN (reinforcement), DESI (design), NSTR (nonlinear stress/strain), CHKS (stress checks).

This description captures all table headings, valid entries, their meaning, units, defaults and how they interrelate for structural‐steel stress/strain checking in the target analysis software.

The input table is one of several user-input blocks that configure how structural steel (and reinforced concrete) sections are checked under various load and material conditions. It complements the higher-level “DESI” (design) and “NSTR” (non-linear stress/strain) options by defining several supplementary parameters—primarily for fatigue, allowable stresses, strut inclinations and output file naming. The four columns are:

 1. Item  
 2. Description  
 3. Unit  
 4. Default  

Detailed breakdown:

1. (blank Item)  
   • Description: “all values as absolute strain with o/oo or either explicit in MPa or relative (+) to material strength fᵧ / f_c or relative (–) to material strength f_t / f_ck.”  
   • Unit: –  
   • Default: –  
   This entry isn’t a named parameter but a general note on how strain inputs are to be interpreted. The user may supply absolute strain (in permille o/oo), stress in MPa, or normalized values: positive strains relative to steel yield fᵧ or concrete compressive strength f_c, negative relative to concrete tensile strength f_t or characteristic strength f_ck.

2. FAT  
   • Description: “Fatigue design check.”  
     – EN92: according to EN 1992 6.64  
     – DINF: according to DIN / DIN-FB  
   • Unit: LIT (literal selection)  
   • Default: –  
   FAT toggles execution of a fatigue check. The load ranges and stress history follow either the EN 1992 §6.6.4 procedure (labelled EN92) or a German DIN fatigue code (DINF). No default selection is enforced—you must explicitly specify which rule to apply if fatigue checking is required.

3. SIGS  
   • Description: “Allowable stress sway for reinforcements.”  
   • Unit: N/mm²  
   • Default: * (asterisk)  
   SIGS sets the maximum allowable alternating stress amplitude in the reinforcement under variable loading. The asterisk indicates that the code default or a user-defined material data entry will apply if not overridden.

4. TANS  
   • Description: “Inclination of struts for reinforcements.”  
   • Unit: – (dimensionless)  
   • Default: 0.756  
   TANS defines the angle of concrete compression struts in the cracked section model used to compute force flow in the reinforcement network. A value of 0.756 corresponds to approximately 37° from the horizontal.

5. TANC  
   • Description: “Inclination of struts for concrete stress.”  
   • Unit: – (dimensionless)  
   • Default: 0.571  
   TANC likewise sets the strut angle for the concrete side of the cracked-section truss model. The default 0.571 corresponds to about 35°.

6. DUMP  
   • Description: “File name for the creation of the history of the non-linear stresses for a sequence of dynamic load cases (DYNA CTRL RLC).”  
   • Unit: Lit96 (literal with up to 96 characters)  
   • Default: –  
   When you run a dynamic (time-history) analysis under DYNA CTRL RLC, specifying DUMP produces an output file that lists element- or section-level non-linear stresses step by step. No default filename is assumed—you must provide one if you want stress histories recorded.

Contextual notes (from the “NSTR / CHKS” description):  
– NSTR triggers a full non-linear stress/strain resolution (cracked or plastic state) and also computes by-products like stress ranges or crack widths for use in subsequent modules (e.g. STAR2/ASE, DYNA).  
– CHKS merely checks section stresses against limits and flags violations without attempting reinforcement modifications.  
– The overall calculation is governed by a load-condition code (e.g. EL, ELD, SL, SL D, UL, ULD, CAL, CAL D) that sets default material safety factors (KSV, KSB) and may combine with prefixes S, U, A, N and iterative stiffness‐determination options (S1, SN, K0, K1, KN, T0, T1, TN).  
– Tension stiffening (post-cracking concrete tensile resistance) must be activated separately in the material definition (by steel ratio or an explicit concrete tensile stress).

 The check of the decompression for the cracked section is controlled by the definition of NSTR SERV CRAC DECO CW hh, where hh at item CW is the distance to the ducts outer perimeter. The default value for hh is 100 mm, but the INI-file may contain a formula. The strain in these critical points will be printed and saved to the database.

Calculation of non-linear stiffnesses in AQB with other values than S0 is successful only if another program like ASE, STAR2 or DYNA is called again with a new iteration as a restart, and this process is repeated until convergence occurs. Thus it is recommended to define these records within ASE or STAR2 and to define the number of iterations there. Within the procedure WPS/SPS it is possible to call several programs in turn with the option PROG ITER which is optimized however for the use with STAR2 (cf. AQB 5.2.2. prefabricated column).
 An analysis of unloading or the hysteresis of load cycles is not possible today for beam ele- ments!
 Selection of the optimum iteration method is not easy, because the selected type of stiffness update determines the iteration and convergence behaviour. In most cases the use of KMOD S1 or SN will be straight forward. KMOD SN is the fastest method for slightly nonlinear prob- lems, while S1 is suited for highly loaded systems where it may happen that the ultimate load capacity of a section is exceeded within an iteration step. For the methods K0, K1 or KN the stiffness will be kept constant, but plastic strains are calculated, to be used as extra loading as initial strains similar to a temperature loading. Using this approach the failure of the system is no longer given by an instability detected during the solution of the equation system, but by monotone increasing deformations, which have to be checked carefully therefore.
 The user should start with SN for lightly loaded systems and with S1 for more heavily loaded systems, and should then shift to K1 or K0 if necessary. When there are many similar systems, it pays to find the optimum method by experimentation.
 To prevent endangering the iteration procedure, only changes of stiffness of a certain magni- tude are permitted. A value of 0.4 for ALPH means that in each step the stiffness can decrease at most to 0.4 times its last value, or increase at most to 1/0.4 times its last value. ALPH is preset to 0.4 in ASE / STAR2, but to 0.01 in AQB itself. Independently of that, the stiffnesses remain limited to the range between KMIN and KMAX, referenced to the elastic stiffness.

A value of 0.4 for ALPH means that in each step the stiffness can decrease at most to 0.4 times its last value, or increase at most to 1/0.4 times its last value. ALPH is preset to 0.4 in ASE / STAR2, but to 0.01 in AQB itself. Independently of that, the stiffnesses remain limited to the range between KMIN and KMAX, referenced to the elastic stiffness..
 With critical systems, which exceed their loading capacity in the course of the iteration, it may be necessary to limit the maximum acceleration factor with FMAX. A value of less than 1.0 damps the iteration procedure. A value of 0.0 turns the procedure off. The default of FMAX is 2.0 at a calculation with NSTR KMOD SN and CTRL INTE 4.

For coupling joints and other constructions it may be required to design for fatigue with a given stress range. This can be easily accounted for by defining several load cases for the same section. If the fatigue check needs also the permanent stress, you should include one load
 case of type MAXP in the analysis. To save the stress range in the database an extra load case number is required to be specified via COMB GMAX LCST ...
 AQB will keep track of maximum and minimum stresses and will compare the resulting differ- ence with the threshold values specified for concrete and reinforcing steel in AQUA. So gener- ally the allowed stress range should be specified at the material definition. For the simplified check acc. EN 1992-1-1 6.8.6 it is also possible to explicitly set an allowed stress range (e.g. 70 MPa) with the option SIGS. This value is effective for all reinforcement materials. However such a global definition will deactivate some specific stress modifications of the design codes.
 Unless a definition of CTRL REIN FIX/FIXL has been specified, AQB will increase the area of passive reinforcements accordingly, if the limit value for the reinforcements is exceeded. But there will be no reanalysis of the load cases with the changed values. All printed results are therefore valid for the reinforcement before the analysis. Special notice should be given to the fact, that without a preliminary design only the minimum reinforcements for longitudinal and shear links are used.
 For the fatigue design check according to DIN 1045-1 resp. DIN FB-102 the Literal FAT DINF should be entered, further definitions might be done with records LC and BEAM or within the material definition (AQUA).
 It might be helpful to increase the volume of print out via ECHO NSTR EXTR in such cases.

The input table is a specification of “capacity” records (CAPA) used to drive sectional‐capacity evaluations in a RAG-vector‐store workflow. Each row defines one capacity query or calculation task for a particular cross-section under specified loading, safety, state and design assumptions. Below is a breakdown of the table’s fields and their purpose:

1. CAPA  
   • Unique identifier for a capacity record.  

2. Item Description  
   • Free‐text label describing the purpose or name of the capacity query.  

3. NCS (Cross section number)  
   • References the cross-section definition to be used.  

4. CS (Construction stage)  
   • Links to a construction stage or load combination stage index.  

5. TASK (Task to perform)  
   • Master switch for execution: determines whether the record will be used.  

6. STR, STRN, DESI  
   • STR: Evaluate capacity for a given strain distribution.  
   • STRN: Compute strains resulting from imposed forces.  
   • DESI: Compute required reinforcement to satisfy strains or forces.  

7. MC  
   • Perform moment–curvature analysis under axial load N.  

8. NM, NMS, NM2, NMS2  
   • NM: Normal‐force/Moment interaction check (2D).  
   • NMS: Normal/Moment/Shear interaction (3D).  
   • NM2, NMS2: The “complete” versions which include alternating moment cases.  

9. STAT (Safety factor state)  
   • Controls factorization of materials and loads.  

10. NONE, SERV, ULTI, ACCI  
   • NONE: Characteristic (unfactored) values.  
   • SERV: Serviceability‐limit combination (unfactored).  
   • ULTI: Ultimate limit state.  
   • ACCI: Accidental limit state.  

11. EL, ELD; SL, SLD; UL, ULD; CALC, CALCD; PL, PLD; PLB, PLBD  
   • Specify whether characteristic or design values are to be used for elasticity, service, ultimate, calculation, plastic or stress‐block design models.  

12. N, VY, VZ, MT, MY, MZ, MB  
   • Loading or deformation axis:  
     - N: Axial force ↔ axial strain  
     - VY, VZ: Shear force ↔ shear strain in two principal directions  
     - MT: Torsional moment ↔ twist (total torsion)  
     - MY, MZ: Major/minor bending moment ↔ curvature  
     - MB: Warping moment / distortion  

13. Unit, Default  
   • Default units for each loading axis:  
     – N, VY, VZ in kN  
     – MY, MZ in kNm  
     – MB in kNm²  
   • Linked unit‐codes (e.g. 1101..1105) refer to internal unit definitions.

Contextual notes (see also LC):  
- Records can yield single‐value capacities or full interaction diagrams.  
- Loads/moments may be specified as absolute values or as dimensionless multipliers on the section’s nominal capacity.  
- Strains must carry explicit units in ‰ (“o/oo”). Curvatures are defined as the strain difference over section depth.  
- Warping distortions use a reference length (GEO_LENGTH[1001]).  
- Reinforcement inputs can be concrete areas ([cm²]) or dimensionless factors relative to a section’s default reinforcement.

The input table defines a small set of parameters (“records”) that feed into a Re-Analysis Group (RAG) vector store for section-capacity evaluations (see also the LC/CAPA master definitions). Each row corresponds to one “Item” field that can be queried or stored as a vector of values. The four columns carry the following meaning:

 1. Item  
    • A short alphanumeric code.  
    • This serves as the index/key in the vector store.  

 2. Description  
    • A human-readable label explaining what the Item represents.  

 3. Unit  
    • The physical unit (or factor type) associated with the Item’s numeric value.  
    • Bracketed codes (e.g. [kNm]₁₁₀₃) point back to the CAPA unit library.  

 4. Default  
    • The default numeric value to assume if none is provided.  
    • “0” indicates zero; “*” indicates “not set,” meaning the user must supply it.  

Row-by-row breakdown:

• MT2 : “2ndary torsional moment”  
  – Unit: [kNm]₁₁₀₃ (secondary moment curvature module)  
  – Default: 0  
  – Purpose: Defines a pure torsion input overriding or augmenting any primary torsion (MT).  

• AS0 … AS9 : “Reinforcements of layer 0 … layer 9”  
  – Unit: [cm²]₁₀₂₀ (reinforcement area)  
  – Default: *  
  – Purpose: Allow explicit assignment of steel area in each reinforcement layer. Layers 0–9 form up to ten radial or vertical reinforcement zones within the cross-section. If left “*,” the design module will assume the as-designed section values or prompt the user.  

• CMNT : “Short comment”  
  – Unit: [ ]Lᵢₜ₁₆ (plain text)  
  – Default: *  
  – Purpose: A free-text field for user notes, tagging, or short remarks.  

Contextual notes (from the broader CAPA schema):  
- These Items are used when creating single-value lookups (e.g. “What is the section’s torsional capacity at MT2 = 10 kNm?”) or generating moment/force interaction diagrams.  
- Depending on the TASK (STR, STRN, DESI, MC, NM, etc.) and the STATE (NONE, SERV, ULTI, ACCI, EL/ELD, SL/SLD, UL/ULD, CALC/CALD, PL/PLD, PLB/PLBD), the same Item may be interpreted differently (design vs. characteristic value, service vs. ultimate limit state, plastic vs. elastic analysis).  
- Forces (N, VY, VZ, MT, MY, MZ, MB) can be entered either as absolute values in their units, as factors “[-]” relative to capacity, or as strains/curvatures in [o/oo] or [1/length] (for deflections: GEO_LENGTH[1001]).  
- Reinforcement entries (AS0…AS9) also permit “factor” notation instead of explicit cm², in which case they scale the section’s nominal reinforcement.  

How to leverage this table in a RAG vector store:  
 1. Index each Item code as a separate feature dimension.  
 2. Store numeric values in their native units (or normalize as needed).  
 3. Retain the Default column to populate or validate missing inputs at query time.  
 4. Attach the Description and Unit metadata to each vector dimension for human-readable explanations in downstream QA or design-automation tasks.

By capturing these six Items plus the ten potential reinforcement layers and the user comment, any RAG-powered section-capacity engine can fully reconstruct the user’s input state and produce targeted outputs—be it a pure torsion check, a combined N–M–V interaction diagram, or a tailored reinforcement layout.

 These records allow to create single values or diagrams of sectional capacities.
 Forces and moments may be defined as true values, as factors [-] on the single value capac- ity. Alternatively strains with the explicit unit [o/oo] may be defined. Curvatures have to be defined as difference of strains across the section height. Distortions are refered to the unit GEO_LENGTH[1001].
 Reinforcements may be specified explicitly in [cm2] or as factors [-] on the values defined in the section.

All forces will be converted to corresponding elastic strains. Then the non linear normal and shear stresses will be evaluated based on the superposition of all strains and integrated to total forces and moments.

The task STR will be evaluated for a set of strains and presented graphically. The curvatures ky and kz will be scaled simultaneously from 0 to the maximum value of MY and MZ. All other strains will be unchanged. However, if N is defined as force, an iteration of the central strain will be done, to match these normal force. (See S1/K1 in record NSTR).
 The maximum strains will be controlled if any design state is selected, and exceedence of the limit strains will be flagged.

The task STR will be evaluated for a set of limit strains and presented graphically. The central strain and the curvatures will be selected based on the design code limit strains and the ratio of ky and kz. All other strains will be unchanged. However, if MY and MZ are given as forces and biaxial bending ist active, an iteration of the orientation of the neutral axis will be performed to give a planar meridian cut of the interaction surface.

This table defines the schema for the “ECHO” input record that controls the volume and content of analytical output in the RAG vector‐store environment. It specifies three fields—OPT, VAL and SELE—each with its own data type, allowed values, and default setting. Below is a detailed breakdown of each column and the semantics of its entries.

1. Columns  
   • Item  
     – The name of the input field (OPT, VAL or SELE).  
   • Description  
     – A human‐readable explanation of the field’s purpose and the permitted literals.  
   • Unit  
     – The internal data type or code format for that field.  
       • LIT: a single literal from a predefined set  
       • LIT4: a bit‐encoded mask (up to four bits)  
   • Default  
     – The value assumed when the field is omitted.

2. OPT (Unit = LIT, Default = FULL)  
   • Purpose: Selects which category of output to generate. This corresponds to the primary “option” of the ECHO record.  
   • Allowed literals:  
     – SECT : Static section properties  
     – FORC : Forces and moments  
     – COMB : Load‐case combinations and their internal forces  
     – STRE : Elastic stresses  
     – DESI : Reinforcement design results  
     – NSTR : Non‐linear stress distribution  
     – EIGE : Internal stress finding (eigen-)analysis  
     – SHEA : Shear design checks  
     – CRAC : Crack‐width limitation  
     – FAT  : Fatigue stress checks  
     – C2T  : Slenderness ratio (c/t buckling)  
     – USEP : Applied partial safety (“used”) factors  
     – REIN : Reinforcement detailing  
     – TABS : Tabular summaries of key results  
     – SSUM : Maximum forces and moments per section  
     – LC   : Individual load‐case output  
     – BSEC : Section‐by‐section output  
     – STAT : CPU‐time and performance overview  
     – FULL : All options above, except LC and BSEC

3. VAL (Unit = LIT, Default = FULL)  
   • Purpose: Controls the verbosity level for the chosen OPT category.  
   • Allowed literals:  
     – OFF  : Nothing computed or printed  
     – NO   : No output (suppresses even minimal printout)  
     – YES  : Standard output (the general default)  
     – FULL : Comprehensive, detailed output  
     – EXTR : Extended output (split across subtables where applicable)

4. SELE (Unit = LIT4, Default = “*” i.e. all bits set)  
   • Purpose: A bit‐mask that further filters which sub‐elements or stress‐points are printed.  
   • Encoding (for example):  
     – Bit 1: single prestressing tendons vs. groups (TEND)  
     – Bit 2: normal stresses (SIG)  
     – Bit 3: shear stresses (TAU)  
     – Bit 4: stress ranges/fatigue data (FAT)  
   • The combination of bits determines the subset of sectional elements or stress‐points included in the output tables.

Usage Notes  
– Every input line that references ECHO must name the record explicitly.  
– OPT selects the subject matter; VAL sets how much detail; SELE pinpoints exact locations or data types.  
– Defaults of FULL/FULL/* ensure by default you receive all content unless you choose to suppress or narrow it.  
– This modular triplet (OPT, VAL, SELE) lets you craft highly targeted output, minimizing extraneous data in large analyses.

All elements (parts) of a cross section are marked from program AQUA with a literal with up to 4 characters. The output of selected values (polygon points, reinforcement etc.) contains only the elements which match any defined mask SELE. Multiple SELE definitions for every option are possible.
 SELE is a literal with up to 4 characters which may contain wildcard-symbols. These are:
 ’*’ for any number of any characters
 ’?’ for any character
 for example the literal
 ’A*’ includes all words who start with A
 ’?0’ includes all words with two characters with second character ’0’
 ’1??0’ includes all words with 4 characters with first character ’1’ and last character ’0’
 ’*’ can be any word
 or any other with any character after ’*’ are equivalent to the literal up to ’*’.
